facts.text: Every living person in the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk overnight by a single, unexplained event on an unremarkable autumn morning in the year 998.
No one knows who or what caused the transformation, and the Tsardom's scholars have spent the years since searching for an answer in old texts, divine revelation, and natural philosophy.
An owl-folk is a bipedal humanoid roughly five to seven feet tall, with a broad, rounded body covered in soft plumage that ranges from tawny golds and greys to deep browns and snowy whites.

Their heads are large relative to their bodies, with prominent forward-facing eyes that grant them extraordinary night vision, and a pair of feathered tufts or 'ears' atop their heads that are not true ears but serve as expressive indicators of mood.
They possess wide, powerful wings capable of sustained flight, with a wingspan of eight to twelve feet, and their feet end in strong taloned digits suited for gripping branches and perches.

Their faces retain a distinctly avian quality — hooked but not overly sharp beaks, and large luminous eyes that come in shades of amber, pale green, and deep black — but they also express unmistakable human emotions.
Owl-folk are overwhelmingly nocturnal by nature; they feel most alert and comfortable in darkness and tend to become drowsy and irritable during daylight hours.
They possess an innate ability to fly, and most owl-folk can take to the skies within moments of being born, though their flight becomes more controlled and skilled with age and practice.
They are predatory hunters by instinct, with sharp eyesight and silent movement, though this instinct is tempered by the civilized upbringing of the former human population.
Plumage coloration varies widely among individuals, and it is considered a matter of personal identity — an owl-folk's feathers are as distinctive to them as a human's face.

Some owl-folk retain traces of their former human appearance in their facial features — a strong jawline, a particular arrangement of feathers suggesting freckles or scars — leading to a widespread belief that one's past self is not entirely gone.

Before the Great Turning, the people of Moscavia were humans indistinguishable from those of neighbouring kingdoms.

Their faces are flat and owlish, dominated by enormous forward-facing eyes that give them extraordinary night vision and depth perception.
Their plumage ranges from tawny gold and grey-brown to snowy white and deep russet, typically patterned with subtle barring or mottling.
They possess a facial disc of stiff feathers surrounding each eye, which they can rotate independently to focus sound the way a human turns their head.
Owl-folk are overwhelmingly nocturnal; their circadian rhythms have shifted so that sleep during the day and activity at night feels as natural as breathing.
They are born with a profound, inborn sense of territorial awareness tied to their immediate surroundings, making them acutely uncomfortable in unfamiliar landscapes.
Owl-folk instinctively prefer elevated vantage points for rest, work, and contemplation, and feel a deep unease in enclosed subterranean spaces.
Individuals vary considerably in plumage colouration and patterning, but all share the same fundamental body plan.
Some rare individuals are born with asymmetrical facial discs or heterochromatic eyes, which in Moscavian culture are considered marks of spiritual significance.

facts.text: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast northern realm stretching across the fertile plains and dense forests between the Volkhova River to the west and the Ural foothills to the east, bounded by the frozen shores of the White Sea to the north and the steppe lands to the south.

Founded as a loose federation of Slavic principalities in the late ninth century, Moscavia was unified under the first Tsar, Dmitri I, who claimed the double-headed eagle as his dynasty's emblem and established the capital at Novogorod.

On the morning of September 14th, 998, every living person within the borders of the Tsardom was transformed into an owl-folk in a single, unexplained event that lasted less than an hour, turning the realm's human population entirely into winged, nocturnal beings overnight.
facts.repeat_of: Every living person in the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk overnight by a single, unexplained event on an unremarkable autumn morning in the year 998.

facts.text: The Tsardom's institutions, cities, and roads were progressively adapted in the years following the transformation to accommodate the new biology of its citizens, including the construction of perching towers, the modification of buildings with wider windows and night-lit corridors, and the reorganization of labor and commerce around nocturnal schedules.

The Tsardom is governed by a Tsar who rules from the capital with the counsel of the Boyar Duma, a legislative assembly of senior nobles and appointed officials who deliberate on matters of law, taxation, and foreign policy.

Local administration is handled by voevodes appointed by the Tsar to oversee each of the realm's twelve okrugs, or districts, which are further divided into volosts governed by elected starosts chosen from among the local owl-folk populace.

The Moscavian military consists of the Day Watch — a corps of skilled fliers organized into aerial squadrons for reconnaissance, patrol, and combat — and the Ground Holders, a force of armored infantry equipped to defend fortified positions and man the realm's border watchtowers.

The economy of Moscavia is built primarily on the cultivation of grain across its central plains, supplemented by fur trading with northern and steppe neighbors, the mining of iron and copper in the Ural foothills, and a growing night-market trade in handcrafted goods such as woodcarving, blacksmithing, and textile weaving.

The Moscavian Legal Code, first codified under Tsar Dmitri II in the year 995 and revised after the transformation in 999, governs all civic matters, including property rights, trade regulations, and the protection of nesting quarters as private domestic space.

Owl-folk culture in Moscavia preserves many pre-transformation traditions — Orthodox Christian worship remains the dominant faith, though services are now held in the small hours of the night and church architecture has been altered with high perches and wide owlish windows to suit the congregation.

The realm's scholars, organized under the Academy of Night Sciences in Novogorod, have devoted the past two years to researching the cause and nature of the 998 transformation, studying everything from ancient texts to astronomical records to the physical properties of owl-folk biology in search of answers.

facts.text: Velikoye is the capital of the Tsardom of Moscavia, a sprawling city of stone and timber nestled in the broad valley of the Kolyma River, where the river bends southward before emptying into the Pale Sea.
The city is built on a series of low, terraced hills that rise gently from the river's east bank, connected by wide stairways and sloping streets that accommodate both flight and ground travel.

Since the Turning of 998, Velikoye's architecture has been thoroughly adapted for owl-folk habitation: buildings feature high perch-walls with handholds and ledges, wide windows for aerial entry, and reinforced rooftops capable of bearing the weight of dozens of roosting birds at once.

The heart of the city is the Great Spiral, a massive stone plaza carved into the central hill in concentric rings, where the Nocturnal Duma holds its sessions beneath a vaulted pavilion of dark timber and silvered iron.
Velikoye's population in the year 1000 is approximately forty thousand owl-folk, making it the largest city in the northern realms and a major hub of trade, learning, and governance.
The city is divided into twelve administrative districts, each named after a pre-Turning human saint and governed by a district elder appointed by the Tsar.
Velikoye's economy depends heavily on its position at the junction of river trade routes and the northern overland trails connecting the Ash Mountains to the Pale Sea coast.
The city contains three major academies, two monasteries of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light, and the headquarters of the Taloned Host's First Aerial Squadron.
By night — when the owl-folk are most active — Velikoye is a spectacle of lantern-lit streets, hovering merchants, and the soft calls of tens of thousands of birds echoing between the rooftops.
Before the Turning, Velikoye was a major human city known as Velikigrad, the seat of the Rurikovich dynasty since the mid-ninth century.

The city suffered significant damage during the weeks immediately following the Turning of 998 as its human infrastructure was hastily converted for avian use, but by the year 999 a comprehensive rebuilding programme had restored and improved it.

Velikoye's building codes, revised in 999, mandate that all new construction include flight corridors, perch-decks, and talon-gripping surfaces as standard features, and that no structure may exceed a height of one hundred and twenty feet to preserve safety during aerial travel.

versions.name: Khorol River

facts.text: The Khorol River is a broad, slow-moving waterway that winds through the western reaches of the Tsardom of Moscavia, flowing generally southward before joining the Kolyma River in the fertile valley east of Velikoye.
facts.repeat_of: Velikoye is the capital of the Tsardom of Moscavia, a sprawling city of stone and timber nestled in the broad valley of the Kolyma River, where the river bends southward before emptying into the Pale Sea.

facts.text: The Khorol has served as a vital trade artery since long before the Turning of 998, its banks dotted with human settlements, dockyards, and market towns that formed part of the northern overland trade network connecting the Ash Mountains to the river ports along the Kolyma.

The river is approximately thirty miles wide at its mouth where it meets the Kolyma, narrowing to roughly twelve miles at its upper reaches near the Ash Mountain foothills, with a gentle gradient that makes it navigable by flat-bottomed barges and shallow-draft vessels throughout most of its length.

The Khorol valley is characterised by dense mixed forests of pine, birch, and aspen along its banks, with open meadowlands and cultivated farmland stretching back from the water on either side, providing some of the most productive agricultural land in Moscavia.

After the Turning of 998, the dockyards and river towns along the Khorol were adapted for owl-folk use, with perch-decks built along the quaysides and reinforced mooring towers erected to accommodate the Taloned Host's river patrols and the expanded civilian fleet.

Moscavian river regulations, revised in 999, mandate that all vessels on the Khorol and its tributaries must carry signal lanterns during nighttime navigation — the primary hours of owl-folk commercial traffic — and must yield to Taloned Host patrol craft on sight.

The river freezes over completely during the harsh winter months, typically from late December to mid-March, when ice-breaker barges clear a navigable channel for essential trade goods and military supplies between Velikoye and the western frontier towns.

Fishermen along the Khorol have reported that the fish populations shifted significantly after the Turning, with cold-water species such as pike and perch thriving while warmer-water stocks declined, likely due to changes in the river's thermal dynamics following widespread deforestation and reconstruction along the banks.

Several important towns and trading posts line the Khorol's course, including the river port of Khorolgrad near the Ash Mountain foothills, the market town of Dvoryanka at the river's midpoint, and the agricultural settlement of Zelenoye just upstream from the Kolyma confluence.

The Khorol's southernmost stretch, where it rounds into the Kolyma valley, is considered one of the most scenic waterways in Moscavia, with limestone bluffs rising sheer from the water on the eastern bank and gentle terraced hills on the western side — terrain that closely resembles the landscape surrounding Velikoye itself.

Owl-folk traders and merchants travelling between the Ash Mountain trade routes and Velikoye typically prefer the Khorol-Kolyma river route over the overland trails, as it reduces transit time by nearly half and allows heavy cargo to be moved by barge rather than cart.

The Khorol basin supports a thriving ecosystem of both terrestrial and aquatic wildlife, and the river's banks are a designated hunting ground for the owl-folk, managed by district elders under regulations that limit nocturnal hunting seasons and protect spawning fish stocks.

facts.text: The Khorol River is a broad, slow-moving waterway that flows through the heart of Velikoye and the broader valley of the Tsardom of Moscavia.
In winter, the upper stretches of the Khorol freeze solid for weeks at a time, halting river trade and forcing merchants to rely on the overland trails instead.
The river's lower reaches, where it bends southward toward the Pale Sea, form part of the navigable waterway shared with the broader Kolyma River system.
Its waters are dark and murky, fed by snowmelt from the Ash Mountains and dozens of tributary streams that drain the dense northern forests.
The Khorol serves as a primary commercial artery, connecting the city's interior markets to the river trade network that links the Ash Mountains to the Pale Sea coast.
Fishing on the Khorol is a major nocturnal occupation for Velikoye's residents, with catches of sterlet, burbot, and pale-sea herring forming a staple of the city's night markets.
Before the Turning of 998, the Khorol's banks in Velikigrad were lined with human wharves and market squares that were subsequently demolished and rebuilt to owl-folk specifications.
The river's banks in Velikoye are lined with stone embankments and timber dockyards, adapted since the Turning to accommodate owl-folk fishermen and merchants who work the waterways at night.
Moscavian fishing regulations, revised after the Turning, require all owl-folk anglers on the Khorol to obtain a nocturnal license from their district elder and observe seasonal catch limits.
Ferry services operate across the river at several points within Velikoye, using flat-bottomed barges fitted with perch-decks so owl-folk passengers can rest mid-crossing.

facts.text: The Nocturnal Duma is the supreme governing council of the Tsardom of Moscavia, established in the aftermath of the Turning of 998 to conduct all official state business during the nighttime hours.
The Duma consists of twelve senior officials appointed by Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III, each chosen for their expertise in a particular domain of governance, commerce, or military affairs.
facts.repeat_of: The Tsardom is governed by Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III, who rules from Velikigrad with the aid of a council of twelve senior officials known as the Nocturnal Duma.

facts.text: All sessions of the Nocturnal Duma are held in the Great Hall of the Tsardom's central administrative building in Velikoye, known as the Nocturnium, a grand structure of pale stone whose towering windows face north to admit the light of the moon and stars.

The Duma's proceedings are conducted entirely in darkness or deep twilight, as owl-folk perception is sharpest during these hours; sessions begin at dusk and typically conclude before the first pale hints of dawn touch the northern sky.
The President of the Nocturnal Duma serves as the Tsar's chief lieutenant in matters of domestic governance and is considered the second most powerful figure in the Tsardom after the Tsar himself.

Each member of the Duma holds a specific portfolio: one oversees the Khorol-Kolyma trade network, another manages relations with the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light, a third commands liaison with the Taloned Host, and so on for all major branches of Moscavian governance.
The Duma has the authority to legislate, adjudicate disputes between provinces, ratify treaties, and levy taxes, though the Tsar retains the power of final veto over all its decrees.

Daytime hours in Velikoye are reserved for rest, private commerce, and family life; government offices and courts remain closed until sunset, when the city's lanterns are lit and the owl-folk begin their waking day.

The Nocturnal Duma inherited many of its procedural traditions from the pre-Turning Boyar Council of the Rurikovich dynasty, though its nocturnal schedule and its adaptation to avian physiology mark a decisive break from those earlier customs.

Seating within the Duma hall is arranged in a wide crescent facing the President's chair, which sits on a raised dais beneath a great owl carved from dark wood — a symbol of the realm's transformation.

The Duma's twelve members are formally referred to as 'Lords of the Night' in diplomatic correspondence, and their collective voice carries the weight of tradition and institutional memory stretching back to the earliest days of owl-folk governance.

In the year 1000, the Nocturnal Duma under Tsar Dmitri III governs a realm of approximately three million owl-folk across dozens of provinces, managing everything from grain tariffs on the Khorol to naval patrols along the Pale Sea.

Runic magic is the art of carving ancient glyphs into stone to bind and direct the forces of frost and wind.
The runes draw their power from the Vostrik Mountains, where the cold is so deep it is said to have memory.
Practitioners are called Frostwardens, and they are trained at the Monastery of the Pale Wind in the city of Khol'sk.
A Frostwarden must spend three winters in solitary carving on the mountain passes before being granted the title.
The runes themselves are not written in any spoken language but in the Oldstone Script, which predates the Tsardom by centuries.
Wind-runes accelerate and redirect air currents for travel, warfare, and weather-shaping over distances of many leagues.
Frost-runes can freeze water, earth, and even stone itself, and when layered in arrays they create barriers of ice that endure for months.
The Tsardom's northern border along the Shelfsea is defended by the Great Rune Wall, a chain of carved monoliths stretching over two hundred miles.

There are three schools of thought among Frostwardens: the Orthodoxy of Deep Carving, which holds that runes must be chiseled into living rock; the Reform of the Drift Script, which permits carving on stone fragments and even bone; and the Quietists, who believe the oldest runes were not carved at all but grew naturally in the mountains.
The faith of the Pale Mother regards the runes as sacred gifts left by the first Frost Queen during the Long Winter that ended the Age of Warring Peoples.
Runic magic cannot be performed in southern climes beyond the River Donova, where the earth is too warm to hold the carvings' charge.
The runic magic of the Tsardom is a discipline rooted in the carving of sacred symbols into stone, which harnesses and binds the elemental forces of frost and wind.
Practitioners, known as Rune-carvers or Frost-scribers, must undergo years of apprenticeship at one of the Tsardom's dedicated scriptoria before they are permitted to inscribe binding rune-work.

The fundamental principle of this magic is that frost and wind are not separate elements but manifestations of a single underlying force—the Breath of the Pale, as the old texts call it—made visible in cold and motion.

Runes are carved using tools fashioned from meteorite iron, quenched in glacial meltwater, because only iron touched by the sky and purified by ice carries enough clarity to channel the Breath without distortion.

A fully inscribed rune-stone can endure for centuries, maintaining its binding long after the carver has died, which is why the Tsardom's oldest monuments still carry active wards against blizzard and avalanche.

There are three recognized schools of thought within the discipline: the Orthodox Line, which holds that rune-work must follow ancient formulae passed down from the First Carvers; the Drift School, which encourages intuitive modification of rune shapes to suit local conditions; and the Severing Faction, which believes that wind and frost should be treated as opposing forces to be held in tension rather than harmony.

The most prestigious institution for the study of runic magic is the Scriptorium of Velikost, nestled in the foothills of the Kholodny Mountains, where apprentices live in stone cells carved from a single massive boulder and train for a minimum of seven years.

Historically, the discipline originated during the reign of Tsar Oleg I of the House of Volkov, who commissioned the first great rune-stones to protect his northern trade routes from catastrophic winter storms that had been destroying caravans for decades.

The Tsardom's military makes extensive use of rune-carved banners and shield-edges, which can deflect enemy arrows by generating localized gusts of wind or coat enemy formations in sheets of black ice.

Frost-scribers of exceptional talent can carve runes into their own skin, creating temporary personal wards, though this practice is considered dangerous because a mistake in the carving can cause frostbite or exposure to uncontrollable gales within the body.

The Tsardom's capital, Moscow, is surrounded by a ring of twelve massive rune-stones erected over the course of a century, each one carved to protect the city from a different direction of attack—elemental or military—and together they form what is called the Pale Circuit.

A rune-carver's work is considered complete only when the stone resonates with a clear, high tone upon being struck, a sound produced by the alignment of the carved channels with the Breath of the Pale; a dull sound means the binding is flawed and must be re-carved.

The Order of the Talon-Scribe is the supreme institution responsible for the study, transcription, preservation, and teaching of the runic script known as the Tsardom's runes.

The Order was founded by Grand Scribe Alaric Vostov during the reign of Tsar Dmitri II of the Volkov Dynasty, after the Great Fire of 742 destroyed most of the Tsardom's written records, forcing a centralized effort to reconstruct and standardize the rune system.
Its seat is the Ataman's Citadel in the capital city of Khorov, a fortress-monastery built into the southern face of the Greymount, overlooking the Dneva River and the Tsardom's central square.
The Order is led by the Ataman of the Quill, a title that combines the roles of spiritual head, chief scholar, and administrative leader, appointed by the Tsar from among the Order's senior members.

Below the Ataman, the Order is divided into three divisions called Quills: the Quill of Memory, which preserves and archives all rune-inscribed texts in the Great Vaults beneath Khorov; the Quill of Teaching, which operates scriptoria and training halls across the Tsardom; and the Quill of the Field, which sends scribes to military campaigns and diplomatic missions to inscribe treaties, battle records, and oaths in the moment of their making.

Each member of the Order takes the Oath of the Unbroken Line, swearing to transmit the runes faithfully without alteration, to never destroy an inscribed text without authorization, and to give their life if needed to protect the knowledge they carry.

The Order maintains twelve chapter houses across the Tsardom, each named after a rune in the First Circle of the Tsardom's script. The oldest and most prestigious is the chapter house of Vekha, named after the rune of foundation, located in the mountain city of Stennik in the Ashgrove Mountains.
Talon-Scribes are identifiable by their grey-and-ochre robes and the talon-shaped iron stylus they wear suspended from their left ear, used for inscribing runes on stone, wood, and parchment.
The Order's motto is 'What is written endures,' and it is carved in the First Circle runes above the entrance to the Ataman's Citadel.

The Order has survived civil wars, foreign invasions, and schisms over the centuries. The most famous crisis was the Rune Famine of 814, when a plague killed half the Order's membership and forced the then-Ataman, Maren Duska, to open apprenticeship to women for the first time, dramatically expanding the Order's capacity.

The Talon-Scribes hold that the Tsardom's runes are not merely a writing system but a living language of the land itself, that each rune carries a fragment of the world's enduring truth, and that to inscribe a rune is to participate in the ongoing creation of reality.

As of the year 1000, the Ataman of the Quill is Sable Korven, a former Field Scribe who distinguished herself during the Border Wars of 987 by inscribing the Treaty of Frostmere in real time as both armies stood down, an act considered one of the most heroic feats in the Order's history.

versions.name: Academy of the Chiseled Moon

facts.text: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a training institution of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, located in the capital city of Velikoye.
It serves as the primary training hall for the Quill of Teaching in Velikoye, preparing new scribes and advancing the studies of those already sworn into the Order.
facts.repeat_of: Below the Ataman, the Order is divided into three divisions called Quills: the Quill of Memory, which preserves and archives all rune-inscribed texts in the Great Vaults beneath Khorov; the Quill of Teaching, which operates scriptoria and training halls across the Tsardom; and the Quill of the Field, which sends scribes to military campaigns and diplomatic missions to inscribe treaties, battle records, and oaths in the moment of their making.

facts.text: The Academy was established in Velikoye during the rebuilding efforts following the Turning of 998, replacing an earlier human scriptorium that had been destroyed in the hasty architectural conversion of the city.

The building itself is a converted human guildhall on the fourth terrace of the city's eastern hill, its stone façade now fitted with wide flight-entrance archways, perch-ledges along every exterior wall, and reinforced rooftop bracing designed to bear the weight of dozens of roosting owl-folk.

Inside, the main lecture hall is a vaulted chamber of grey stone, its walls lined with alcoves containing inscribed tablets — practice texts carved by generations of students since the Academy's founding.

The hall features twelve long desks arranged in concentric semicircles around a raised dais where the master scribe stands, each desk equipped with a sloping writing surface, a tray of iron styluses, and a block of pale limestone for rune practice.
Admission to the Academy requires a letter of recommendation from a Talon-Scribe of the Quill of Memory or Quill of the Field, attesting to the candidate's literacy and aptitude for rune-inscription.

Students at the Chiseled Moon train for a minimum of two years, during which they learn the First Circle runes, the foundational scripts of the Tsardom, and advance to the more complex Frostward Runes used in military and diplomatic inscription work.

The Academy's curriculum also includes history, calligraphy, and the philosophical tenets of the Order, including the significance of the Oath of the Unbroken Line and the belief that runes are a living language of the land itself.
The head of the Academy holds the title of Master of the Chiseled Moon, appointed by the Ataman of the Quill in consultation with the Quill of Teaching's senior scribes.
facts.repeat_of: The Order is led by the Ataman of the Quill, a title that combines the roles of spiritual head, chief scholar, and administrative leader, appointed by the Tsar from among the Order's senior members.

facts.text: By the year 1000, the Academy has graduated over three hundred Talon-Scribes, many of whom have gone on to distinguished careers in all three Quills of the Order.

The Academy's motto, carved above its main entrance in deep ochre paint against grey stone, reads: 'What is written endures' — the same phrase that adorns the entrance to the Ataman's Citadel in Khorov.
facts.repeat_of: The Order's motto is 'What is written endures,' and it is carved in the First Circle runes above the entrance to the Ataman's Citadel.

Froststeel is a rare metal mined from the deep veins of the Ashenmount Range and is said to remain sharp for decades without dulling.
The White Talon has fought in every major conflict involving Velmaris since its founding, earning a reputation for holding ground that other forces cannot.
Its current commander is General Maren Voss, a veteran of the Thornwall Border War who took command in the year 984 after the previous commander fell to illness.
The regiment's war cry is 'By the Tusk!', referencing the legendary mammoth tusk from which the officers' gauntlets are made.
At its peak strength, the White Talon numbers approximately 1,200 soldiers, organized into twelve companies of one hundred each.
The regiment's barracks are located in the fortress city of Greymarch, the military capital of Velmaris, where it maintains a permanent garrison year-round.

versions.name: The Frosted Wing

facts.text: The Frosted Wing is an elite regiment of the Taloned Host, the military arm of the Tsardom of Moscavia, stationed at the glacier edge of the northern frontier.
Every soldier in the regiment is an owl-folk archer, selected for exceptional eyesight, wing strength, and marksmanship in the punishing conditions near the Pale Sea.
The regiment takes its name from the thick rime of frost that coats the plumage of its members during winter patrols, giving them a glittering, spectral appearance against the snow.

Archers of the Frosted Wing carry recurved longbows of ashwood and yew, tipped with obsidian arrowheads that do not shatter in the extreme cold, capable of striking targets at ranges exceeding four hundred paces.

The regiment was formed in the year 999 under the command of Colonel Maren Snezhanka to defend the northern glacier passes against raids by the Frostborn skirmishers, who had begun probing the Tsardom's borders for resources and slaves.

Frosted Wing soldiers train extensively in nocturnal combat, leveraging their superior night vision and silent flight to ambush and harass enemies in darkness, before melting back into the frozen landscape.

Each archer is equipped with a hooded lantern strapped to the left wrist, its dim blue light used for signaling between squad members during blizzard conditions when visual communication is impossible.
The regiment's standard is a pennant of deep indigo silk bearing a white owl in flight against a crescent moon, sewn with silver thread that glints in moonlight.
Recruits must pass the Trial of the Howling Wind, spending three nights exposed on the glacier's edge without shelter while maintaining a patrol route, before being admitted to the regiment.

The Frosted Wing operates from a network of stone watchtowers built into the cliff faces above the ice, each tower heated by braziers of slow-burning peat and stocked with dried rations and arrow caches.

Members of the Frosted Wing develop a distinctive gait when grounded — a wide, deliberate stance with talons sunk deep into packed snow — to resist the treacherous crosswinds that sweep across the glacier.

The regiment enjoys a reputation among the civilian population of Moscavia as both fearsome warriors and quiet guardians; folk songs from the interior provinces often feature the Frosted Wing as protectors who appear in blizzards to shield villages from raiders, vanishing before dawn.

elsewhere.text: The Frosted Wing is one of several specialized regiments within the Taloned Host, distinguished by its arctic deployment and its role in northern border defense.

versions.name: Frosted Wing

facts.text: The Frosted Wing is a regiment of eared owl-folk archers stationed along the glacier edge of the Tsardom of Moscavia, tasked with defending the northern frontier where the frozen shores of the Pale Sea meet the Ash Mountains.

The regiment draws its name from the rime and frost that perpetually coats the feathers of its soldiers, who spend much of their service in subzero conditions on the ice shelves and frozen ridgelines above the Pale Sea.

Every soldier in the Frosted Wing is an owl-folk archer, selected for exceptional eyesight and flight endurance, with specialized training in cold-weather combat and long-range marksmanship across icy terrain.

The regiment was established in the year 999, just one year after the Turning, when the new Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III recognized that Moscavia's northern glacier frontier required a dedicated garrison to patrol the frozen expanses where human settlers had once mined for pale stone.

Frosted Wing archers are equipped with composite bows built from Ash Mountain yew and sinew, reinforced with a thin lacquer of seal oil to resist cracking in the cold, paired with arrows tipped in obsidian or hardened steel.

Their plumage, naturally adapted to the frigid northern climate, ranges from deep snowy whites and pale greys to soft blue-greys that blend seamlessly with the ice and cloud cover of the glacier edge, making them nearly invisible to enemies during nighttime patrols.

The Frosted Wing operates under the command of the Taloned Host's northern wing, reporting to the garrison commander of the Icewatch Fort at the mouth of the Kolyma River system, where the river meets the Pale Sea.

Soldiers of the Frosted Wing sleep in shifts during the daylight hours within heated stone barracks built into the cliff faces of the northern escarpment, their quarters lined with thick pelts and heated by braziers of slow-burning peat.

The regiment's most celebrated tradition is the Nightwatch Vigil, a ceremonial patrol conducted on the longest night of winter by the twelve most senior archers, who fly in a silent circle above the frozen coastline without rest until dawn.

Frosted Wing recruits undergo a grueling eight-month training period at the Icewatch Fort, during which they learn to navigate crevasses by moonlight, hunt seals and polar hares for sustenance, and hold their aim in winds that howl at speeds exceeding fifty miles per hour.

The regiment has earned a fearsome reputation among neighboring polities for its ability to strike from complete darkness — owl-folk archers of the Frosted Wing can loose accurate arrows at targets up to three hundred paces away using only the light of the moon and stars.

A common saying among Moscavian soldiers is 'May your feathers frost before your courage,' a phrase attributed to the Frosted Wing's first commander, who reportedly led a sortie bare-chested into a blizzard to rally his frightened troops.

elsewhere.text: The Taloned Host's northern wing maintains the Frosted Wing regiment along the glacier edge of the Pale Sea, a deployment considered one of the most demanding postings in the entire Moscavian military due to the extreme cold and isolation.

versions.name: The Frostwing Host

facts.text: The Frostwing Host is the standing army of the Tsardom of Moscavia, established in the years following the Turning of 998 to defend the realm and project its power across the northern lands.

Its name derives from the frost-white plumage and ice-hardened talons that characterize the owl-folk soldiers who serve within it, evoking both the transformed nature of Moscavian citizens and the harsh northern climate they defend.

The Host operates under the direct authority of the Tsar and is administered by the Nocturnal Duma's Military Committee, a standing sub-council of three senior officials who oversee recruitment, provisioning, and deployment.

Its headquarters are co-located with the Tsar's palace in Velikoye, where the General Staff maintains a vast hall of war-tables, aerial maps, and ice-glass scrying instruments for tracking enemy movements across the northern frontier.

The Host maintains a standing strength of approximately 40,000 soldiers across its aerial, ground, and naval branches, supplemented by militia levies from the provincial towns and river settlements along the Khorol and Kolyma systems.

Its aerial squadrons are its most prestigious arm, comprising highly trained owl-folk fliers who carry light lances and talon-bolts into battle, striking from above with devastating speed and precision.

Ground infantry regiments are equipped with talon-gripping gauntlets and armored boots that allow owl-folk soldiers to scale walls, dig into frozen earth, and engage in close-quarters combat with both natural talons and steel-edged weapons.

The Host's navy sails from Pale Sea ports and along the frozen waterways of the north, with high perch-decks built atop each vessel so that owl-folk officers can take flight to survey the ice, coordinate fleet movements, and engage enemy scouts at altitude.

Among its most decorated regiments is the Frosted Wing, an elite arctic formation stationed at the northern glacier edge, tasked with defending the Pale Sea coast and monitoring the movements of the Frostborn raiders beyond it.
The White Talon is the Host's heaviest and most elite heavy infantry regiment, serving as the Tsar's personal guard and the final line of defense in any siege or pitched battle.

facts.text: The Frostwing Host is the standing army of the Tsardom of Moscavia, fielded to defend the realm's borders and enforce its sovereignty across the northern reaches.
It is organized into multiple specialized regiments, each tailored to the unique demands of Moscavia's terrain, from frozen glacier edges to dense boreal forests.

Every soldier of the Frostwing Host was once a human citizen of Moscavia who underwent the Turning of 998, and the army's doctrine reflects the blend of human tactical tradition and avian perceptual abilities inherited from that transformation.
The Host maintains permanent garrisons along the Ash Mountains in the west, the northern glacier edge bordering the Pale Sea, and at key river crossing points along the Khorol and Kolyma systems.

Aerial squadrons constitute the Host's primary strike force, utilizing the natural flight capabilities of the owl-folk to conduct reconnaissance, rapid deployment, and high-altitude bombardment using modified siege equipment.

Ground infantry regiments are equipped with talon-gripping harnesses and reinforced armor plating designed to allow owl-folk soldiers to scale cliffs, ice faces, and vertical structures with devastating speed.

The Host's navy operates a fleet of high-deck vessels along the Khorol and Kolyma rivers as well as the northern coast of the Pale Sea, with elevated command platforms built into the rigging for owl-folk officers to survey the battlefield.

Training for the Frostwing Host takes place at military academies in Velikoye and at regional garrison forts, where recruits are drilled in both the ancient human arts of warfare and the instinct-driven combat techniques unique to owl-folk physiology.
The Host answers ultimately to Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III and the Nocturnal Duma, with operational command delegated to a High Marshal appointed by the Tsar.

facts.text: Elite regiments within the Host, such as the Frosted Wing and the White Talon, receive specialized training for arctic warfare and heavy assault respectively, and are considered the finest fighting forces in the known north.

versions.name: Plumage Signaling

facts.text: Plumage Signaling, known commonly as the Feather Language, is the custom by which the owl-folk of the Tsardom of Moscavia communicate through the deliberate raising, settling, fanning, and positioning of their body feathers.

Every owl-folk possesses a unique plumage pattern that serves as both personal identification and a palette of communicative expression, much as a human face conveys identity while also betraying emotion through blushes, frowns, and other involuntary signals.

The Feather Language is not merely a supplement to verbal speech but a primary mode of communication among owl-folk, particularly in formal settings such as sessions of the Nocturnal Duma, where it allows members to express nuance, emphasis, and dissent without disrupting the speaker or breaking the decorum of darkness.
A fully fanned tail spread wide indicates confidence or authority, while feathers pressed flat against the body signify submission, grief, or the acknowledgment of a grave matter.

The ear-tufts, though not true ears, play a central role in Plumage Signaling: their position and tension convey alertness, curiosity, skepticism, or displeasure, and they are often the first feature an owl-folk observer reads in a social exchange.

Among the aristocratic families of Velikoye, mastery of the Feather Language is considered an essential social skill, and young owl-folk are trained in its subtleties from an early age, much as human-era nobility once studied dance and etiquette.

The Grand Owl Hall of the Tsar's Palace is specifically designed to accommodate Plumage Signaling, with wide aisles, high ceilings, and smooth stone walls that allow feather displays to be seen clearly by all members even in total darkness.

During Duma sessions, members frequently signal their votes, objections, and amendments through feather movements rather than speaking aloud, enabling multiple threads of formal and informal communication to occur simultaneously in the darkness.

There exist regional variations in the Feather Language across Moscavia, with owl-folk from the northern provinces near the Ash Mountains employing different conventions than those of the river valleys around Velikoye, leading to occasional misunderstandings between travelers and officials from different parts of the Tsardom.

The Orthodox Church of the Northern Light has formalized certain religious gestures within the Feather Language, such as the Pilgrim's Spread — wings half-open and head bowed — which signifies devotion and supplication during worship.

Scholars at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon have attempted to compile comprehensive grammars of the Feather Language, but the custom's inherent fluidity and the influence of individual plumage patterns make standardization difficult, and no single authoritative text has been accepted.

The Feather Language is believed to have emerged organically in the weeks following the Turning of 998, as the newly transformed owl-folk discovered that their plumage responded to emotional states in ways that were visible to others, and gradually learned to control those responses deliberately.

elsewhere.text: Members of the Nocturnal Duma frequently employ Plumage Signaling during sessions to express agreement, dissent, or the urgency of a matter without breaking the silence maintained for the sake of the visually impaired human-era advisors who were once present and whose accommodations, though no longer needed, remain a vestige of pre-Turning protocol.

The Grand Owl Hall features tiered stone galleries lined with smooth perches, each carved with individual owl-folk crest-rests that allow members to display their plumage at full extension during formal votes — a visual spectacle visible even in the hall's characteristic total darkness.

elsewhere.target: Orthodox Church of the Northern Light
elsewhere.text: The Church's formalization of religious gestures in the Feather Language has led to the development of liturgical plumage choreography, in which clergy perform elaborate synchronized feather displays during the Northern Light services, a practice that draws on both pre-Turning Christian iconography and the newly discovered expressive potential of owl-folk plumage.

The Academy maintains a department dedicated to the study of Plumage Signaling, where students learn to decode the feather-language of historical figures by studying preserved plumage samples and contemporaneous accounts written by human-era observers who witnessed the early days of the custom's development.

facts.text: Plumage Signaling is the primary means of nonverbal communication among the owl-folk of the Tsardom of Moscavia, in which meaning is conveyed through the deliberate raising, settling, fanning, and positioning of feathers on the body, wings, and head tufts.

facts.repeat_of: An owl-folk is a bipedal humanoid roughly five to seven feet tall, with a broad, rounded body covered in soft plumage that ranges from tawny golds and greys to deep browns and snowy whites.

facts.text: The feathered tufts atop an owl-folk's head, often called 'ears' though they are not true ears, are among the most expressive elements used in Plumage Signaling, serving as visible indicators of mood, intent, and emotional state.
A fully raised crest of head feathers signals alertness, surprise, or heightened attention, while a flattened crest indicates submission, calm, or grief.

Fanning the wings partially while keeping the body still is a gesture of display used to communicate authority, confidence, or a formal declaration of intent, commonly seen when members of the Nocturnal Duma wish to speak without words during deliberations.
The ruffling of breast and shoulder feathers in a rapid, agitated pattern conveys irritation or disagreement, and is frequently observed during heated debates in the Grand Owl Hall.
Smoothing all feathers flat against the body is a gesture of acknowledgment or assent, often used in place of verbal agreement during formal proceedings of the Night Court.

Among the aristocratic families of Velikoye, mastery of Plumage Signaling is considered essential to social competence, and children of the old human-era noble houses are trained in its subtleties from a young age.

The custom emerged naturally in the years following the Turning of 998, as the transformed population developed new modes of expression suited to their changed bodies, and it has since become deeply embedded in Moscavian social and political life.

In the Grand Owl Hall, where all sessions of the Nocturnal Duma are conducted in darkness, Plumage Signaling supplements the members' keen night-vision and acute hearing, providing an additional channel of communication in an environment where spoken words can carry unintended echoes off the vast stone walls.

Certain combinations of feather movements have been codified into formal protocol within the Night Court, with specific gestures reserved for particular occasions, such as the opening and closing of sessions, the announcement of a vote, and the declaration of a Tsar's tiebreaking decision.

The Orthodox Church of the Northern Light has blessed Plumage Signaling as a divinely sanctioned gift, interpreting the transformation of feathers as evidence of God's continued presence in the lives of the owl-folk, and incorporating feather gestures into certain liturgical rites.

steps.prompt: its winter markets and what they sell

facts.text: Velikoye's winter markets operate under canvas awnings stretched between the upper perch-walls of the merchant quarter on the river's east bank, where vendors sell dried fish and salted river crayfish from the Kolyma alongside smoked meats and root vegetables preserved through the frost months.

By tradition, the winter markets are opened each year on the first night of the Frost Moon by the district elder of Saint Illarion's Quarter, who rings a bell of silvered iron from a high balcony to signal that the stalls may begin trading.

Among the most prized wares at the winter markets are pelts — ermine, wolverine, and snow leopard — brought south from the Ash Mountains along the overland trails and traded by merchants who arrive with caravans of laden ravens and hawks.

The markets also serve as informal gathering places where owl-folk meet to share news and gossip, with small performance stages set up along the main thoroughfare where traveling musicians and storytellers perform for crowds who perch along the overhead ledges.

During the long northern winters, Velikoye's three great covered markets — the Frost Rink Bazaar on Saint Nicholas Hill, the Pellet & Plumage Exchange near the Khorol dockyards, and the Warmth Hall beneath the old human cathedral of the Annunciation — open their iron-barred stalls to tens of thousands of owl-folk seeking provisions against the cold.

The winter markets specialize in salted fish from the Pale Sea fleet, smoked meats and dried herbs from the Ash Mountain trails, tallow candles and lamp oil in every grade, thick felted cloaks dyed in deep greens and ochres, and bundles of dried moss used as insulation for perch-walls and nest-boxes.

Merchants flying in from the northern provinces bring rare goods to the Frost Rink Bazaar — amber from the tundra rivers, falcon-bone carvings, bolts of spider-silk cloth, and jars of preserved nightberries that glow faintly in the dark.

The Pellet & Plumage Exchange, situated close to the river docks, trades primarily in bulk commodities: grain from the southern farmlands, dried fish, building timber, and the dense river clay that Velikoye's masons use for winter repair work on flight corridors and rooftop nesting ledges.

Market hours in winter are strictly regulated by the Tsar's nightwatch bell-towers, which ring the First Hoot at dusk and the Last Hoot before dawn, and all trade must conclude before the morning light forces the owl-folk indoors.

steps.prompt: a failed uprising of the human nobles against the owl-folk Tsar

facts.text: In the summer of 997, a coalition of human noble houses led by Prince Yaroslav Volkov of the northern marches launched a surprise uprising against Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III, denouncing the owl-folk as usurpers and demanding the restoration of human rule.

The conspirators, numbering roughly forty minor lords and their retainers, attempted to seize Velikigrad's Grand Roost during the twilight transition between day and night shifts, believing the owl-folk guards would be at their most vulnerable during the change of watch.

The uprising was crushed within three days when the Taloned Host's aerial squadrons encircled the rebel-held districts and Tsar Dmitri personally negotiated the surrender of Prince Volkov, who was subsequently exiled to the frozen island of Kholm Ogny rather than executed, in keeping with the Tsardom's revised legal tradition of mercy toward former humans.

The failure of the 997 uprising is widely regarded as the definitive end of organized human resistance within Moscavia, though its memory remains a source of tension in certain northern provinces where human-born families retain influence in local merchant guilds.

After the uprising, Tsar Dmitri commissioned the construction of the Pale Watchtowers — a network of stone observation posts along the northern frontier — both as a military precaution and as a symbolic statement that the Tsardom would never again be caught unawares by those who refused the Turning.

In the spring of 997, a coalition of human noble houses led by Prince Yury of Novgorod and the boyar Kazarin launched a coordinated revolt against Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III, protesting what they called the 'unnatural tyranny' of owl-folk rule and demanding the restoration of human governance.

The uprising, known as the Human Dawn Conspiracy, sought to seize control of Velikigrad by exploiting the fact that the owl-folk had not yet fully adapted the capital's defenses for aerial combat, relying instead on hastily reinforced ground fortifications.

The conspirators secured the loyalty of several provincial garrisons and the merchant quarter of Velikigrad, but their plans were betrayed by Metropolitan Ilya of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light, who had secretly pledged his allegiance to the Tsar.

Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III personally commanded the Taloned Host's suppression of the revolt, deploying aerial squadrons to cut off the human rebels' retreat along the Khorol River valley and besieging their stronghold in the old Kremlin quarter of Velikigrad.

Prince Yury of Novgorod was executed publicly on the steps of the Duma Hall in Velikigrad on 12 August 997, and the surviving human noble conspirators were stripped of their titles and lands, which were redistributed among loyalist owl-folk families, an act that profoundly reshaped the aristocratic hierarchy of the Tsardom.

steps.prompt: two taverns where owl-folk and humans drink together

rows.name: The Blinking Lantern
rows.line: A warmly lit tavern on the lower ring of the Great Spiral, where human and owl-folk patrons share long tables carved from pale birchwood, its walls hung with oil lanterns that flicker in a rhythm resembling owl-sign, and its cellar stocked with honeyed mead and frozen vodka from the northern steppes.

rows.name: Moshka's Nest
rows.line: A raucous, smoky establishment wedged between two old stone tenements on the eastern bank of the Kolyma River, run by a heavyset human woman named Moshka who keeps a pet barn owl named Duma on the bar counter, famous for its roasted pheasant and its tradition of owl-folk and human patrons sharing a single tankard to seal any deal struck over the table.

rows.name: The Hollow Lantern
rows.line: A tavern nestled in the lower terraces of the Great Spiral, the Hollow Lantern is a warm-stoned building with a round door and windows set high in the walls for owl-folk entry, where human and owl-folk patrons share long tables over roasted root vegetables, honeyed mead, and a house brew called Kolyma Fog that glows faintly amber in the cup.

rows.name: The Drowsy Falcon
rows.line: Situated on the eastern bank of the Khorol River, just within Velikoye's outer wall, the Drowsy Falcon is a timber-and-daub establishment built into the remnants of a pre-Turning human tavern, its reinforced upper floor serving as a communal roost for owl-folk regulars while its ground floor bar caters to human drinkers, with a shared hearth and a long counter where both species order from the same barkeep, a broad-shouldered human woman named Masha who speaks passable plumage-sign.

Velikoye's winter markets operate under canvas awnings stretched between the upper perch-walls of the merchant quarter on the river's east bank, where vendors sell dried fish and salted river crayfish from the Kolyma alongside smoked meats and root vegetables preserved through the frost months.

The heart of the city is the Great Spiral, a massive stone plaza carved into the central hill in concentric rings, where the Nocturnal Duma holds its sessions beneath a vaulted pavilion of dark timber and silvered iron.

By tradition, the winter markets are opened each year on the first night of the Frost Moon by the district elder of Saint Illarion's Quarter, who rings a bell of silvered iron from a high balcony to signal that the stalls may begin trading.

The city suffered significant damage during the weeks immediately following the Turning of 998 as its human infrastructure was hastily converted for avian use, but by the year 999 a comprehensive rebuilding programme had restored and improved it.

Velikoye's building codes, revised in 999, mandate that all new construction include flight corridors, perch-decks, and talon-gripping surfaces as standard features, and that no structure may exceed a height of one hundred and twenty feet to preserve safety during aerial travel.
The city is divided into twelve administrative districts, each named after a pre-Turning human saint and governed by a district elder appointed by the Tsar.
The city is built on a series of low, terraced hills that rise gently from the river's east bank, connected by wide stairways and sloping streets that accommodate both flight and ground travel.
The Grand Owl Hall in the Tsar's Palace serves as the meeting chamber for the Nocturnal Duma.
By night — when the owl-folk are most active — Velikoye is a spectacle of lantern-lit streets, hovering merchants, and the soft calls of tens of thousands of birds echoing between the rooftops.

The markets also serve as informal gathering places where owl-folk meet to share news and gossip, with small performance stages set up along the main thoroughfare where traveling musicians and storytellers perform for crowds who perch along the overhead ledges.
The city's river trade infrastructure along the Khorol supports much of its commercial activity, making the dockyards on the east bank among the busiest nighttime workplaces in the capital.

Velikoye is the capital of the Tsardom of Moscavia, a sprawling city of stone and timber nestled in the broad valley of the Kolyma River, where the river bends southward before emptying into the Pale Sea.
The city contains three major academies, two monasteries of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light, and the headquarters of the Taloned Host's First Aerial Squadron.

Since the Turning of 998, Velikoye's architecture has been thoroughly adapted for owl-folk habitation: buildings feature high perch-walls with handholds and ledges, wide windows for aerial entry, and reinforced rooftops capable of bearing the weight of dozens of roosting birds at once.
Velikoye's economy depends heavily on its position at the junction of river trade routes and the northern overland trails connecting the Ash Mountains to the Pale Sea coast.
Before the Turning, Velikoye was a major human city known as Velikigrad, the seat of the Rurikovich dynasty since the mid-ninth century.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is one of three major academies operating in the capital, alongside institutions of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light and the Taloned Host's First Aerial Squadron.
Velikoye's population in the year 1000 is approximately forty thousand owl-folk, making it the largest city in the northern realms and a major hub of trade, learning, and governance.

steps.prompt: a chapter house of the Order in another city of the Tsardom

rows.name: Chapter House of Lethka
rows.line: The Chapter House of Lethka, named after the rune of passage, is the Order's newest chapter house, established in the year 997 in the river-trade city of Velmora on the eastern bank of the Dneva, serving as a center for the transcription and teaching of runic script in the Tsardom's most commercially vital region.

rows.name: Chapter House of Orsya
rows.line: The Chapter House of Orsya, named after the rune of the open hand, is the twelfth and youngest chapter house of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, established in the river port city of Velikost in 994 to serve the Tsardom's growing maritime trade and the naval garrison along the southern Dneva.

facts.text: Its seat is the Ataman's Citadel in the capital city of Khorov, a fortress-monastery built into the southern face of the Greymount, overlooking the Dneva River and the Tsardom's central square.

Below the Ataman, the Order is divided into three divisions called Quills: the Quill of Memory, which preserves and archives all rune-inscribed texts in the Great Vaults beneath Khorov; the Quill of Teaching, which operates scriptoria and training halls across the Tsardom; and the Quill of the Field, which sends scribes to military campaigns and diplomatic missions to inscribe treaties, battle records, and oaths in the moment of their making.
The Order's motto is 'What is written endures,' and it is carved in the First Circle runes above the entrance to the Ataman's Citadel.

Each member of the Order takes the Oath of the Unbroken Line, swearing to transmit the runes faithfully without alteration, to never destroy an inscribed text without authorization, and to give their life if needed to protect the knowledge they carry.

The Order maintains twelve chapter houses across the Tsardom, each named after a rune in the First Circle of the Tsardom's script. The oldest and most prestigious is the chapter house of Vekha, named after the rune of foundation, located in the mountain city of Stennik in the Ashgrove Mountains.

The Order was founded by Grand Scribe Alaric Vostov during the reign of Tsar Dmitri II of the Volkov Dynasty, after the Great Fire of 742 destroyed most of the Tsardom's written records, forcing a centralized effort to reconstruct and standardize the rune system.

The Talon-Scribes hold that the Tsardom's runes are not merely a writing system but a living language of the land itself, that each rune carries a fragment of the world's enduring truth, and that to inscribe a rune is to participate in the ongoing creation of reality.
Talon-Scribes are identifiable by their grey-and-ochre robes and the talon-shaped iron stylus they wear suspended from their left ear, used for inscribing runes on stone, wood, and parchment.
The Order of the Talon-Scribe is the supreme institution responsible for the study, transcription, preservation, and teaching of the runic script known as the Tsardom's runes.
The Order is led by the Ataman of the Quill, a title that combines the roles of spiritual head, chief scholar, and administrative leader, appointed by the Tsar from among the Order's senior members.

The Order has survived civil wars, foreign invasions, and schisms over the centuries. The most famous crisis was the Rune Famine of 814, when a plague killed half the Order's membership and forced the then-Ataman, Maren Duska, to open apprenticeship to women for the first time, dramatically expanding the Order's capacity.

As of the year 1000, the Ataman of the Quill is Sable Korven, a former Field Scribe who distinguished herself during the Border Wars of 987 by inscribing the Treaty of Frostmere in real time as both armies stood down, an act considered one of the most heroic feats in the Order's history.

The Blinking Lantern, a warmly lit tavern on the Spiral's lower ring, serves honeyed mead and frozen vodka to human and avian patrons. The Academy of the Chiseled Moon occupies the upper terraces overlooking the Spiral and the Kolyma River.

The militaries of the Tsardom of Moscavia collectively form the Taloned Host, the realm's armed forces established after the Turning of 998. The First Aerial Squadron is based in the capital Velikigrad, where the Nocturnal Duma's Military Committee administers the Host under the Tsar's authority.

A single establishment, Moshka's Nest, sits on the Kolyma's eastern bank.

versions.name: Wattles

facts.text: Wattles are clusters of soft, elongated feathers that grow along the neck and chin of owl-folk, and their presence, absence, or arrangement serves as a visible marker of social status, age, and personal identity among the owl-folk of Velikoye.
Every owl-folk develops wattles by the time they reach maturity, typically between their seventeenth and twentieth year, though the exact timing varies by individual.

Wattles grow in a variety of colors and patterns that often echo the overall plumage of the individual owl-folk, though some exhibit striking contrasts — a snowy-white owl may develop russet or deep brown wattles, and vice versa.

Among the owl-folk of Velikoye, the length and fullness of one's wattles are commonly used as informal indicators of age and experience, with elder district officials and members of the Nocturnal Duma often displaying particularly voluminous wattles.

It is customary for owl-folk to groom and arrange their wattles with care, and the use of specially formulated feather balms — made from rendered tallow and aromatic herbs — is a widespread daily practice, particularly before attending public gatherings or market events.

Wattles are considered an intimate part of personal appearance, and it is regarded as a grave social transgression to touch or interfere with another owl-folk's wattles without explicit permission, comparable in seriousness to certain violations of physical privacy among pre-Turning humans.

The district elder of Saint Illarion's Quarter, who traditionally opens the winter markets each year, is expected to present immaculately maintained wattles as part of the ceremony, serving as a visible symbol of the quarter's order and prosperity.
facts.repeat_of: By tradition, the winter markets are opened each year on the first night of the Frost Moon by the district elder of Saint Illarion's Quarter, who rings a bell of silvered iron from a high balcony to signal that the stalls may begin trading.

facts.text: Some owl-folk take pride in cultivating unusually elaborate wattles through selective grooming techniques passed down within family lines, and particularly striking wattle arrangements have become a form of sartorial self-expression, akin to the wearing of fine clothing in pre-Turning human society.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon includes a brief study of wattle biology and cultural significance in its curriculum on avian physiology, though the subject remains a minor component of the broader academic programme.

Owl-folk who have recently undergone significant life changes — the death of a close relative, a marriage, the birth of offspring — sometimes allow their wattles to grow untrimmed for a period, as a visible expression of grief or transition, a practice known colloquially as 'wearing the rough down.'

Merchants in Velikoye's winter markets sell specialized combs and oils designed for wattle maintenance, and the trade in premium wattle-care products has become a modest but steady commercial niche within the capital's economy.

versions.name: Wattles

facts.text: The wattle custom of Velikoye's owl-folk is the practice of adorning oneself with plaited braids of soft, dyed feathers woven into the breast and neck plumage, typically performed before important social gatherings, seasonal festivals, and the opening of the winter markets.

Wattles are crafted from the breast feathers of the wearer, carefully separated from the body plumage, washed in warm water scented with juniper oil, and then braided together with supplementary feathers dyed in colors that carry symbolic meaning.

The colors used in wattle-braiding follow a traditional code: white signifies purity and new beginnings; deep blue represents wisdom and age; gold denotes prosperity and hospitality; and red, rarely used, marks mourning or solemn oath-taking.

Skilled wattle-weavers, known as okraschivateli, operate small workshops in the merchant quarter near the east bank dockyards, where they prepare braids for clients who sit on low perches while the work is done.

The wattle custom arose in the months immediately following the Turning of 998, as the newly transformed owl-folk sought ways to maintain social rituals that had previously relied on clothing and personal adornment no longer applicable to their changed bodies.

By the winter market season of 999, the practice had become so widespread that the district elder of Saint Illarion's Quarter formally acknowledged it by incorporating a wattle-wearing ceremony into the Frost Moon opening rituals.
facts.repeat_of: By tradition, the winter markets are opened each year on the first night of the Frost Moon by the district elder of Saint Illarion's Quarter, who rings a bell of silvered iron from a high balcony to signal that the stalls may begin trading.

facts.text: Wattles are worn across the upper chest and along the sides of the neck, secured with fine sinew threads that loop through the remaining breast feathers, and they are meant to be removed and replaced for each occasion rather than worn permanently.

The complexity of a wattle arrangement reflects the wearer's status and the formality of the event: simple single-braid wattles suffice for casual evening outings, while elaborate multi-stranded wattles with gold and blue threads are reserved for sessions of the Nocturnal Duma and the Tsar's court.

Among the owl-folk, a freshly wattled individual is considered especially striking, and it is customary for onlookers to offer a soft trill of approval — a low, vibrating call produced by vibrating the throat feathers — when admiring someone's craftsmanship.

The wattle custom has been absorbed into the liturgical practices of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light, which uses white wattles for clergy during midnight vigils and blue-black wattles for funeral processions along the Kolyma's east bank.
Young owl-folk typically receive their first wattles from a parent or guardian on the eve of their first winter market, marking their full participation in the social life of Velikoye.

elsewhere.text: The wattle custom is one of the defining social practices that emerged in Velikoye during the rebuilding period following the Turning of 998, alongside the development of the Feather Language and the adaptation of the Great Spiral for nocturnal governance.

The wattle custom reflects the owl-folk's deep investment in personal appearance and social signaling, channeling the former human practice of clothing and jewelry into a form compatible with their transformed physiology.

Members of the Nocturnal Duma wear elaborate multi-stranded wattles in deep blue and gold during formal sessions held beneath the vaulted pavilion of dark timber and silvered iron at the heart of Velikoye.

versions.name: Anastasiya Koroleva

facts.text: She was born in the year 958 in the mountain city of Stennik to a family of stonecutters who carved decorative runes for the local temple of Vekha.
She entered the Order of the Talon-Scribe at age seventeen, training at the Chapter House of Vekha, where she distinguished herself in the reconstruction of damaged rune inscriptions.

Her hand is extraordinarily steady, and she can inscribe runes with a precision that most scribes achieve only after decades of practice, earning her the unofficial title of 'the Sure Hand' among her peers.
She is lean and weathered, with deep-set grey eyes and a face lined by decades of squinting over parchment and stone in dimly lit vaults.
Her dark hair, once black, has gone iron-grey and she keeps it pulled back tightly under her scribe's cowl, though a few stubborn strands escape near her temples.
She speaks with a clipped, deliberate cadence, choosing her words as carefully as she chooses the strokes of her stylus, and she has a dry, understated wit that catches people off guard.

She is deeply disciplined and fiercely protective of knowledge, but she carries a quiet restlessness — a sense that the Order's current orthodoxy has made the runes safer while draining them of something vital.
She was briefly mentored by the late Grand Scribe Alaric Vostov in his final years and inherited his private notes on pre-Fire rune variants, which she has studied in secret for over a decade.
She is well-regarded by Ataman Sable Korven, who values her expertise in paleographic reconstruction, though he does not know the full extent of her private work.
She rose to the position of Chief Scribe in the year 995, responsible for overseeing the transcription and verification of all rune texts entered into the Great Vaults beneath Khorov.

In a hidden workshop beneath her quarters, she carves runes using techniques and glyphs drawn from fragments predating the Great Fire of 742, runes that the Order officially considers corrupted or apocryphal.

exceptions.text: She privately disputes the Order's official position that all pre-Fire rune fragments are unreliable, and she continues to study and carve glyphs the Order has declared obsolete.

elsewhere.text: Sable Korven relies on Anastasiya's expertise in paleographic reconstruction for several key restoration projects in the Great Vaults, and he considers her one of the Order's most valuable scholars.

elsewhere.text: Anastasiya has sworn the Oath of the Unbroken Line and takes it seriously, but she believes that faithfully transmitting the runes also means preserving every surviving fragment, even those the Order has chosen to exclude from the standardized canon.

Beneath the Ataman's Citadel in Khorov, the Great Vaults stretch deep into the bedrock of Greymount, a labyrinth of stone chambers where the Order stores its most precious rune-inscribed texts, sealed behind iron doors and warded by standing glyphs.

She is considered the finest living carver of Frostward Runes, capable of inscribing runes on stone so precisely that they glow faintly in winter air.

She was once close to Maren Duska, a fellow scribe who died during the Border Wars of 987, and she has never fully spoken about the loss.

versions.name: Vasha Dorin

facts.text: Vasha is lean and wiry, standing barely five feet tall with sun-darkened skin and close-cropped black hair that she keeps shorn to her scalp in the military fashion she learned from her father, a border infantryman.
Her left ear bears the Order's talon-shaped iron stylus, its curved blade catching the light whenever she tilts her head, though she still flinches when it brushes the cartilage.

Her grey-and-ochre robes are perpetually travel-worn, the ochre band along her sleeves frayed to near-white threads, and she has taken to rolling the hem above her ankles to keep from tripping on muddy roads.
Vasha is restless and sharp-tongued, quick to judge strangers but slow to hold grudges, and she has a habit of drumming her fingers against hard surfaces as if counting something only she can hear.

She carries a deep, quiet guilt over the death of her father during the Border Wars, which she believes she could have prevented if she had arrived at the frontier garrison one day sooner with a dispatch that was ultimately delayed by a snowstorm.

Born in 978 to a soldier and a seamstress in the border town of Verkhov, Vasha grew up in a household where her father taught her to read Tsardom runes from carved wooden blocks and her mother taught her to mend torn leather.

She entered the Order of the Talon-Scribe at age sixteen after the local chapter house in Verkhov accepted her as an apprentice scribe, drawn by her rapid and accurate hand and her ability to memorize entire documents after a single reading.

Vasha is an exceptional runner and navigator, able to find her way across unfamiliar terrain using landmarks and the subtle directional clues embedded in rune-carved waystones along the Tsardom's trade roads.

She can inscribe basic runes with speed and clarity, though her paleographic mastery remains limited to the First and Second Circles; she struggles with the archaic Third Circle glyphs used in diplomatic correspondence.

Vasha maintains a tense but respectful working relationship with Senior Scribe Anastasiya Koroleva, who oversees her assignments from the Ataman's Citadel and has noted her potential while finding her temperament difficult.

She is close to a fellow courier named Yurii Malenkov, a broad-shouldered man from the southern steppe towns who shares her sense of humor and covers the eastern route from Khorov to the chapter house of Lethka.

facts.text: Born in 978 in the river town of Mylino to a fisherman father and a mother who worked as a scribe's assistant at the local chapter house, Vasha grew up handling ink and parchment before she could read.

She can inscribe the First Circle of the Tsardom's runes in under four minutes using her talon-stylus, a speed that places her in the upper tier of field scribes.

She has an exceptional memory for routes and geography, able to navigate between any two of the twelve chapter houses without a map, a skill she maintains through meticulous mental mapping during every journey.
She reports to Field Scribe Maren Duska, a veteran of the Border Wars who oversees courier operations out of Chapter House Lethka.
She speaks in short, precise sentences and avoids embellishment, though she occasionally drops a folk expression from her Mylino upbringing when startled or irritated.

local.name: Chief Scribe Elara Voss
facts: A tall, sharp-featured woman in her mid-forties with silver-streaked brown hair pulled into a severe braid, Elara Voss has served as Chief Scribe of the Academy of the Chiseled Moon for six years. She is known for her exacting standards and her quiet, almost predatory patience when evaluating a scribe's work.

She wears the grey-and-ochre robes of a senior member of the Order, her talon-stylus suspended from her left ear, and keeps a leather-bound journal in which she records every student's progress — and every failure.

extras.name: Academy students
facts: A dozen or so young scribes in plain grey robes move between halls, some practicing rune-carving on limestone slabs, others seated in alcoves reading from reference texts. A few glance up as Vasha enters, noting the talon-stylus on her ear — she is clearly not a student.

setup.goal: Vasha must deliver a sealed letter to the Chief Scribe and determine whether its contents warrant urgency or routine filing.
setup.intro: The morning light catches the iron blade of Vasha's talon-stylus as she pushes through the wide arched entrance of the Academy, stepping from the hilltop's cool wind into the warm, chalk-scented air of the corridor beyond. Students at nearby workbenches look up from their carving — a few with curiosity, one with open suspicion — before returning to the shallow grooves they are cutting into soft limestone. The crescent halls stretch in both directions, their grey fieldstone walls lined with deep-set windows that admit pale beams of sunlight. Somewhere deeper in the building, a voice is reciting from a text in the archaic cadence of the Third Circle, the syllables echoing off stone. Vasha rolls her shoulders, adjusts the leather satchel slung across her chest, and drums her fingers once against the doorframe — a quick, restless tattoo. The letter inside the satchel is sealed with black wax and the angular imprint of Senior Scribe Koroleva's signet. It arrived at the Verkhov chapter house three days ago, marked for the Chief Scribe here at the Chiseled Moon, and the seal has not been broken. But the way Anastasiya had looked at her when handing it over — that measured, calculating look — had told Vasha there was more to this letter than a simple request.
