In narration and dialogue, call things by their everyday names: where a name is followed by "usually called ...", use that name, and keep the full name for formal moments.
Goal: Vasha must deliver a sealed letter to the Chief Scribe and determine whether its contents warrant urgency or routine filing.
Place: Academy of the Chiseled Moon (usually called Chiseled Moon)
- The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a prestigious institution of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, located in the capital city of Velikoye.
- It occupies a converted timber-and-stone complex on the upper terraces of Velikoye's central hill, overlooking the Great Spiral and the Kolyma River to the east.
- The building is a broad, low structure of grey fieldstone with a reinforced slate roof designed to support the weight of roosting owl-folk, featuring wide arched windows that allow aerial entry into the lecture halls.
- Above the main entrance, carved in deep relief into a moon-shaped lintel of pale marble, is the image of a chiseled rune — the rune of the Academy's namesake — surrounded by a border of interlocking talon-motifs.
- The Academy is operated under the authority of the Quill of Teaching, one of the three divisions of the Order of the Talon-Scribe.
- It serves as the primary training facility in Velikoye for new scribes and apprentices, teaching them the theory and practice of the Tsardom's runic script.
- Students at the Academy learn to inscribe runes on stone, wood, and parchment using iron talon-styli, and study the philosophical underpinnings of the runic tradition as articulated by Grand Scribe Alaric Vostov.
- The curriculum includes courses in rune grammar, inscription techniques, the history of the Order, and the Oath of the Unbroken Line, which all graduates must swear before receiving their grey-and-ochre robes and talon-styli.
- Instruction takes place in a series of interconnected halls arranged in a crescent shape around an open courtyard, where students practice carving runes on slabs of soft limestone set into workbenches built at talon-gripping height.
- The Academy also houses a small library of reference texts and a scriptorium where advanced students produce inscribed copies of important documents for the Quill of Memory.
- As one of the three major academies in Velikoye, the Chiseled Moon plays a vital role in training the next generation of Talon-Scribes for service across the Tsardom of Moscavia.
- The current head of the Academy answers to the Quill of Teaching's senior administrator, who reports in turn to Ataman Sable Korven in Khorov.
- The Academy maintains a department dedicated to the study of Plumage Signaling, where students learn to decode the feather-language of historical figures by studying preserved plumage samples and contemporaneous accounts written by human-era observers who witnessed the early days of the custom's development.

What this scene touches: keep what these say true, and bring it in only where the scene calls for it.
Velikoye (capital)
- Velikoye is the capital of the Tsardom of Moscavia, a sprawling city of stone and timber nestled in the broad valley of the Kolyma River, where the river bends southward before emptying into the Pale Sea.
- Before the Turning, Velikoye was a major human city known as Velikigrad, the seat of the Rurikovich dynasty since the mid-ninth century.
- The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is one of three major academies operating in the capital, alongside institutions of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light and the Taloned Host's First Aerial Squadron.
- Since the Turning of 998, Velikoye's architecture has been thoroughly adapted for owl-folk habitation: buildings feature high perch-walls with handholds and ledges, wide windows for aerial entry, and reinforced rooftops capable of bearing the weight of dozens of roosting birds at once.
- The heart of the city is the Great Spiral, a massive stone plaza carved into the central hill in concentric rings, where the Nocturnal Duma holds its sessions beneath a vaulted pavilion of dark timber and silvered iron.
- In 999: Ferry services operate across the river at several points within Velikoye, using flat-bottomed barges fitted with perch-decks so owl-folk passengers can rest mid-crossing.
- In 999: Moscavian fishing regulations, revised after the Turning, require all owl-folk anglers on the Khorol to obtain a nocturnal license from their district elder and observe seasonal catch limits.
- In 999: Scholars at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon have attempted to compile comprehensive grammars of the Feather Language, but the custom's inherent fluidity and the influence of individual plumage patterns make standardization difficult, and no single authoritative text has been accepted.

Runic Magic of the Tsardom (lore, usually called Frostward Runes)
- Runic magic is the art of carving ancient glyphs into stone to bind and direct the forces of frost and wind.
- Practitioners are called Frostwardens, and they are trained at the Monastery of the Pale Wind in the city of Khol'sk.
- The runes draw their power from the Vostrik Mountains, where the cold is so deep it is said to have memory.
- The runes themselves are not written in any spoken language but in the Oldstone Script, which predates the Tsardom by centuries.
- Runic magic cannot be performed in southern climes beyond the River Donova, where the earth is too warm to hold the carvings' charge.
- In 842: The Tsardom's northern border along the Shelfsea is defended by the Great Rune Wall, a chain of carved monoliths stretching over two hundred miles.
- In 975: She entered the Order of the Talon-Scribe at age seventeen, training at the Chapter House of Vekha, where she distinguished herself in the reconstruction of damaged rune inscriptions.
- In 995: She rose to the position of Chief Scribe in the year 995, responsible for overseeing the transcription and verification of all rune texts entered into the Great Vaults beneath Khorov.

Tsardom of Moscavia (nation, usually called Moscavia)
- The Tsardom of Moscavia is a sprawling northern realm stretching across the forests and river valleys between the Ash Mountains to the west and the frozen shores of the Pale Sea to the north.
- Before the Turning, Moscavia was a powerful human kingdom ruled by the Rurikovich dynasty, with a long history of warfare, trade, and cultural exchange along the northern routes.
- The Khorol and the Kolyma system are central to Moscavia's economy, connecting its interior provinces to the Ash Mountain trade routes and the Pale Sea ports.
- The Tsardom's government operates on a nocturnal schedule, with the Nocturnal Duma conducting all official business between dusk and dawn.
- In 1000: In the year 1000, Moscavia stands as a prosperous and stable realm, its transformation now a generation old, with a new culture that blends human memory with avian instinct.
- In 1000: The regiment enjoys a reputation among the civilian population of Moscavia as both fearsome warriors and quiet guardians; folk songs from the interior provinces often feature the Frosted Wing as protectors who appear in blizzards to shield villages from raiders, vanishing before dawn.
- In 1000: The Host maintains a standing strength of approximately 40,000 soldiers across its aerial, ground, and naval branches, supplemented by militia levies from the provincial towns and river settlements along the Khorol and Kolyma systems.

The Order of the Talon-Scribe (institution, usually called Talon-Scribes)
- The Order of the Talon-Scribe is the supreme institution responsible for the study, transcription, preservation, and teaching of the runic script known as the Tsardom's runes.
- In 742: The Talon-Scribes hold that the Tsardom's runes are not merely a writing system but a living language of the land itself, that each rune carries a fragment of the world's enduring truth, and that to inscribe a rune is to participate in the ongoing creation of reality.
- In 814: The Order has survived civil wars, foreign invasions, and schisms over the centuries. The most famous crisis was the Rune Famine of 814, when a plague killed half the Order's membership and forced the then-Ataman, Maren Duska, to open apprenticeship to women for the first time, dramatically expanding the Order's capacity.
- In 996: As of the year 1000, the Ataman of the Quill is Sable Korven, a former Field Scribe who distinguished herself during the Border Wars of 987 by inscribing the Treaty of Frostmere in real time as both armies stood down, an act considered one of the most heroic feats in the Order's history.

[end of world]

roles.role: courier of the Quill of the Field

turns.direction: Vasha is shown inside and led through the Academy toward the Chief Scribe's office; show what he sees and who he passes.

runs.output:
Vasha follows the corridor past a row of practice halls, where the rhythmic scratch of iron on stone rises and falls like breathing. A group of first-year apprentices huddle around a workbench near the wall, their limestone slabs already scored with a few wobbly attempts at the Rune of Gathering. One of them — barely old enough to have finished fledging, with down still visible at the joints of both wings — glances up at Vasha's satchel and goes wide-eyed before being pulled back to his work by a sharp word from the student beside him.

The hallway turns, and the quality of the light changes. Here, the windows face east, toward the Kolyma, and the morning sun cuts through at a low angle, throwing long rectangles of gold across the floor. Vasha's footsteps echo in a way that says the corridor is older than the rest — the stonework is tighter, the mortar darker with age, and the ceiling vaults higher than the reinforced slate roofs she's been passing beneath. A carved notice board on the left displays several parchments pinned under clips shaped like curved talons: class schedules, a reminder about the upcoming examination on Third Circle inscriptions, and a flyer advertising a public lecture on the Plumage Studies of Grand Scribe Volkov. Vasha slows to read the last one. Volkov's name she knows — his work on the Feather Language of the early Tsars is considered foundational, though she's heard whispers that newer scholars find his classifications too rigid.

At the end of the passage, a door stands slightly ajar, warm amber light spilling from within. Above it, a small brass plate reads CHIEF SCRIBE in blocky Tsardom script. Vasha can hear the scrape of a stylus on vellum from inside, steady and unhurried, the sound of someone who has all the time in the world. She pushes the door open. The office is cluttered in a way that suggests not neglect but deliberate accumulation — shelves lined with bound volumes and loose stacks of parchment, a wide desk dominated by a reading lamp whose flame gutters faintly in some draft she can't identify. Behind the desk sits a broad-shouldered man with a close-cropped beard going grey at the chin, wearing the grey-and-ochre robes of a senior Talon-Scribe.

The corridor branches ahead, and Vasha turns left, following the faint sound of shuffling papers and the occasional creak of a heavy drawer. A young apprentice — barely more than a fledgling by the scuffed condition of his robes and the unsteady way he grips his talon-stylus — freezes mid-groove when he sees her, then quickly averts his eyes to his workbench as if he's been caught at something. She doesn't blame him. Outsiders aren't common here, and the grey-and-ochre robes she wears mark her as a member of a different chapter house, which makes her neither student nor teacher — an uncomfortable in-between.

She passes through an archway into the open courtyard, where the morning air is noticeably cooler and carries the mineral tang of limestone dust. A dozen students practice at their workbenches in the open air, their talon-styli clicking against stone in a rhythm that almost sounds like breathing. One woman near the far wall is carving with unusual speed, her feathers ruffled in concentration, each stroke precise and deliberate. The courtyard's crescent shape funnels the sound forward, so that Vasha can hear every tap and scrape as she crosses.

Ahead, on the far side of the courtyard, a narrow staircase ascends the inner wall — the kind built with wide, shallow steps and deep handholds, designed for taloned feet. A wooden sign nailed to the wall beside the stairs reads CHIEF SCRIBE'S OFFICE — THIRD LANDING in both standard script and the older angular forms of the First Circle. Beneath it, someone has scratched a smaller note in informal hand: Knock twice. He's deaf on the left side.

Vasha climbs, her talons finding the handholds with practiced ease, and arrives on the third landing to find a heavy oak door, slightly ajar, with warm candlelight spilling through the gap. She can hear the scratching of a quill inside — or perhaps a stylus on slate — steady and unhurried. She raps her knuckles against the doorframe twice, then waits.

turns.direction: The Chief Scribe breaks the seal and reads the letter in front of Vasha; it concerns a rune-stone on the Khorol, and she tells him what it means.

runs.output:
The man behind the desk looks up as the door swings inward, his stylus pausing mid-stroke on whatever document he'd been working through. He's older than she expected — the Chief Scribe of the Chiseled Moon, yet he carries himself with the quiet ease of someone who learned long ago that the weight of a title doesn't need to be performed. His eyes, dark and sharp beneath a heavy brow, travel from Vasha's face to the satchel at her chest.

"You must be the courier from Verkhov," he says, setting his stylus down with a deliberate click against the edge of his desk. He gestures to the chair across from him — a sturdy thing of carved oak, its armrests worn smooth by generations of visitors. "Sit. That satchel of yours has been looking at me like it's carrying something important, and I'd rather not guess."

Vasha settles into the chair and reaches into the satchel, pulling out the sealed letter. The black wax is still intact, still bearing the angular press of Koroleva's signet — a talon flanked by two vertical bars, the mark of the Verkhov chapter house. She places it on the desk between them. The Chief Scribe picks it up, turns it once in his broad hands, then breaks the seal with his thumbnail. He unfurls the vellum and reads, his expression shifting almost imperceptibly — the faintest narrowing of his eyes, a slight forward lean of his shoulders — as though the words on the page are pulling him in. When he finishes, he sets the letter flat on the desk and reads it a second time, slower.

"The Khorol rune-stone," he says at last, looking up at Vasha. "The one at the old crossing below Staroye. Someone's been tampering with it." He taps the vellum with one finger. "Koroleva's field team found the inscriptions degraded — not worn, degraded, as if someone tried to alter the binding without understanding what they were unraveling. The Rune of Tethering has been partially overwritten with something that doesn't match any recognized script." He leans back, rubbing the grey at his chin. "That's the rune-stone that holds the frost-ward along the lower Khorol valley."

The Chief Scribe — his nameplate on the desk reads Dmitri Yefimov — looks up from his work as Vasha enters, and his stylus pauses mid-stroke. His eyes move immediately to the satchel, then to her face, then back to the satchel. He sets the stylus down with care, aligns it parallel to the edge of his desk, and leans back in his chair.

"You have a letter for me, I take it." It isn't a question. He extends one thick hand across the desk, palm up, fingers slightly curled. Vasha unclasps the satchel and withdraws the sealed parchment — the black wax still smooth, still bearing Koroleva's sharp-edged signet. Yefimov takes it between two fingers, holds it up to the lamplight for a moment as if checking the seal for any sign of tampering, then brings a small knife from his desk set to the wax. The blade catches the light, and the seal cracks cleanly, splitting along its natural grain.

He unfurls the letter and reads. His eyes move steadily across the lines, but there's a subtle change in his posture — the way a talon-tip might twitch involuntarily. By the second paragraph, his brow furrows. He reads the third paragraph a second time, slower, his lips barely moving. When he finishes, he folds the letter deliberately along its original creases and sets it face-down on the desk, his hand resting on it for a moment as if to keep it from disappearing.

"The Khorol rune-stone at Verkhov," he says, and his voice carries the particular gravity of a man who has just learned something he wasn't expecting to learn this morning. "Koroleva's survey team found it during their seasonal inspection of the river markers — a stone that shouldn't exist, inscribed with a rune variant that doesn't match any entry in the Third Circle canon or any of the regional supplements." He meets Vasha's eyes. "She's asking me to cross-reference it against the Chiseled Moon's working archive and determine whether it's an ancient inscription that's been overlooked, or something... newer." He lets that word hang in the air between them, heavy with implication. "Either way, if it's genuine, it changes things."

## Task
Write the description entry of a reference profile for Owl-folk, a species in a story world.

Who the species is (for consistency only; do NOT describe these here):
- Named Owl-folk.

Facts for this entry:
- Every living person in the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk overnight by a single, unexplained event on an unremarkable autumn morning in the year 998.
- No one knows who or what caused the transformation, and the Tsardom's scholars have spent the years since searching for an answer in old texts, divine revelation, and natural philosophy.
- An owl-folk is a bipedal humanoid roughly five to seven feet tall, with a broad, rounded body covered in soft plumage that ranges from tawny golds and greys to deep browns and snowy whites.
- Their heads are large relative to their bodies, with prominent forward-facing eyes that grant them extraordinary night vision, and a pair of feathered tufts or 'ears' atop their heads that are not true ears but serve as expressive indicators of mood.
- They possess wide, powerful wings capable of sustained flight, with a wingspan of eight to twelve feet, and their feet end in strong taloned digits suited for gripping branches and perches.
- Their faces retain a distinctly avian quality — hooked but not overly sharp beaks, and large luminous eyes that come in shades of amber, pale green, and deep black — but they also express unmistakable human emotions.
- Owl-folk are overwhelmingly nocturnal by nature; they feel most alert and comfortable in darkness and tend to become drowsy and irritable during daylight hours.
- They possess an innate ability to fly, and most owl-folk can take to the skies within moments of being born, though their flight becomes more controlled and skilled with age and practice.
- They are predatory hunters by instinct, with sharp eyesight and silent movement, though this instinct is tempered by the civilized upbringing of the former human population.
- Plumage coloration varies widely among individuals, and it is considered a matter of personal identity — an owl-folk's feathers are as distinctive to them as a human's face.
- Some owl-folk retain traces of their former human appearance in their facial features — a strong jawline, a particular arrangement of feathers suggesting freckles or scars — leading to a widespread belief that one's past self is not entirely gone.
- The Tsardom of Moscavia continues to function as a political entity under the transformed population, with its cities, roads, and institutions adapted for winged, nocturnal citizens.

Rules:
- This is a reference entry like a character sheet or encyclopedia, NOT a scene.
- Present tense, third person. State what is true; do not narrate a moment.
- No setting, no actions happening right now, no dialogue, no other characters.
- Use only the facts; keep their specific wording where natural; invent nothing new.
- One paragraph, at most about 90 words.

Standing roughly five to seven feet tall, they possess broad, rounded bodies covered in soft plumage of varying colors, prominent forward-facing eyes, and feathered tufts atop their heads. Their wings span eight to twelve feet, enabling sustained flight. Despite their avian nature, owl-folk retain distinctly human emotional expressions and, in some cases, subtle traces of their former human appearance. They are predominantly nocturnal, predatory by instinct but civilized in behavior. The Tsardom continues to function as a political entity under their governance.

## Scene

The morning light catches the iron blade of Vasha's talon-stylus as she pushes through the wide arched entrance of the Academy, stepping from the hilltop's cool wind into the warm, chalk-scented air of the corridor beyond. Students at nearby workbenches look up from their carving — a few with curiosity, one with open suspicion — before returning to the shallow grooves they are cutting into soft limestone. The crescent halls stretch in both directions, their grey fieldstone walls lined with deep-set windows that admit pale beams of sunlight. Somewhere deeper in the building, a voice is reciting from a text in the archaic cadence of the Third Circle, the syllables echoing off stone. Vasha rolls her shoulders, adjusts the leather satchel slung across her chest, and drums her fingers once against the doorframe — a quick, restless tattoo. The letter inside the satchel is sealed with black wax and the angular imprint of Senior Scribe Koroleva's signet. It arrived at the Verkhov chapter house three days ago, marked for the Chief Scribe here at the Chiseled Moon, and the seal has not been broken. But the way Anastasiya had looked at her when handing it over — that measured, calculating look — had told Vasha there was more to this letter than a simple request.
Vasha follows the corridor past a row of practice halls, where the rhythmic scratch of iron on stone rises and falls like breathing. A group of first-year apprentices huddle around a workbench near the wall, their limestone slabs already scored with a few wobbly attempts at the Rune of Gathering. One of them — barely old enough to have finished fledging, with down still visible at the joints of both wings — glances up at Vasha's satchel and goes wide-eyed before being pulled back to his work by a sharp word from the student beside him.

The hallway turns, and the quality of the light changes. Here, the windows face east, toward the Kolyma, and the morning sun cuts through at a low angle, throwing long rectangles of gold across the floor. Vasha's footsteps echo in a way that says the corridor is older than the rest — the stonework is tighter, the mortar darker with age, and the ceiling vaults higher than the reinforced slate roofs she's been passing beneath. A carved notice board on the left displays several parchments pinned under clips shaped like curved talons: class schedules, a reminder about the upcoming examination on Third Circle inscriptions, and a flyer advertising a public lecture on the Plumage Studies of Grand Scribe Volkov. Vasha slows to read the last one. Volkov's name she knows — his work on the Feather Language of the early Tsars is considered foundational, though she's heard whispers that newer scholars find his classifications too rigid.

At the end of the passage, a door stands slightly ajar, warm amber light spilling from within. Above it, a small brass plate reads CHIEF SCRIBE in blocky Tsardom script. Vasha can hear the scrape of a stylus on vellum from inside, steady and unhurried, the sound of someone who has all the time in the world. She pushes the door open. The office is cluttered in a way that suggests not neglect but deliberate accumulation — shelves lined with bound volumes and loose stacks of parchment, a wide desk dominated by a reading lamp whose flame gutters faintly in some draft she can't identify. Behind the desk sits a broad-shouldered man with a close-cropped beard going grey at the chin, wearing the grey-and-ochre robes of a senior Talon-Scribe.

Each soldier of the White Talon carries a tower shield of lacquered ashwood, reinforced with iron bands and painted in the regiment's colors of white and pale blue.
The regiment is divided into four companies: Dawnclaw, Midwinter, Ironbeak, and Palefang.
The White Talon has never been routed in open battle since its founding in 784, a record that has earned it the title 'Unbroken.'
The White Talon is the heaviest and most elite heavy infantry regiment of the Frostwing Host, the standing army of the Kingdom of Aelthar.

New soldiers who complete the Frost March are formally inducted in a ceremony called the Binding, where they swear an oath on a blade drawn from the Frostwing Host's founding sword, Oathkeeper.
The regiment takes its name from the Aelthari phrase 'Gorath Vaelin,' meaning 'White Talon,' which was the war cry of its founding commander, General Maren Frostveil.

facts.text: Archers of the Frosted Wing carry recurved longbows of ashwood and yew, tipped with obsidian arrowheads that do not shatter in the extreme cold, capable of striking targets at ranges exceeding four hundred paces.

Members of the Frosted Wing develop a distinctive gait when grounded — a wide, deliberate stance with talons sunk deep into packed snow — to resist the treacherous crosswinds that sweep across the glacier.
Every soldier in the regiment is an owl-folk archer, selected for exceptional eyesight, wing strength, and marksmanship in the punishing conditions near the Pale Sea.
The regiment takes its name from the thick rime of frost that coats the plumage of its members during winter patrols, giving them a glittering, spectral appearance against the snow.

Frosted Wing soldiers train extensively in nocturnal combat, leveraging their superior night vision and silent flight to ambush and harass enemies in darkness, before melting back into the frozen landscape.

Each archer is equipped with a hooded lantern strapped to the left wrist, its dim blue light used for signaling between squad members during blizzard conditions when visual communication is impossible.
The Frosted Wing is an elite regiment of the Taloned Host, the military arm of the Tsardom of Moscavia, stationed at the glacier edge of the northern frontier.
The regiment's standard is a pennant of deep indigo silk bearing a white owl in flight against a crescent moon, sewn with silver thread that glints in moonlight.

The regiment was formed in the year 999 under the command of Colonel Maren Snezhanka to defend the northern glacier passes against raids by the Frostborn skirmishers, who had begun probing the Tsardom's borders for resources and slaves.

The Frosted Wing operates from a network of stone watchtowers built into the cliff faces above the ice, each tower heated by braziers of slow-burning peat and stocked with dried rations and arrow caches.
Recruits must pass the Trial of the Howling Wind, spending three nights exposed on the glacier's edge without shelter while maintaining a patrol route, before being admitted to the regiment.

The regiment enjoys a reputation among the civilian population of Moscavia as both fearsome warriors and quiet guardians; folk songs from the interior provinces often feature the Frosted Wing as protectors who appear in blizzards to shield villages from raiders, vanishing before dawn.

Among its most decorated regiments is the Frosted Wing, an elite arctic formation stationed at the northern glacier edge, tasked with defending the Pale Sea coast and monitoring the movements of the Frostborn raiders beyond it.

Its aerial squadrons are its most prestigious arm, comprising highly trained owl-folk fliers who carry light lances and talon-bolts into battle, striking from above with devastating speed and precision.

Ground infantry regiments are equipped with talon-gripping gauntlets and armored boots that allow owl-folk soldiers to scale walls, dig into frozen earth, and engage in close-quarters combat with both natural talons and steel-edged weapons.
Recruitment into the Host is mandatory for all able-bodied owl-folk citizens between the ages of eighteen and twenty, though volunteers and career soldiers form the backbone of the elite regiments.

Training emphasizes both the avian instincts inherited from the Turning — night vision, silent flight, acute hearing — and the disciplined use of Moscavia's refined military arts, including siege engineering, naval tactics, and coordinated aerial warfare.

The Host operates under the direct authority of the Tsar and is administered by the Nocturnal Duma's Military Committee, a standing sub-council of three senior officials who oversee recruitment, provisioning, and deployment.

The Host's navy sails from Pale Sea ports and along the frozen waterways of the north, with high perch-decks built atop each vessel so that owl-folk officers can take flight to survey the ice, coordinate fleet movements, and engage enemy scouts at altitude.

Its name derives from the frost-white plumage and ice-hardened talons that characterize the owl-folk soldiers who serve within it, evoking both the transformed nature of Moscavian citizens and the harsh northern climate they defend.

Its headquarters are co-located with the Tsar's palace in Velikoye, where the General Staff maintains a vast hall of war-tables, aerial maps, and ice-glass scrying instruments for tracking enemy movements across the northern frontier.
The White Talon is the Host's heaviest and most elite heavy infantry regiment, serving as the Tsar's personal guard and the final line of defense in any siege or pitched battle.
The Frostwing Host is the standing army of the Tsardom of Moscavia, established in the years following the Turning of 998 to defend the realm and project its power across the northern lands.

The Host maintains a standing strength of approximately 40,000 soldiers across its aerial, ground, and naval branches, supplemented by militia levies from the provincial towns and river settlements along the Khorol and Kolyma systems.
Its seat is the Ataman's Citadel in the capital city of Khorov, a fortress-monastery built into the southern face of the Greymount, overlooking the Dneva River and the Tsardom's central square.

Below the Ataman, the Order is divided into three divisions called Quills: the Quill of Memory, which preserves and archives all rune-inscribed texts in the Great Vaults beneath Khorov; the Quill of Teaching, which operates scriptoria and training halls across the Tsardom; and the Quill of the Field, which sends scribes to military campaigns and diplomatic missions to inscribe treaties, battle records, and oaths in the moment of their making.
The Order's motto is 'What is written endures,' and it is carved in the First Circle runes above the entrance to the Ataman's Citadel.

Each member of the Order takes the Oath of the Unbroken Line, swearing to transmit the runes faithfully without alteration, to never destroy an inscribed text without authorization, and to give their life if needed to protect the knowledge they carry.

The Order maintains twelve chapter houses across the Tsardom, each named after a rune in the First Circle of the Tsardom's script. The oldest and most prestigious is the chapter house of Vekha, named after the rune of foundation, located in the mountain city of Stennik in the Ashgrove Mountains.

The Order was founded by Grand Scribe Alaric Vostov during the reign of Tsar Dmitri II of the Volkov Dynasty, after the Great Fire of 742 destroyed most of the Tsardom's written records, forcing a centralized effort to reconstruct and standardize the rune system.

The Talon-Scribes hold that the Tsardom's runes are not merely a writing system but a living language of the land itself, that each rune carries a fragment of the world's enduring truth, and that to inscribe a rune is to participate in the ongoing creation of reality.
Talon-Scribes are identifiable by their grey-and-ochre robes and the talon-shaped iron stylus they wear suspended from their left ear, used for inscribing runes on stone, wood, and parchment.
The Order of the Talon-Scribe is the supreme institution responsible for the study, transcription, preservation, and teaching of the runic script known as the Tsardom's runes.
The Order is led by the Ataman of the Quill, a title that combines the roles of spiritual head, chief scholar, and administrative leader, appointed by the Tsar from among the Order's senior members.

The Order has survived civil wars, foreign invasions, and schisms over the centuries. The most famous crisis was the Rune Famine of 814, when a plague killed half the Order's membership and forced the then-Ataman, Maren Duska, to open apprenticeship to women for the first time, dramatically expanding the Order's capacity.

As of the year 1000, the Ataman of the Quill is Sable Korven, a former Field Scribe who distinguished herself during the Border Wars of 987 by inscribing the Treaty of Frostmere in real time as both armies stood down, an act considered one of the most heroic feats in the Order's history.

facts.text: The Church's formalization of religious gestures in the Feather Language has led to the development of liturgical plumage choreography, in which clergy perform elaborate synchronized feather displays during the Northern Light services, a practice that draws on both pre-Turning Christian iconography and the newly discovered expressive potential of owl-folk plumage.

Instruction takes place in a series of interconnected halls arranged in a crescent shape around an open courtyard, where students practice carving runes on slabs of soft limestone set into workbenches built at talon-gripping height.

Students at the Academy learn to inscribe runes on stone, wood, and parchment using iron talon-styli, and study the philosophical underpinnings of the runic tradition as articulated by Grand Scribe Alaric Vostov.
As one of the three major academies in Velikoye, the Chiseled Moon plays a vital role in training the next generation of Talon-Scribes for service across the Tsardom of Moscavia.
The current head of the Academy answers to the Quill of Teaching's senior administrator, who reports in turn to Ataman Sable Korven in Khorov.

The curriculum includes courses in rune grammar, inscription techniques, the history of the Order, and the Oath of the Unbroken Line, which all graduates must swear before receiving their grey-and-ochre robes and talon-styli.
The Academy is operated under the authority of the Quill of Teaching, one of the three divisions of the Order of the Talon-Scribe.

The Academy maintains a department dedicated to the study of Plumage Signaling, where students learn to decode the feather-language of historical figures by studying preserved plumage samples and contemporaneous accounts written by human-era observers who witnessed the early days of the custom's development.
The Academy also houses a small library of reference texts and a scriptorium where advanced students produce inscribed copies of important documents for the Quill of Memory.

The building is a broad, low structure of grey fieldstone with a reinforced slate roof designed to support the weight of roosting owl-folk, featuring wide arched windows that allow aerial entry into the lecture halls.

Above the main entrance, carved in deep relief into a moon-shaped lintel of pale marble, is the image of a chiseled rune — the rune of the Academy's namesake — surrounded by a border of interlocking talon-motifs.
The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a prestigious institution of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, located in the capital city of Velikoye.
It occupies a converted timber-and-stone complex on the upper terraces of Velikoye's central hill, overlooking the Great Spiral and the Kolyma River to the east.
The Khorol River is a broad, slow-moving waterway that flows through the heart of Velikoye and the broader valley of the Tsardom of Moscavia.
In winter, the upper stretches of the Khorol freeze solid for weeks at a time, halting river trade and forcing merchants to rely on the overland trails instead.
The river's lower reaches, where it bends southward toward the Pale Sea, form part of the navigable waterway shared with the broader Kolyma River system.
Its waters are dark and murky, fed by snowmelt from the Ash Mountains and dozens of tributary streams that drain the dense northern forests.
The Khorol serves as a primary commercial artery, connecting the city's interior markets to the river trade network that links the Ash Mountains to the Pale Sea coast.
Fishing on the Khorol is a major nocturnal occupation for Velikoye's residents, with catches of sterlet, burbot, and pale-sea herring forming a staple of the city's night markets.
Before the Turning of 998, the Khorol's banks in Velikigrad were lined with human wharves and market squares that were subsequently demolished and rebuilt to owl-folk specifications.
The river's banks in Velikoye are lined with stone embankments and timber dockyards, adapted since the Turning to accommodate owl-folk fishermen and merchants who work the waterways at night.
Moscavian fishing regulations, revised after the Turning, require all owl-folk anglers on the Khorol to obtain a nocturnal license from their district elder and observe seasonal catch limits.
Ferry services operate across the river at several points within Velikoye, using flat-bottomed barges fitted with perch-decks so owl-folk passengers can rest mid-crossing.

Among the most prized wares at the winter markets are pelts — ermine, wolverine, and snow leopard — brought south from the Ash Mountains along the overland trails and traded by merchants who arrive with caravans of laden ravens and hawks.

Velikoye's winter markets operate under canvas awnings stretched between the upper perch-walls of the merchant quarter on the river's east bank, where vendors sell dried fish and salted river crayfish from the Kolyma alongside smoked meats and root vegetables preserved through the frost months.

The heart of the city is the Great Spiral, a massive stone plaza carved into the central hill in concentric rings, where the Nocturnal Duma holds its sessions beneath a vaulted pavilion of dark timber and silvered iron.

By tradition, the winter markets are opened each year on the first night of the Frost Moon by the district elder of Saint Illarion's Quarter, who rings a bell of silvered iron from a high balcony to signal that the stalls may begin trading.

The city suffered significant damage during the weeks immediately following the Turning of 998 as its human infrastructure was hastily converted for avian use, but by the year 999 a comprehensive rebuilding programme had restored and improved it.

Velikoye's building codes, revised in 999, mandate that all new construction include flight corridors, perch-decks, and talon-gripping surfaces as standard features, and that no structure may exceed a height of one hundred and twenty feet to preserve safety during aerial travel.
The city is divided into twelve administrative districts, each named after a pre-Turning human saint and governed by a district elder appointed by the Tsar.
The city is built on a series of low, terraced hills that rise gently from the river's east bank, connected by wide stairways and sloping streets that accommodate both flight and ground travel.
The Grand Owl Hall in the Tsar's Palace serves as the meeting chamber for the Nocturnal Duma.
By night — when the owl-folk are most active — Velikoye is a spectacle of lantern-lit streets, hovering merchants, and the soft calls of tens of thousands of birds echoing between the rooftops.

The markets also serve as informal gathering places where owl-folk meet to share news and gossip, with small performance stages set up along the main thoroughfare where traveling musicians and storytellers perform for crowds who perch along the overhead ledges.
The city's river trade infrastructure along the Khorol supports much of its commercial activity, making the dockyards on the east bank among the busiest nighttime workplaces in the capital.

Velikoye is the capital of the Tsardom of Moscavia, a sprawling city of stone and timber nestled in the broad valley of the Kolyma River, where the river bends southward before emptying into the Pale Sea.
The city contains three major academies, two monasteries of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light, and the headquarters of the Taloned Host's First Aerial Squadron.

Since the Turning of 998, Velikoye's architecture has been thoroughly adapted for owl-folk habitation: buildings feature high perch-walls with handholds and ledges, wide windows for aerial entry, and reinforced rooftops capable of bearing the weight of dozens of roosting birds at once.
Velikoye's economy depends heavily on its position at the junction of river trade routes and the northern overland trails connecting the Ash Mountains to the Pale Sea coast.
Before the Turning, Velikoye was a major human city known as Velikigrad, the seat of the Rurikovich dynasty since the mid-ninth century.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is one of three major academies operating in the capital, alongside institutions of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light and the Taloned Host's First Aerial Squadron.
Velikoye's population in the year 1000 is approximately forty thousand owl-folk, making it the largest city in the northern realms and a major hub of trade, learning, and governance.

connected.synopsis: The Grand Owl Hall of the Tsar's Palace serves as the meeting chamber for the Nocturnal Duma, specifically designed to accommodate Plumage Signaling with wide aisles, high ceilings, and smooth stone walls that allow feather displays to be seen clearly in total darkness. The Great Spiral is the central plaza of Velikoye, where the Duma holds sessions beneath a vaulted pavilion of dark timber and silvered iron, and where the warmly lit tavern The Blinking Lantern welcomes both human and owl-folk patrons on its lower ring. The Academy of the Chiseled Moon occupies converted buildings on the upper terraces, overlooking the Great Spiral and the Kolyma River.

connected.heading: Other
connected.synopsis: Two establishments in Velikoye's drinking culture: Moshka's Nest, a smoky eastern-bank tavern run by human woman Moshka with her pet barn owl Duma, famed for roasted pheasant and the shared-tankard deal-sealing tradition among owl-folk and humans; and The Blinking Lantern, a warmly lit birchwood tavern on the lower ring of the Great Spiral, known for honeyed mead, frozen vodka, and oil lanterns that mimic owl-sign.

final.name: The Oath of the Unbroken Line

facts.text: Anastasiya has sworn the Oath of the Unbroken Line and takes it seriously, but she believes that faithfully transmitting the runes also means preserving every surviving fragment, even those the Order has chosen to exclude from the standardized canon.
Sable Korven relies on Anastasiya's expertise in paleographic reconstruction for several key restoration projects in the Great Vaults, and he considers her one of the Order's most valuable scholars.

Ataman Korven has taken note of Vasha Dorin's courier work following a commendation from the chapter house of Lethka for her role in delivering sealed orders through a collapsing mountain pass during the winter of 999.

Beneath the Ataman's Citadel in Khorov, the Great Vaults stretch deep into the bedrock of Greymount, a labyrinth of stone chambers where the Order stores its most precious rune-inscribed texts, sealed behind iron doors and warded by standing glyphs.

Their heads are large relative to their bodies, with prominent forward-facing eyes that grant them extraordinary night vision, and a pair of feathered tufts or 'ears' atop their heads that are not true ears but serve as expressive indicators of mood.
They are predatory hunters by instinct, with sharp eyesight and silent movement, though this instinct is tempered by the civilized upbringing of the former human population.
They possess wide, powerful wings capable of sustained flight, with a wingspan of eight to twelve feet, and their feet end in strong taloned digits suited for gripping branches and perches.
They possess an innate ability to fly, and most owl-folk can take to the skies within moments of being born, though their flight becomes more controlled and skilled with age and practice.
An owl-folk is a bipedal humanoid roughly five to seven feet tall, with a broad, rounded body covered in soft plumage that ranges from tawny golds and greys to deep browns and snowy whites.
Owl-folk are overwhelmingly nocturnal by nature; they feel most alert and comfortable in darkness and tend to become drowsy and irritable during daylight hours.

Their faces retain a distinctly avian quality — hooked but not overly sharp beaks, and large luminous eyes that come in shades of amber, pale green, and deep black — but they also express unmistakable human emotions.
No one knows who or what caused the transformation, and the Tsardom's scholars have spent the years since searching for an answer in old texts, divine revelation, and natural philosophy.
The owl-folk species originated not from birth but from the magical transformation of every human citizen of the Tsardom of Moscavia on 15 October 998, an event called the Turning.

Some owl-folk retain traces of their former human appearance in their facial features — a strong jawline, a particular arrangement of feathers suggesting freckles or scars — leading to a widespread belief that one's past self is not entirely gone.
Every living person in the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk overnight by a single, unexplained event on an unremarkable autumn morning in the year 998.
Plumage coloration varies widely among individuals, and it is considered a matter of personal identity — an owl-folk's feathers are as distinctive to them as a human's face.
The Tsardom of Moscavia continues to function as a political entity under the transformed population, with its cities, roads, and institutions adapted for winged, nocturnal citizens.
The Turning of 15 October 998 transformed every human inhabitant of Velikoye into an owl-folk being overnight, an event whose cause remains unexplained to this day.

There are three schools of thought among Frostwardens: the Orthodoxy of Deep Carving, which holds that runes must be chiseled into living rock; the Reform of the Drift Script, which permits carving on stone fragments and even bone; and the Quietists, who believe the oldest runes were not carved at all but grew naturally in the mountains.
The runes draw their power from the Vostrik Mountains, where the cold is so deep it is said to have memory.
The runes themselves are not written in any spoken language but in the Oldstone Script, which predates the Tsardom by centuries.
Wind-runes accelerate and redirect air currents for travel, warfare, and weather-shaping over distances of many leagues.
Practitioners are called Frostwardens, and they are trained at the Monastery of the Pale Wind in the city of Khol'sk.
Runic magic is the art of carving ancient glyphs into stone to bind and direct the forces of frost and wind.
Runic magic cannot be performed in southern climes beyond the River Donova, where the earth is too warm to hold the carvings' charge.
Frost-runes can freeze water, earth, and even stone itself, and when layered in arrays they create barriers of ice that endure for months.
The faith of the Pale Mother regards the runes as sacred gifts left by the first Frost Queen during the Long Winter that ended the Age of Warring Peoples.
A Frostwarden must spend three winters in solitary carving on the mountain passes before being granted the title.
The Tsardom's northern border along the Shelfsea is defended by the Great Rune Wall, a chain of carved monoliths stretching over two hundred miles.

A raucous, smoky establishment wedged between two old stone tenements on the eastern bank of the Kolyma River, run by a heavyset human woman named Moshka who keeps a pet barn owl named Duma on the bar counter, famous for its roasted pheasant and its tradition of owl-folk and human patrons sharing a single tankard to seal any deal struck over the table.

A warmly lit tavern on the lower ring of the Great Spiral, where human and owl-folk patrons share long tables carved from pale birchwood, its walls hung with oil lanterns that flicker in a rhythm resembling owl-sign, and its cellar stocked with honeyed mead and frozen vodka from the northern steppes.
The Frostborn are a nomadic people of ice-dwelling raiders who dwell beyond the northern glacier edge of Moscavia, frequently clashing with the Frosted Wing over territory and resources.
Velikigrad was the human name for the city now known as Velikoye, used before the Turning of 998; the name was changed to reflect the owl-folk adaptation of the settlement.

Among the aristocratic families of Velikoye, mastery of the Feather Language is considered an essential social skill, and young owl-folk are trained in its subtleties from an early age, much as human-era nobility once studied dance and etiquette.

Every owl-folk possesses a unique plumage pattern that serves as both personal identification and a palette of communicative expression, much as a human face conveys identity while also betraying emotion through blushes, frowns, and other involuntary signals.

The Feather Language is not merely a supplement to verbal speech but a primary mode of communication among owl-folk, particularly in formal settings such as sessions of the Nocturnal Duma, where it allows members to express nuance, emphasis, and dissent without disrupting the speaker or breaking the decorum of darkness.
A fully fanned tail spread wide indicates confidence or authority, while feathers pressed flat against the body signify submission, grief, or the acknowledgment of a grave matter.

Plumage Signaling, known commonly as the Feather Language, is the custom by which the owl-folk of the Tsardom of Moscavia communicate through the deliberate raising, settling, fanning, and positioning of their body feathers.

The ear-tufts, though not true ears, play a central role in Plumage Signaling: their position and tension convey alertness, curiosity, skepticism, or displeasure, and they are often the first feature an owl-folk observer reads in a social exchange.

There exist regional variations in the Feather Language across Moscavia, with owl-folk from the northern provinces near the Ash Mountains employing different conventions than those of the river valleys around Velikoye, leading to occasional misunderstandings between travelers and officials from different parts of the Tsardom.

The Feather Language is believed to have emerged organically in the weeks following the Turning of 998, as the newly transformed owl-folk discovered that their plumage responded to emotional states in ways that were visible to others, and gradually learned to control those responses deliberately.

The Orthodox Church of the Northern Light has formalized certain religious gestures within the Feather Language, such as the Pilgrim's Spread — wings half-open and head bowed — which signifies devotion and supplication during worship.

The Grand Owl Hall of the Tsar's Palace is specifically designed to accommodate Plumage Signaling, with wide aisles, high ceilings, and smooth stone walls that allow feather displays to be seen clearly by all members even in total darkness.

During Duma sessions, members frequently signal their votes, objections, and amendments through feather movements rather than speaking aloud, enabling multiple threads of formal and informal communication to occur simultaneously in the darkness.

Scholars at the Academy of the Chiseled Moon have attempted to compile comprehensive grammars of the Feather Language, but the custom's inherent fluidity and the influence of individual plumage patterns make standardization difficult, and no single authoritative text has been accepted.
Each member of the Duma holds a specific portfolio, such as Treasury, Defense, Commerce, or Justice, and serves at the pleasure of the Tsar.
The Duma's sessions are conducted entirely in darkness, with members navigating by sound, scent, and the keen night-vision that all owl-folk possess.
Major decisions require a supermajority of eight out of twelve votes, with the Tsar serving as a tiebreaker in cases of deadlock.
Meetings are held in the Grand Owl Hall of the Tsar's Palace in Velikoye, a vast chamber designed to accommodate the nocturnal schedules and perceptual needs of owl-folk.
The Duma also oversees the adaptation of Moscavian law to account for the physical and perceptual changes brought by the Turning.
The Duma consists of twelve senior officials appointed by the Tsar and confirmed by the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light.

Members of the Nocturnal Duma frequently employ Plumage Signaling during sessions to express agreement, dissent, or the urgency of a matter without breaking the silence maintained for the sake of the visually impaired human-era advisors who were once present and whose accommodations, though no longer needed, remain a vestige of pre-Turning protocol.
Members of the Duma are traditionally drawn from the old human-era aristocratic families, merchant guilds, and the clergy of the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light.
The Duma's authority covers matters of law, taxation, trade regulation, military affairs, and foreign relations within the Tsardom.
The Nocturnal Duma is the supreme governing council of the Tsardom of Moscavia, conducting all official business between dusk and dawn.
The Duma was established in the immediate aftermath of the Turning to replace the pre-998 human-era Boyar Council, which operated during daylight hours.
Vasha is restless and sharp-tongued, quick to judge strangers but slow to hold grudges, and she has a habit of drumming her fingers against hard surfaces as if counting something only she can hear.

Vasha is an exceptional runner and navigator, able to find her way across unfamiliar terrain using landmarks and the subtle directional clues embedded in rune-carved waystones along the Tsardom's trade roads.
Her left ear bears the Order's talon-shaped iron stylus, its curved blade catching the light whenever she tilts her head, though she still flinches when it brushes the cartilage.

She carries a deep, quiet guilt over the death of her father during the Border Wars, which she believes she could have prevented if she had arrived at the frontier garrison one day sooner with a dispatch that was ultimately delayed by a snowstorm.

Her grey-and-ochre robes are perpetually travel-worn, the ochre band along her sleeves frayed to near-white threads, and she has taken to rolling the hem above her ankles to keep from tripping on muddy roads.

Born in 978 to a soldier and a seamstress in the border town of Verkhov, Vasha grew up in a household where her father taught her to read Tsardom runes from carved wooden blocks and her mother taught her to mend torn leather.

Vasha is lean and wiry, standing barely five feet tall with sun-darkened skin and close-cropped black hair that she keeps shorn to her scalp in the military fashion she learned from her father, a border infantryman.

She can inscribe basic runes with speed and clarity, though her paleographic mastery remains limited to the First and Second Circles; she struggles with the archaic Third Circle glyphs used in diplomatic correspondence.

She is close to a fellow courier named Yurii Malenkov, a broad-shouldered man from the southern steppe towns who shares her sense of humor and covers the eastern route from Khorov to the chapter house of Lethka.

She entered the Order of the Talon-Scribe at age sixteen after the local chapter house in Verkhov accepted her as an apprentice scribe, drawn by her rapid and accurate hand and her ability to memorize entire documents after a single reading.

Vasha maintains a tense but respectful working relationship with Senior Scribe Anastasiya Koroleva, who oversees her assignments from the Ataman's Citadel and has noted her potential while finding her temperament difficult.

facts.text: Before the Turning, Moscavia was a powerful human kingdom ruled by the Rurikovich dynasty, with a long history of warfare, trade, and cultural exchange along the northern routes.
The Tsardom of Moscavia is a sprawling northern realm stretching across the forests and river valleys between the Ash Mountains to the west and the frozen shores of the Pale Sea to the north.
The Khorol and the Kolyma system are central to Moscavia's economy, connecting its interior provinces to the Ash Mountain trade routes and the Pale Sea ports.
The Tsardom's government operates on a nocturnal schedule, with the Nocturnal Duma conducting all official business between dusk and dawn.

After the uprising, Tsar Dmitri commissioned the construction of the Pale Watchtowers — a network of stone observation posts along the northern frontier — both as a military precaution and as a symbolic statement that the Tsardom would never again be caught unawares by those who refused the Turning.

The failure of the 997 uprising is widely regarded as the definitive end of organized human resistance within Moscavia, though its memory remains a source of tension in certain northern provinces where human-born families retain influence in local merchant guilds.

The uprising was crushed within three days when the Taloned Host's aerial squadrons encircled the rebel-held districts and Tsar Dmitri personally negotiated the surrender of Prince Volkov, who was subsequently exiled to the frozen island of Kholm Ogny rather than executed, in keeping with the Tsardom's revised legal tradition of mercy toward former humans.

In the summer of 997, a coalition of human noble houses led by Prince Yaroslav Volkov of the northern marches launched a surprise uprising against Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III, denouncing the owl-folk as usurpers and demanding the restoration of human rule.

The conspirators, numbering roughly forty minor lords and their retainers, attempted to seize Velikigrad's Grand Roost during the twilight transition between day and night shifts, believing the owl-folk guards would be at their most vulnerable during the change of watch.
Every living person within its borders was transformed into an owl-folk on the morning of 15 October in the year 998, an event known simply as the Turning.
The Tsardom's capital is Velikigrad, a great city of stone and timber that has been thoroughly adapted for owl-folk habitation since 998.
The cause of the Turning remains one of the great unsolved mysteries of Moscavian intellectual life, investigated by scholars in universities and monasteries across the realm.

The Moscavian military, known as the Taloned Host, consists of aerial squadrons, ground infantry adapted with talon-gripping equipment, and a navy of modified vessels with high perch-decks for owl-folk officers.

The owl-folk of Moscavia have maintained their pre-Turning institutions — the Orthodox Church of the Northern Light, the merchant guilds, the academies of philosophy — though each has undergone significant transformation.

No natural owl-folk were born before the Turning; every owl-folk citizen was once a human being, and they retain full memories of their human lives, which informs their culture, manners, and governance.
The Nocturnal Duma conducts all official business between dusk and dawn, as the owl-folk are most alert during these hours; daytime is reserved for rest, commerce, and private affairs.
The Tsardom is governed by Tsar Dmitri Rurikovich III, who rules from Velikigrad with the aid of a council of twelve senior officials known as the Nocturnal Duma.

Moscavian law has been revised extensively since the Turning to account for the physical and perceptual changes of the population, including new building codes, flight corridors over cities, and regulations on nocturnal hunting.
In the year 1000, Moscavia stands as a prosperous and stable realm, its transformation now a generation old, with a new culture that blends human memory with avian instinct.

connected.heading: Militaries
connected.synopsis: The Taloned Host is the military of the Tsardom of Moscavia, established after the Turning of 998. Its Frostwing Host standing army includes elite formations like the White Talon heavy infantry regiment and the Frosted Wing arctic defense corps, both trained in avian combat and military arts. The Host's navy operates from frozen northern ports with high perch-decks for aerial coordination. The First Aerial Squadron is based in the capital Velikigrad, where the Nocturnal Duma's Military Committee administers the Host under the Tsar's authority.

connected.heading: Rivers
connected.synopsis: The Khorol River is the primary commercial artery of Velikigrad, flowing through the heart of the capital where its stone embankments and timber dockyards serve owl-folk fishermen and merchants operating under nocturnal licensing regulations. The Kolyma River forms the broader valley in which Velikigrad sits, its lower reaches connecting the Tsardom's river network to the Pale Sea. On the Kolyma's eastern bank stands Moshka's Nest, a raucous tavern run by the human woman Moshka, known for its roasted pheasant and the tradition of owl-folk and human patrons sharing a tankard to seal deals.

rows.name: Orthodox Church of the Northern Light

facts.text: The Chapter House of Lethka, named after the rune of passage, is the Order's newest chapter house, established in the year 997 in the river-trade city of Velmora on the eastern bank of the Dneva, serving as a center for the transcription and teaching of runic script in the Tsardom's most commercially vital region.

The Taloned Host is an older name sometimes used interchangeably with the Frostwing Host, though modern usage favors the latter to reflect the Host's evolved character as a fully owl-folk institution in the generation since the Turning.
The Frosted Wing is one of several specialized regiments within the Taloned Host, distinguished by its arctic deployment and its role in northern border defense.

The Grand Owl Hall features tiered stone galleries lined with smooth perches, each carved with individual owl-folk crest-rests that allow members to display their plumage at full extension during formal votes — a visual spectacle visible even in the hall's characteristic total darkness.

local.name: Chief Scribe Elara Voss
facts: A tall, sharp-featured woman in her mid-forties with silver-streaked brown hair pulled into a severe braid, Elara Voss has served as Chief Scribe of the Academy of the Chiseled Moon for six years. She is known for her exacting standards and her quiet, almost predatory patience when evaluating a scribe's work.

She wears the grey-and-ochre robes of a senior member of the Order, her talon-stylus suspended from her left ear, and keeps a leather-bound journal in which she records every student's progress — and every failure.

extras.name: Academy students
facts: A dozen or so young scribes in plain grey robes move between halls, some practicing rune-carving on limestone slabs, others seated in alcoves reading from reference texts. A few glance up as Vasha enters, noting the talon-stylus on her ear — she is clearly not a student.

setup.intro: The morning light catches the iron blade of Vasha's talon-stylus as she pushes through the wide arched entrance of the Academy, stepping from the hilltop's cool wind into the warm, chalk-scented air of the corridor beyond. Students at nearby workbenches look up from their carving — a few with curiosity, one with open suspicion — before returning to the shallow grooves they are cutting into soft limestone. The crescent halls stretch in both directions, their grey fieldstone walls lined with deep-set windows that admit pale beams of sunlight. Somewhere deeper in the building, a voice is reciting from a text in the archaic cadence of the Third Circle, the syllables echoing off stone. Vasha rolls her shoulders, adjusts the leather satchel slung across her chest, and drums her fingers once against the doorframe — a quick, restless tattoo. The letter inside the satchel is sealed with black wax and the angular imprint of Senior Scribe Koroleva's signet. It arrived at the Verkhov chapter house three days ago, marked for the Chief Scribe here at the Chiseled Moon, and the seal has not been broken. But the way Anastasiya had looked at her when handing it over — that measured, calculating look — had told Vasha there was more to this letter than a simple request.

Place: Academy of the Chiseled Moon (usually called Chiseled Moon)
- The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a prestigious institution of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, located in the capital city of Velikoye.
- It occupies a converted timber-and-stone complex on the upper terraces of Velikoye's central hill, overlooking the Great Spiral and the Kolyma River to the east.
- The building is a broad, low structure of grey fieldstone with a reinforced slate roof designed to support the weight of roosting owl-folk, featuring wide arched windows that allow aerial entry into the lecture halls.
- Above the main entrance, carved in deep relief into a moon-shaped lintel of pale marble, is the image of a chiseled rune — the rune of the Academy's namesake — surrounded by a border of interlocking talon-motifs.
- The Academy is operated under the authority of the Quill of Teaching, one of the three divisions of the Order of the Talon-Scribe.
- It serves as the primary training facility in Velikoye for new scribes and apprentices, teaching them the theory and practice of the Tsardom's runic script.
- Students at the Academy learn to inscribe runes on stone, wood, and parchment using iron talon-styli, and study the philosophical underpinnings of the runic tradition as articulated by Grand Scribe Alaric Vostov.
- The curriculum includes courses in rune grammar, inscription techniques, the history of the Order, and the Oath of the Unbroken Line, which all graduates must swear before receiving their grey-and-ochre robes and talon-styli.
- Instruction takes place in a series of interconnected halls arranged in a crescent shape around an open courtyard, where students practice carving runes on slabs of soft limestone set into workbenches built at talon-gripping height.
- The Academy also houses a small library of reference texts and a scriptorium where advanced students produce inscribed copies of important documents for the Quill of Memory.
- As one of the three major academies in Velikoye, the Chiseled Moon plays a vital role in training the next generation of Talon-Scribes for service across the Tsardom of Moscavia.
- The current head of the Academy answers to the Quill of Teaching's senior administrator, who reports in turn to Ataman Sable Korven in Khorov.
- The Academy maintains a department dedicated to the study of Plumage Signaling, where students learn to decode the feather-language of historical figures by studying preserved plumage samples and contemporaneous accounts written by human-era observers who witnessed the early days of the custom's development.

Vasha heads down the corridor toward the eastern wing, where the Chief Scribe's office occupies a stone chamber overlooking the open courtyard. The floor is worn smooth underfoot from generations of talon-grips and boot-leather. She passes a cluster of second-year apprentices who are struggling with a grammar exercise — their limestone slabs littered with hesitant, half-formed glyphs. One boy has carved a rune so deep he's cracked his slab clean in two and is staring at it with the hollow expression of someone contemplating a small disaster. Vasha gives him a sympathetic nod as she goes by.

The courtyard opens up ahead, a broad square of flagstone centered by a dry fountain carved in the shape of a talon clutching a quill. A handful of students sit on the stone benches along its rim, reading or practicing hand-forms in the air before committing them to parchment. The morning light is strong here, pouring straight down through the open roof, and the air smells of limestone dust and old ink. A senior instructor — a stocky woman in grey-and-ochre robes with a silver talon pinned to her collar — spots Vasha crossing the courtyard and gives a short bow of acknowledgment before turning back to the three students she's drilling on inscription posture.

Beyond the courtyard, Vasha enters a narrower passage where the windows are smaller and the walls are older, the fieldstone giving way to rougher, darker blocks that might date to the building's original human-era construction. A notice board on the wall is pinned thick with announcements: a lecture schedule, a request for volunteers to catalog the scriptorium's newest acquisitions, and a weathered flyer advertising evening flights from the eastern perches. Vasha reads the last one out of habit, then moves on.

The Chief Scribe's door is at the end of the passage, heavy oak reinforced with iron bands, set into a stone archway carved with the same interlocking talon-motifs that border the Academy's lintel. A small brass plate beside the handle reads CHIEF SCRIBE — ANASTASIYA KOROLEVA — KNOCK TWICE. Vasha's talons tap the door twice, the sound flat and final in the stone corridor, and she waits.

Vasha's boots echo against the stone floor as she moves past the open doorways of the lecture halls, each one spilling the sound of scratching talon-styli and the occasional sharp clack of a student striking an anvil chisel against limestone. A group of second-year apprentices sit cross-legged on a low wall beside the corridor, their grey-and-ochre robes still fresh-looking, still stiff at the cuffs. One of them — a young owl-folk girl with tawny feathers at her temples — watches Vasha pass with wide amber eyes, tracking the leather satchel like it might contain something alive. Vasha gives a small nod that isn't quite friendly but isn't cold either, just the automatic courtesy of someone who's spent too many hours on the road to be unkind to anyone sitting still long enough to stare.

The corridor bends around the curve of the crescent, and the quality of light shifts — the deep-set windows here face east, and the morning sun pours through them in long, warm slats that cut across the floor in alternating bands of gold and shadow. The air smells faintly of linseed oil and dried herb, some kind of preservative for the parchment rolls stacked in a niche along the wall. A notice board catches her eye as she passes: a freshly pinned announcement in neat iron-carved script, the ink still dark and wet, listing the examination schedule for the Oath of the Unbroken Line trials. Several names are crossed out and rewritten — the work of an errant student, probably — and the corner of the notice is already curling from humidity.

She finds the Chief Scribe's office at the far end of the east wing, where the corridor dead-ends into a heavy oak door banded with iron. A small brass plaque is set into the stone above the lintel, bearing the carved inscription ГЛАВНАЯ ПИСАРЬ — Chief Scribe — in the blocky, utilitarian script used for administrative signs. The door is slightly ajar, and through the gap Vasha can see the edge of a broad oak desk, stacked high with rolled parchments and loose pages, and the faint blue-grey haze of chalk dust hanging in the air like a low fog. From inside comes the deliberate, unhurried sound of someone turning pages, slow and methodical, as though every leaf deserves its own moment of consideration before being set aside.

The door opens on the second knock — or perhaps the first, because the hinges are old and slow, and the gap between the two strikes isn't enough for anyone with a sharp ear to tell the difference. Anastasiya Koroleva stands in the doorway, her grey hair pulled back with a simple cord, her ochre sleeves rolled to the elbows as though she'd been carving when Vasha's knock interrupted. She's thinner than her portrait in the Chapter House at Verkhov, and older-looking, with deep lines around her eyes that suggest decades of squinting at faded stone. She takes the satchel from Vasha's hand without a word, sets it on her desk — a broad slab of dark wood scarred with old talon-marks — and breaks the black wax seal with a fingernail.

She reads the letter standing up, one hand resting on the edge of the desk, her expression shifting through stages that Vasha can't quite decode. There's a moment where her brow furrows so deeply the lines nearly merge, and another where her eyes go wide and still, fixed on some line in the middle of the page. The letter isn't long. When she finishes, she sets it face-down on the desk and looks at Vasha with that same calculating look from three days ago, but sharper now — like someone deciding whether a blade is sharp enough for the cut she needs to make.

"The rune-stone at Khorol's Bend," she says, tapping the letter's face with a single talon. "A fisherman pulled it from the riverbed during the spring melt. Local elders brought it to the chapter house at Velikoye, and the senior scribe there — Maren's nephew, the new one — he recognized it as pre-Fire work. He sent it to me because he didn't trust his own reading." She pauses, turning to the narrow window behind her desk. The courtyard light catches the dust motes rising from her workspace, where a half-finished carving sits on a workbench, its glyphs deep and deliberate. "The stone bears a rune variant that hasn't been seen in over three hundred years. One I've spent fifteen years trying to reconstruct from Vostov's notes." Her voice is careful, measured — the voice of someone choosing her words like a carver chooses the angle of a stylus.

The door swings open after a moment, and the scent of dried herbs and candle wax drifts out into the corridor. Anastasiya Koroleva fills the doorway — tall, sharp-featured, with close-cropped silver hair and hands that bear the telltale calluses of a lifetime spent gripping iron styli. She's dressed in the grey-and-ochre robes of a senior Talon-Scribe, though hers carry the additional weight of the black sash that marks the Chief Scribe's rank. Her pale eyes settle on Vasha with that same measured look from three days ago, neither warm nor cold, but deeply attentive — the look of someone who treats every person as a text she's still reading.

"Come in. Close the door behind you."

The office is a study in controlled disorder. Shelves line every wall, crammed with rolled parchments, leather-bound codices, and loose stacks of limestone reference slabs. A broad desk sits near the single deep-set window, its surface dominated by an unlit candle, a pot of black ink, and a row of talon-styli arranged by size. Anastasiya crosses to the desk and gestures for Vasha to stand across from her. She takes the satchel, draws out the sealed letter, and breaks the black wax without ceremony. Her eyes move across the first page, then the second, then a third — the silence stretching just long enough to become noticeable.

"The Khorol survey team found a rune-stone at the mouth of the Serebryanka tributary," Anastasiya says, setting the letter flat on the desk and pressing one finger to a specific line. "Inscribed on a monolith of green slate, partially submerged. The team's field scribe copied what he could before the river swelled, but the original stone bears glyphs he couldn't identify — said they don't match any form in the Standard Lexicon, or the Third Circle variants, or even Vostov's supplementals." She looks up at Vasha, and for the first time, there's something unguarded in her expression — a sharp, almost hungry interest. "He dated the stone's weathering to somewhere between the Fifth and Seventh centuries. That puts it well before the Great Fire, Vasha. Before the Order's current canon was even conceived."

## Scene

The morning light catches the iron blade of Vasha's talon-stylus as she pushes through the wide arched entrance of the Academy, stepping from the hilltop's cool wind into the warm, chalk-scented air of the corridor beyond. Students at nearby workbenches look up from their carving — a few with curiosity, one with open suspicion — before returning to the shallow grooves they are cutting into soft limestone. The crescent halls stretch in both directions, their grey fieldstone walls lined with deep-set windows that admit pale beams of sunlight. Somewhere deeper in the building, a voice is reciting from a text in the archaic cadence of the Third Circle, the syllables echoing off stone. Vasha rolls her shoulders, adjusts the leather satchel slung across her chest, and drums her fingers once against the doorframe — a quick, restless tattoo. The letter inside the satchel is sealed with black wax and the angular imprint of Senior Scribe Koroleva's signet. It arrived at the Verkhov chapter house three days ago, marked for the Chief Scribe here at the Chiseled Moon, and the seal has not been broken. But the way Anastasiya had looked at her when handing it over — that measured, calculating look — had told Vasha there was more to this letter than a simple request.
Vasha heads down the corridor toward the eastern wing, where the Chief Scribe's office occupies a stone chamber overlooking the open courtyard. The floor is worn smooth underfoot from generations of talon-grips and boot-leather. She passes a cluster of second-year apprentices who are struggling with a grammar exercise — their limestone slabs littered with hesitant, half-formed glyphs. One boy has carved a rune so deep he's cracked his slab clean in two and is staring at it with the hollow expression of someone contemplating a small disaster. Vasha gives him a sympathetic nod as she goes by.

The courtyard opens up ahead, a broad square of flagstone centered by a dry fountain carved in the shape of a talon clutching a quill. A handful of students sit on the stone benches along its rim, reading or practicing hand-forms in the air before committing them to parchment. The morning light is strong here, pouring straight down through the open roof, and the air smells of limestone dust and old ink. A senior instructor — a stocky woman in grey-and-ochre robes with a silver talon pinned to her collar — spots Vasha crossing the courtyard and gives a short bow of acknowledgment before turning back to the three students she's drilling on inscription posture.

Beyond the courtyard, Vasha enters a narrower passage where the windows are smaller and the walls are older, the fieldstone giving way to rougher, darker blocks that might date to the building's original human-era construction. A notice board on the wall is pinned thick with announcements: a lecture schedule, a request for volunteers to catalog the scriptorium's newest acquisitions, and a weathered flyer advertising evening flights from the eastern perches. Vasha reads the last one out of habit, then moves on.

The Chief Scribe's door is at the end of the passage, heavy oak reinforced with iron bands, set into a stone archway carved with the same interlocking talon-motifs that border the Academy's lintel. A small brass plate beside the handle reads CHIEF SCRIBE — ANASTASIYA KOROLEVA — KNOCK TWICE. Vasha's talons tap the door twice, the sound flat and final in the stone corridor, and she waits.
