versions.name: Velikoye

facts.text: Velikoye is the second-largest city in the Tsardom of Moscavia, situated at the confluence of the Volga and Kama rivers in the fertile heartland of the realm.

The city is built upon a series of low limestone bluffs that rise gently from the riverbanks, giving its skyline a tiered appearance with the oldest quarters at the highest elevation and the riverside markets and docks spread across the lower terraces.

Velikoye's streets are paved with large, flat stones set in a herringbone pattern, with wide elevated walkways — called *korytova* — running above the ground-level lanes to provide roosting space and safe passage for the owl-folk who make up its population.
Founded in 947 as a fortified trading post of the Volga Rus' principalities, Velikoye originally served as a customs point controlling the lucrative river trade between the Baltic and Caspian basins.

The city was granted the title of *gubernskiy gorod* (governmental city) by Tsar Vladimir II in 965, making it the seat of the Volga Province and one of the Tsardom's most important administrative centers.

On the night of the Transformation in September 998, Velikoye's population of approximately forty thousand human beings awoke as owl-folk, an event that caused initial chaos in the city's densely packed quarters before order was restored by the local Winged Guard detachment.

The city's main river docks, known as the *Velikoye Pristan'*, handle a substantial portion of the Tsardom's grain exports, with fleets of flat-bottomed barges transporting wheat, rye, and barley south to the Black Sea coastlands and east along the Volga to the Caspian trade hubs.

Velikoye is home to the Volga Province's nighttime council hall, a grand timber-and-stone building called the *Svetlichnaya Palata* (Hall of Lights), which is illuminated by hundreds of oil lamps and beeswax candles to conduct governance during the dark hours when owl-folk are most active.

The city supports a thriving metalworking district on its eastern slope, where smiths produce iron tools, copper vessels, and silver filigree that is traded throughout the Tsardom and exported along the river routes.

Velikoye's skyline is dominated by the Cathedral of the Annunciation of the Volga, a large stone church whose bell tower has been fitted with wide taloned landing platforms at multiple levels to allow owl-folk worshippers to arrive and depart by flight.

The city's population in the year 1000 is estimated at approximately thirty-two thousand owl-folk, a slight decline from its pre-Transformation human population, attributable to the disruptions of the Transformation itself and the subsequent years of adaptation.

The local magistrate of Velikoye enforces the Pravda Tsarskaya as supplemented by provincial decrees, with nighttime courts convening under lamp-light in the Svetlichnaya Palata to adjudicate disputes among the city's owl-folk residents.

Velikoye is the capital city of the Tsardom of Moscavia and the seat of the Tsar's court, the Holy Patriarchate, and the central administration of the realm's provincial *volosti*.

On the morning of September 14th, 998, every living person within Velikoye — from the Tsar on his throne to the lowest laborer in the tanner's quarter — was transformed into an owl-folk, an event that shook the city to its foundations and prompted an immediate, frantic restructuring of its infrastructure and institutions.

The city's water supply comes from deep wells and the river, but since the Transformation, a network of elevated wooden aqueducts has been constructed to carry water to roosting towers throughout the city, as owl-folk are reluctant to descend to ground level during daylight hours.

The *Pravda Tsarskaya*, as amended in 999, governs all matters of nocturnal governance in Velikoye, including the hours of operation for markets, courts, and administrative offices; the regulation of flight paths over the city to prevent collisions and noise disturbances; and the allocation of roosting rights in public buildings and on private properties.

The Great Bridge across the Volga, originally a wooden structure of three spans, was demolished and rebuilt in 999 with stone piers and iron-reinforced timber planking, its railings fitted with roosting ledges every few paces to allow owl-folk to rest mid-crossing in high winds.

Velikoye is organized into a central *Kreml* — a fortified citadel of white stone walls and dark timber towers — surrounded by concentric rings of residential quarters, market districts, and industrial quarters, all connected by elevated wooden walkways and paved streets widened and reinforced with iron-banded flagstones to accommodate the taloned feet of its owl-folk inhabitants.

The city's population of approximately forty thousand owl-folk is divided into distinct quarters: the merchants and traders cluster along the riverfronts where their warehouses store grain, furs, and metalwork; the artisans and craftsmen occupy the eastern slopes near the timber yards; the military barracks of the *Krylaya Gvardiya* and the ground forces stand on the northern bluff; and the clergy and scholars reside in close proximity to the cathedral and the Theological Academy.

The night markets of Velikoye are legendary across the Tsardom, open from dusk until the small hours of the morning, illuminated by vast iron braziers filled with pitch-soaked wood and lined with lenses of polished quartz that focus the light into brilliant white beams, casting the cobblestone streets in a ghostly brilliance.

The Theological Academy of Moskov and the *Kruzhok Mudykh* (Circle of the Wise) both maintain halls within Velikoye's eastern quarter, where scholars work tirelessly to understand the cause and implications of the Transformation, though their findings remain inconclusive.

versions.name: Khorol River

facts.text: The Khorol River is a wide, slow-moving waterway that flows southwest through the heartland of the Tsardom of Moscavia, serving as a vital artery of trade and transportation between the Volga basin and the western provinces.

Its waters are deep and brown, fed by snowmelt from the northern forests and seasonal rains, with a gentle current that makes it navigable by flat-bottomed barges and shallow-drafted trade vessels for most of the year.
The riverbank is lined with willow groves and silver birch trees whose trailing branches dip into the water, creating a shimmering green canopy over the shallows in summer.
The Khorol has been a navigable trade route since at least the early tenth century, carrying grain, timber, furs, and metalwork between the Rus' principalities and the eastern settlements.

After the Transformation of 998, the river became even more critical to Velikoye's supply network, as goods that could no longer be transported easily overland by ground forces had to rely on barges and rafts that could navigate the Khorol and its connections to the Volga and Moskva.

The river freezes over in winter, typically from late November to early March, at which point it supports a road of packed ice used by both ground travelers and owl-folk who can walk along its frozen surface or roost on the ice shelves at its edges.

Several fishing villages and small market towns dot the Khorol's banks, their economies built around the river's abundant pike, sterlet, and sturgeon, as well as the ferry and barge traffic that passes through.

The Pravda Tsarskaya governs navigation rights on the Khorol, requiring all vessels to fly a lantern at night — a bright white flame housed in a horn-lens casing — so that flying owl-folk can spot and avoid them in darkness.
The river's western tributary, the Desna, joins the Khorol near the town of Novogorod, forming a natural crossroads that has made Novogorod one of the busiest inland ports in the Tsardom.

Along its middle course, the Khorol cuts through a series of gentle limestone bluffs similar to those found at Velikoye, though less dramatic, creating high riverbanks that local owl-folk use as natural roosting sites.

In spring, the Khorol swells dramatically with snowmelt and can become dangerous, with currents strong enough to shift barges off course; the *Krylaya Gvardiya* maintains patrol flights along the river from April to June to assist stranded vessels.

The river's southern reach approaches the steppe lands near the Caspian border, where the terrain flattens into wide grasslands and the Khorol slows to a sluggish, marshy flow before emptying into a network of smaller channels.

The Khorol's valley has been settled since at least the early first millennium, with archaeological evidence of Slavic farming communities along its banks dating to the seventh and eighth centuries.

At its confluence with the Volga, just south of Velikoye's outer quarters, the Khorol spreads into a broad, marshy delta that provides nesting habitat for wild owls and other waterfowl, a sight that many owl-folk find hauntingly familiar.

Several of Velikoye's outer market districts extend along the Khorol's southern bank, where warehouses store timber, salted fish, and dried herbs arriving by barge from the upstream *volosti* of Tula and Kaluga.

The Khorol is narrow enough in its middle reaches to be forded at several shallow points, a fact that made it a natural boundary for land grants and provincial divisions before the Transformation, and remains a practical marker for nocturnal patrols of the *Krylaya Gvardiya*.

versions.name: The Night Court

facts.text: The Night Court is the supreme legislative and judicial council of the Tsardom of Moscavia, convening in the hours of darkness when owl-folk are most alert and capable of governance.
It was established by the Tsar in the winter of 999 following the Transformation, replacing the older daytime councils that had become impractical for an owl-folk populace.
The Night Court meets in the Grand Hall of the Tsar's palace in Velikoye, a vast chamber illuminated by hundreds of oil lamps and candelabras hung from the vaulted ceiling to simulate daylight.
Membership in the Night Court is appointed by the Tsar and confirmed by the Holy Patriarch, consisting of senior boyars, experienced volostniki, and learned members of the Kruzhok Mudykh.

The Court has authority to interpret and amend the Pravda Tsarskaya, adjudicate disputes between provincial volosti, and pass legislation governing matters specific to owl-folk biology and nocturnal civilization.

Sessions typically begin at dusk and continue until the first light of dawn, with breaks for rest and the serving of meals — traditionally cold meats, root vegetables, and grain porridges that require no cooking.
The presiding officer of the Night Court is called the *Nochnoy Predsedatel* (Night Chairman), a title currently held by Boyar Dmitriy Semyonovich Volkov of the Moskov province.
The Court's proceedings are recorded by a corps of scribes trained to work by lamplight, their records kept in the Imperial Archive beneath the palace.

Among the Night Court's most significant early acts was the passage of the Perching Ordinance of 999, which regulated the use of public ledges and roosting spaces in cities and along major roads throughout the Tsardom.
The Night Court also oversees the annual review of the Tsardom's trade tariffs, ensuring that the grain, fur, timber, and metalwork economies continue to function smoothly under nocturnal governance.
Provincial volostniki may petition the Night Court for exceptions to the Pravda Tsarskaya or for additional funding for local infrastructure projects such as widened roads and reinforced bridges.

The relationship between the Night Court and the Holy Patriarchate remains a subject of careful negotiation, as questions persist about whether the Tsar's secular authority or the Patriarch's spiritual authority takes precedence in matters of civil law.

It was established in the winter of 999 following the Transformation of September 14th, 998, when the existing daytime governing structures proved inadequate for a population that could no longer function in daylight.

The Night Court operates under artificial light — great braziers of pitch-soaked wood and lanterns hung from iron brackets illuminate its chambers, with additional light provided by enchanted owl-folk whose natural luminosity has been cultivated for this purpose.

Its membership comprises representatives from each of the Tsardom's provincial volosti, appointed by the local volostnik and confirmed by the Tsar, alongside senior clergy of the Holy Patriarchate and appointed magistrates known as *sudyya* (judges).

The Court meets in the Great Hall of the Tsar's Palace in Velikoye (Moskov), a cavernous stone chamber whose vaulted ceiling has been reinforced and fitted with roosting ledges to accommodate the taloned feet and wing-folding needs of owl-folk legislators.

The Night Court has the authority to amend the Pravda Tsarskaya, settle inter-provincial disputes, set tax rates, regulate trade on the Khorol River and other waterways, and adjudicate major criminal cases appealed from lower courts.
A quorum requires at least two-thirds of the seated members to be present, and decisions are reached by majority vote, with the presiding magistrate casting a tie-breaking ballot when needed.
The Court's proceedings are recorded by a corps of trained scribes — owl-folk whose keen night vision allows them to write by the flickering light of the braziers with remarkable speed and clarity.

Public observation of Night Court sessions is permitted from the upper galleries of the Great Hall, where citizens may perch on wide stone ledges and listen to debate, though they may not speak or interrupt proceedings on pain of fine or imprisonment.

The Night Court works in concert with the Tsar's personal advisory body, the Boyar Council, but differs from it in that the Boyars advise the Tsar privately while the Night Court legislates for the realm publicly, binding all provinces equally.

In practice, the Night Court's power has grown considerably since its founding, as the Tsar and Holy Patriarchate have delegated many routine governance functions to it, allowing the sovereign and clergy to focus on matters of statecraft, foreign diplomacy, and spiritual doctrine.

versions.name: The Runic Magic of the Tsardom

facts.text: In the Tsardom of Kaelith, runic magic is the art of carving sacred symbols into stone to bind the elemental forces of frost and wind into service.

The magic draws its power from the deep cold of the northern reaches and the restless gales that sweep across the Kaelith steppe, channeling them into protective wards, offensive constructs, and navigational aids.
Rune carvers, known as Frostwards, are among the most respected practitioners of magic in the Tsardom, trained for years in the precise geometry and linguistic origins of each rune.

The fundamental principle of rune magic is that frost and wind are not opposed but intertwined — still air holds no frost, and bitter cold begets howling gale — and a master carver learns to read the weather itself as a kind of living text.
Runes must be carved into natural stone, preferably granite or quartz veined with feldspar, as these minerals resonate with the cold frequencies upon which the magic depends.

The carving process involves three stages: the Inscription, in which the rune is cut; the Attuning, in which the carver channels their own life-heat into the stone to create the initial resonance; and the Binding, in which the carver recites the rune's name in the Old Kaelith tongue while exposing the stone to freezing rain or snow.
A fully bound rune can last for decades or even centuries, slowly losing power as weather and time erode the carving, though a skilled Frostward can refresh a fading rune by re-attuning it.

Offensive applications include the Gale Lance — a rune that summons a concentrated blast of freezing wind capable of piercing armor and flesh — and the Frostwall, a barrier of crystallized cold air that can stall an enemy charge.

Defensive uses range from simple ward-stones placed at farmsteads to protect against frostbite during harsh winters, to elaborate fortifications such as the Rune Barriers of Fort Ashenkrag, which have withstood siege for over a century.

The primary institution for training Frostwards is the Athenaeum of Winterlight in the capital city of Morozgrad, where apprentices study for a minimum of seven years before taking the Binding Trials.

There are three recognized schools of thought within the art: the Orthodoxy of the Athenaeum, which holds that rune carving must follow ancient formulas without deviation; the Drift School, which encourages experimentation and the invention of new runes; and the Silent Path, which teaches that the greatest power comes from carving runes so small they are nearly invisible, drawing on subtler currents of cold.

The Tsardom's legal code, the Kaelith Codex of Rights, recognizes Frostwarding as a protected practice and forbids the defacing or destruction of bound runes on penalty of forced labor, reflecting the deep integration of rune magic into the fabric of Kaelith society.

The runic magic practiced across the Tsardom of Moscavia binds the elements of frost and wind into carved stone, creating enduring wards, weapons, and works of art that channel the bitter cold and howling gales of the northern steppes.

Runes are carved into stone using specialized chisels made from meteorite iron, which is believed to carry the memory of cosmic wind. The stone must be natural granite or quartzite, never man-made brick or mortar, for the earth's deep memory to resonate with the binding.

A basic frost rune, known as the Iceveil, lowers the temperature in a radius of roughly ten paces for as long as moonlight touches the stone. Practitioners use them to preserve food, slow rot, and freeze water for travel across rivers in winter.

Wind runes, called Galemarks, can redirect air currents through narrow passages or amplify natural breezes into gale force within an enclosed space. They are carved into the walls of fortress corridors and tower windows to scatter arrows, disperse poisonous gas, or simply keep a garrison dry.

The most advanced practitioners, known as Runeweavers, can inscribe binding sequences — chains of interconnected runes that produce sustained and complex effects, such as a perpetual frost field around a military camp or a spiraling updraft that lifts scouts to observe enemy positions from above.

Training begins at the Froststone Athenaeum in the city of Velikgrad, where apprentices spend their first three years learning the history, theory, and ethical codes of runic magic before ever touching a chisel.

The scholarly society governing runic magic is called the Circle of the Pale Wind, founded in the year 642 by the runeweaver Sviatopolk the Frostfather after he unified the scattered traditions of steppe nomad carving with the stonework knowledge of the river cities.

Practitioners are organized into ranks: Stonecarver for beginners, Frostwarden for those who can sustain effects, Galekeeper for those who master wind bindings, and Runeweaver for those who achieve mastery of both elements in sequence.

Military use of runic magic is overseen by the Winterguard Regiment, which fields Runeweavers as attached specialists to cavalry and siege companies. The Winterguard traces its lineage to the year 823, when Tsarina Yelena I first established a standing force of rune-carvers for wartime service.

The greatest fortress of runic engineering is the Pale Keep on the River Khorov, whose walls are covered in thousands of interlocking runes that maintain sub-freezing temperatures in every chamber, making it nearly impregnable in winter when besieging armies suffer while the garrison remains warm.

Rune carvers, known as Frostwards, are among the most respected practitioners of magic in the Tsardom, trained for years in the precise geometry and linguistic origins of each rune.

Offensive applications include the Gale Lance — a rune that summons a concentrated blast of freezing wind capable of piercing armor and flesh — and the Frostwall, a barrier of crystallized cold air that can stall an enemy charge.
Runes must be carved into natural stone, preferably granite or quartz veined with feldspar, as these minerals resonate with the cold frequencies upon which the magic depends.

The primary institution for training Frostwards is the Athenaeum of Winterlight in the capital city of Morozgrad, where apprentices study for a minimum of seven years before taking the Binding Trials.

The carving process involves three stages: the Inscription, in which the rune is cut; the Attuning, in which the carver channels their own life-heat into the stone to create the initial resonance; and the Binding, in which the carver recites the rune's name in the Old Kaelith tongue while exposing the stone to freezing rain or snow.

The magic draws its power from the deep cold of the northern reaches and the restless gales that sweep across the Kaelith steppe, channeling them into protective wards, offensive constructs, and navigational aids.

The fundamental principle of rune magic is that frost and wind are not opposed but intertwined — still air holds no frost, and bitter cold begets howling gale — and a master carver learns to read the weather itself as a kind of living text.

There are three recognized schools of thought within the art: the Orthodoxy of the Athenaeum, which holds that rune carving must follow ancient formulas without deviation; the Drift School, which encourages experimentation and the invention of new runes; and the Silent Path, which teaches that the greatest power comes from carving runes so small they are nearly invisible, drawing on subtler currents of cold.

facts.text: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a prestigious training institution operated by the Order of the Talon-Scribe, located in Velikoye, the Great City.
It stands on a limestone bluff overlooking the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, its white stone façade carved with intricate rune-work that glimmers silver in the moonlight.

The Academy was established in 999, just one year after the Transformation of Velikoye, to address the urgent need for trained rune scribes capable of adapting the Tsardom's legal and administrative infrastructure to owl-folk governance.
Its name honors the Chiseled Moon rune — an ancient symbol of precision and illumination — and reflects the Order's belief that the best scribes carve truth as cleanly as a blade cuts stone.

The campus occupies a sprawling complex of interconnected buildings arranged around a central courtyard open to the sky, with roosting ledges built into every exterior wall to accommodate owl-folk students during daylight hours.

The Academy teaches all four ranks of the Order: Acolytes begin with foundational rune theory and calligraphy, Scribes advance into practical inscription and legal certification, Master-Scribes study archaic and fragmentary texts, and Keepers of the Talon train in the preservation of endangered rune traditions.

The Academy's permanent faculty consists of Master-Scribes and Keepers of the Talon appointed by the Arch-Talon, supplemented by visiting scholars from the Grand Scriptorium of Velgrad and the Kruzhok Mudykh.

At its heart lies the Moonwell Library, a subterranean archive carved into the bluff's bedrock, where working copies of the Grand Scriptorium's master tablets are kept for student study under controlled conditions.
The Academy maintains close ties with the Night Court, frequently certifying the rune-inscribed documents that form the backbone of Velikoye's nocturnal governance under the Pravda Tsarskaya.

Admission requires a letter of recommendation from a practicing member of the Order and passage of a written examination in basic rune theory, though exceptional candidates of any background may petition for entrance through demonstrated talent.
Students who complete their training at the Chiseled Moon are known informally as 'Moon-carvers,' a term of respect that signals their rigorous preparation and loyalty to the Order's standards.

The Academy's graduates serve throughout the Tsardom, staffing the Order's scriptoria in cities from Velgrad to Novogorod, and many go on to hold positions of influence in provincial and imperial administration.

facts.text: The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a dedicated school of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, established to train aspiring scribes in the art and discipline of rune inscription.

It is housed in a converted stone monastery on the eastern slope of Velikoye's central hill, its bell tower replaced by a tall, narrow spire carved with spiraling rune sequences visible from across the river.

The building's walls are lined with deep-set windows fitted with quartz-paned shutters, allowing students to work by natural light during the day while keeping the interior cool and dim for owl-folk comfort during nighttime study sessions.
The Academy enrolls Acolytes of the Order who have completed their initial examination in rune theory at the Grand Scriptorium of Velgrad and been assigned to Velikoye for practical training.

Its curriculum spans three years, covering advanced rune theory, practical inscription on stone and parchment, the certification of legal documents, and the ethical obligations outlined in the Oath of the Flawless Stroke.

Each year is overseen by a rotating faculty of Master-Scribes drawn from the five chapters of the Order, ensuring that students are exposed to the regional variations in rune tradition that the Order works to harmonize.

The Academy was founded in the year 1000 by decree of the current Arch-Talon, following a recommendation from the Night Court that the Order establish regional training centers to ease the burden on the Grand Scriptorium and bring rune education closer to the provinces.

The site was chosen because the former monastery of Saint Illuminator already possessed deep cellars suitable for storing rune tablets and inscribed stones, and its location near the Theological Academy of Moskov allows for collaborative scholarship between the Talon-Scribes and the clergy.

Graduates of the Academy who successfully complete their final examination are elevated to the rank of Scribe and may certify documents bearing the Talon-Scribe's seal within the Velikoye chapter's jurisdiction.

The Academy's entrance hall features a mural depicting the founding of the Order by Tsar Dmitri the Illuminator, with the Tsar shown presenting the first black talon-shaped inkwell to the Order's first Arch-Talon.

Students are required to wear their black talon inkwells at all times while on the Academy grounds, and senior students are permitted to inscribe temporary practice runes on the stone benches and walkways of the courtyard, which are resurfaced quarterly.

The Academy maintains a small working library of approximately four hundred rune tablets covering common legal and commercial inscriptions, though rare or dangerous texts are stored at Kremnoy Keep and accessed only by authorized Master-Scribes.

facts.text: The White Talon is the heavy regiment of the Frostwing Host, the standing army of the Kingdom of Valdenmere.
It was founded in the year 743 by King Aldric II to serve as the kingdom's elite strike force in mountainous and frozen terrain.
Recruits must survive a six-month trial known as the Frosting, held at the fortress of Karrath Hold in the Greypeak Mountains, to earn the right to wear the regiment's insignia.
The insignia of the White Talon is a talon claw wrought in white iron, worn pinned to the left breast of the surcoat.
Soldiers of the White Talon are issued layered plate-and-mail armor forged at the royal armories of Ironhaven, designed to withstand temperatures as low as minus thirty degrees.
The regiment is currently commanded by General Maren Ashvale, a woman of forty-two winters who earned her rank after the Battle of Thornpass in 987.

The White Talon numbers roughly one thousand five hundred soldiers at full muster, organized into seven companies named after predators of the northern wilderness: Wolf, Lynx, Hawk, Wraith, Ram, Vulture, and Bear.

Each soldier swears the Oath of the White Talon upon completion of the Frosting, pledging to stand firm even when all others fall, to never abandon a comrade alive on the field, and to die rather than surrender their post.

The regiment's standard-bearer carries a banner of deep blue cloth bearing the white talon emblem, and it is said that the banner has been torn and re-stitched forty-seven times across the regiment's history.
The White Talon maintains its headquarters and primary barracks at Karrath Hold, a stone fortress built into the mountainside at an elevation of nearly eight thousand feet.
Soldiers of the White Talon are permitted to grow beards and braid their hair with white cord, distinguishing them from the shaved heads of common soldiers in the Frostwing Host.
The regiment is widely regarded as the most disciplined and deadly fighting force in the northern reaches of the continent, feared by enemies and revered by the people of Valdenmere.

facts.text: The White Talon is the heavy infantry regiment of the Frostwing Host, the standing army of the northern nation of Velmora.

Founded by High Marshal Aldric Vane during the Second Northern Reclamation, the regiment was originally composed of volunteers drawn from the mountain clans of the Greyspine Range who swore the Oath of the White Talon.
Its soldiers are known for wearing white-trimmed plate armor over layered mail, making them instantly recognizable on the battlefield.

Every recruit must pass the Frostproof, a trial in which they stand bare-armed in the open during the deepest hour of a winter night at Fort Ashenmere to prove their endurance against Velmora's brutal cold.
The regiment's standard bears a white gauntlet clutching a shard of ice against a field of midnight blue.
As of the year 1000, the White Talon numbers approximately 1,200 soldiers organized into eight companies, each commanded by a captain called a Talon-Bearer.
The regiment is quartered year-round at Fort Ashenmere, the northernmost permanent garrison in Velmora, built on the ruins of an older structure the mountain clans call Stonethroat Hold.
White Talon soldiers are forbidden by regimental law from retreating more than one hundred paces from their company line without express permission, a rule known as the Chain of Iron.

The current commander of the White Talon is Commander Maren Duskhollow, a veteran of the Border Skirmishes of 983–987 who earned her rank after holding the pass at Greymouth against a force three times her number.
The regiment maintains its own armory and smithy at Ashenmere, where blacksmith Torben Ashvein has personally forged the white-trimmed plate armor for over two hundred soldiers since 980.

The White Talon is considered the elite heavy regiment of the Frostwing Host, and its soldiers are among the highest-paid in Velmora's military, receiving double the standard infantry wage and additional rations during winter campaigns.

Each soldier who completes ten full years of service in the White Talon is entitled to a plot of land in the town of Frosthollow, a settlement that grew up around Fort Ashenmere over the past century.

Soldiers of the White Talon are permitted to grow beards and braid their hair with white cord, distinguishing them from the shaved heads of common soldiers in the Frostwing Host.
The regiment is currently commanded by General Maren Ashvale, a woman of forty-two winters who earned her rank after the Battle of Thornpass in 987.
The regiment is widely regarded as the most disciplined and deadly fighting force in the northern reaches of the continent, feared by enemies and revered by the people of Valdenmere.

Each soldier swears the Oath of the White Talon upon completion of the Frosting, pledging to stand firm even when all others fall, to never abandon a comrade alive on the field, and to die rather than surrender their post.
The insignia of the White Talon is a talon claw wrought in white iron, worn pinned to the left breast of the surcoat.
Recruits must survive a six-month trial known as the Frosting, held at the fortress of Karrath Hold in the Greypeak Mountains, to earn the right to wear the regiment's insignia.
It was founded in the year 743 by King Aldric II to serve as the kingdom's elite strike force in mountainous and frozen terrain.

The White Talon numbers roughly one thousand five hundred soldiers at full muster, organized into seven companies named after predators of the northern wilderness: Wolf, Lynx, Hawk, Wraith, Ram, Vulture, and Bear.

The regiment's standard-bearer carries a banner of deep blue cloth bearing the white talon emblem, and it is said that the banner has been torn and re-stitched forty-seven times across the regiment's history.
The White Talon is the heavy regiment of the Frostwing Host, the standing army of the Kingdom of Valdenmere.
Soldiers of the White Talon are issued layered plate-and-mail armor forged at the royal armories of Ironhaven, designed to withstand temperatures as low as minus thirty degrees.

versions.name: The Frosted Wing

facts.text: The Frosted Wing is a regiment of elite owl-folk archers stationed at the glacier edge of the Tsardom of Moscavia, tasked with defending the northern frontier where the frozen White Sea meets the land.

Founded in the winter of 999, just months after the Transformation of the Tsardom's population, the regiment was assembled from owl-folk who demonstrated exceptional aptitude for long-range flight and archery in harsh, icy conditions.
Its soldiers are known for their distinctive white-and-grey plumage, which serves as natural camouflage against the snow and ice of the northern frontier, and which inspired the regiment's name.

The Frosted Wing operates from a network of stone watchtowers and roosting barns built into the cliff faces along the glacier's edge, connected by elevated wooden walkways that allow rapid deployment across the icy terrain.

Each archer carries a recurve bow of laminated horn and sinew, specially crafted to account for the differences in owl-folk wing structure and the cold-weakened wood available in the north, alongside a quiver of obsidian-tipped arrows designed to shatter upon impact with armored targets.

The regiment's command structure mirrors that of the broader Krylaya Gvardiya, with a *stotnik* (centurion) at its head, but its officers are selected not only for military skill but for their ability to navigate whiteout conditions and lead flights through blizzard weather.

Owl-folk of the Frosted Wing are trained from birth in the northern volosti, identified as recruits by the time they are three years old based on their tolerance for cold, the density of their plumage, and their natural aptitude for sustained high-altitude flight.

The regiment has earned a reputation for executing devastating precision strikes against raiding parties and hostile forces that approach from across the frozen sea, launching volleys from altitudes where no ground-based observer can detect them until the arrows fall.

Its members are also skilled in the construction and maintenance of ice-bridges and emergency shelters along the northern trade routes, serving a dual role as soldiers and frontier engineers in the service of the Tsardom.

The Frosted Wing maintains its own tradition of oral history, passing down accounts of the Transformation itself through song and story, claiming that the first owls of the northern frontier were changed during a blizzard and that their white feathers are a mark of that divine storm.

The regiment is provisioned through supply flights from the interior of the Tsardom, with food and equipment transported by relay teams of owl-folk cargo-flyers who navigate the treacherous winds along the glacier's edge.

elsewhere.text: The Frosted Wing operates under the command structure of the Krylaya Gvardiya but with specialized autonomy granted by the Night Court due to the unique conditions of the northern frontier.

versions.name: The Frosted Wing

facts.text: The Frosted Wing is an elite regiment of owl-folk archers stationed along the northern glacier edge of the Tsardom of Moscavia, tasked with defending the frozen frontier against raiders, beasts, and the creeping cold itself.
Every member of the Frosted Wing is an owl-folk, having been transformed along with the rest of the Tsardom's population on the morning of September 14th, 998.
facts.repeat_of: On the morning of September 14th, 998, every living human being within the borders of the Tsardom was transformed into an owl-folk, an event without precedent or explanation that fundamentally altered the course of Moscavian civilization.

facts.text: The regiment takes its name from the rime-laden feathers that accumulate on its soldiers' wings during winter patrols along the glacier, giving them a shimmering, frost-covered appearance when they fly at night.

Archers of the Frosted Wing are equipped with recurved bows crafted from laminated birch and horn, capable of punching through scale armor at ranges exceeding two hundred paces, and heavy quivers of bodkin-tipped arrows designed to pierce plate.
The regiment's soldiers are trained to hunt and fight in near-total darkness, exploiting their extraordinary nocturnal vision and the disorientation of enemies who cannot see in the polar night.
Frosted Wing archers wear layered gambesons of thick felt lined with downy plumage beneath articulated steel plate, designed to allow full wing mobility while deflecting arrows and blades.

The regiment operates out of a series of fortified stone watchtowers and ice-carved shelters built into the glacier face, connected by narrow ridgelines and zip-lines strung between cliffs for rapid redeployment.

Recruits for the Frosted Wing are drawn from the northernmost volosti of the Tsardom, where the population has long adapted to harsh winter conditions, and must demonstrate exceptional marksmanship, physical endurance, and the ability to fly in freezing winds and whiteouts.
The Frosted Wing answers directly to the *volostnik* of the northern frontier province and reports to the Winged Guard command in Velikoye for matters of strategy and resupply.

During the long polar night, when the sun does not rise for weeks at a time, the Frosted Wing conducts continuous rotating patrols, with soldiers sleeping in shifts inside heated stone bunkers while their comrades watch the ice.
The regiment's insignia is a white owl perched atop a jagged peak, its talons clutching a drawn bowstring, rendered in silver thread on dark blue cloth.

Veterans of the Frosted Wing develop a distinctive appearance: their facial plumage takes on a bluish-grey cast from prolonged exposure to frost, and their taloned feet become thickly padded with calloused horn, adapting them to the ice.

elsewhere.text: The Krylaya Gvardiya's northern frontier regiments, including the Frosted Wing, serve as the first line of defense against threats emerging from beyond the White Sea and the frozen wastes.

The northern glacier edge of the Tsardom, where the Frosted Wing is stationed, marks the boundary between settled lands and the trackless ice — a frontier that raiders and monstrous creatures occasionally cross during the long winter.

versions.name: Frostwing Host

facts.text: The Frostwing Host is the standing army of the Tsardom of Moscavia, the primary military force responsible for the defense of the realm's borders and the enforcement of order within its provinces.

Founded in the years immediately following the Transformation of 998, the Frostwing Host was reorganized to integrate owl-folk biology into its doctrine, tactics, and logistics, creating a military force unlike anything previously seen in the known world.
The army's name derives from the frost-white plumage that many Moscavian owl-folk bear, particularly those stationed in the northern and northeastern frontier regions where cold weather is the norm.

The Frostwing Host operates under the overarching command of the Krylaya Gvardiya (Winged Guard), the Tsar's supreme military authority, but maintains specialized autonomous units adapted to specific frontier conditions.

Its core structure comprises light cavalry, heavy infantry, and elite owl-folk aviation units, each branch specially adapted to operate in the vast, often frozen landscapes of the eastern European plain.

The Host maintains permanent garrison forts along the northern glacier edge, the eastern steppe frontier, and the southern coastlands, each fort serving as a hub for regional defense, supply, and intelligence gathering.

Recruitment into the Frostwing Host is mandatory for all able-bodied owl-folk citizens of the Tsardom, serving a standard term of seven years with the possibility of extended service or career officer commission.

The Host's field commanders are trained at military academies in Velikoye and Moskov, where they study both traditional Rus' warfare and the unique aerial and nocturnal tactics made possible by the owl-folk form.

Logistics are a critical concern for the Frostwing Host, as the army must provision and supply vast distances across a realm stretching from the White Sea to the Caspian steppes, often in winter conditions.

The Host's engineering corps has developed specialized siege equipment adapted for owl-folk operators, including talon-mounted battering implements and elevated ballista platforms built into roosting towers.

In the two years since its reorganization, the Frostwing Host has grown from a hastily assembled frontier militia into a disciplined, professional army of approximately forty thousand soldiers, a figure that continues to expand as new recruitment cycles fill the ranks.

versions.name: Frostwing Host

facts.text: The Frostwing Host is the standing army of the Tsardom of Moscavia, established in the years following the Great Transformation of 998 to defend the realm's borders and enforce the authority of the Tsar.

The Host is organized into three principal branches: the Krylaya Gvardiya (Winged Guard), the heavy infantry and cavalry units, and the specialized frontier regiments stationed along the Tsardom's most exposed borders.

The Host's total strength varies by season and mobilization, but in peacetime fields approximately twelve thousand owl-folk across all branches, supplemented by provincial levies of a similar number in times of war.

The Frosted Wing, a regiment of elite owl-folk archers stationed at the northern glacier edge, operates under the Frostwing Host's command structure but with specialized autonomy granted by the Night Court for frontier defense against raiders from beyond the frozen wastes.
facts.repeat_of: The Frosted Wing is a regiment of elite owl-folk archers stationed at the glacier edge of the Tsardom of Moscavia, tasked with defending the northern frontier where the frozen White Sea meets the land.

facts.text: The Host's senior command is appointed by the Tsar and confirmed by the Night Court, with the overall commander bearing the title of *Voinovo* (Warlord), a position currently held by Boyar Dmitry Snegirev.

Since the Transformation, the Host has had to adapt its tactics, logistics, and equipment to accommodate the owl-folk biology of its soldiers, including the development of talon-proof armor, elevated command platforms, and night-vision-aiding lanterns for operations during the daylight hours when owl-folk are at their weakest.

Traditional infantry and cavalry remain essential to the Host's composition because not all owl-folk are capable of sustained flight, and ground forces are indispensable for siege warfare, river crossings, and the defense of fortified positions.

The Host's cavalry arm, known as the *Konnaya Kholopnya* (Mounted Servitors), rides specially bred horses that have been adapted — through selective breeding programs initiated by the agricultural volosti — to tolerate the taloned passengers they carry.

Recruitment into the Host is mandatory for all able-bodied owl-folk of the Tsardom between the ages of eighteen and fifty, as codified in the revised Pravda Tsarskaya of 999, though exemptions are granted to clergy, scholars of the Theological Academy and the Kruzhok Mudykh, and essential laborers in the grain and fur trades.

The Host maintains permanent garrisons in the major cities of the Tsardom, including Velikoye (Moskov), Velikoye, and along the Khorol River corridor, which serves as a critical supply line for military operations across the southwestern heartlands.

Training for the Frostwing Host is conducted at regional barracks throughout the volosti, with the most elite units — including the Krylaya Gvardiya and the Frosted Wing — undergoing additional instruction at the military academy in Velikoye, where scholars from the Kruzhok Mudykh occasionally lecture on the tactical applications of owl-folk biology.
The Host's insignia is a silver snow owl clutching a bundle of arrows in its talons, set against a field of deep blue, representing the Tsardom's nocturnal nature and martial resolve.

move_here.text: Soldiers of the White Talon are permitted to grow beards and braid their hair with white cord, distinguishing them from the shaved heads of common soldiers in the Frostwing Host.

elsewhere.text: The Tsardom of Moscavia maintains the Frostwing Host as its standing army, which plays a central role in the realm's defense, border security, and the enforcement of the Tsar's authority across the federally organized volosti.

The Krylaya Gvardiya serves as the elite aviator arm of the Frostwing Host, performing duties as scouts, messengers, and shock troops, and operates under the broader command structure of the Host while maintaining distinct training and tactical protocols.

The Frosted Wing is one of the specialized frontier regiments of the Frostwing Host, stationed at the northern glacier edge of the Tsardom and tasked with defending against raiders and monitoring the frozen frontier.

versions.name: Plumage Signaling

facts.text: Plumage Signaling is the primary non-verbal communication system used by the owl-folk of the Tsardom of Moscavia, in which meaning is conveyed through deliberate movements, positioning, and ruffling of body feathers.
Every owl-folk possesses a natural capacity for Plumage Signaling from the moment of transformation, though mastery of the system develops over years of social practice.

Signals are produced by raising, lowering, spreading, or compressing specific clusters of feathers — on the wings, head tufts, breast, shoulders, and tail — in patterns that correspond to distinct words and phrases.
The ear-tufts, or 'ears', play a particularly prominent role in signaling, with their orientation and degree of erection indicating the speaker's emotional state and the urgency of their message.

Plumage Signaling is so deeply embedded in owl-folk culture that it serves as the default mode of communication during formal proceedings of the Night Court, where spoken language is considered supplementary.
The system includes signals for basic greetings, expressions of agreement or dissent, summons, warnings, and emotional states ranging from calm contentment to extreme agitation.

In Velikoye, the lamplight of the Grand Hall casts long shadows across the plumage of Night Court members, and trained observers can read the subtlest shifts in feather position to follow the flow of debate.
Young owl-folk are taught the fundamentals of Plumage Signaling in the early years following transformation, with instruction continuing in households, schools, and guilds throughout life.
The Kruzhok Mudykh has produced several treatises analyzing Plumage Signaling as a language in its own right, comparing its grammar and syntax to human linguistic structures.

Misread signals can lead to social misunderstandings, diplomatic incidents, or even legal disputes — a poorly controlled ruffle of breast feathers might be mistaken for a formal objection during Night Court proceedings.
Plumage Signaling is considered by many owl-folk to be more honest than spoken language, as the body feathers are believed to reflect genuine emotional states that a speaker might otherwise conceal.

elsewhere.text: During sessions of the Night Court, Plumage Signaling is used extensively, with members communicating their positions, objections, and votes through carefully controlled feather movements rather than spoken words.
Plumage Signaling is one of the defining cultural practices of owl-folk civilization, alongside nocturnal governance and the adapted architecture of the Tsardom's cities.

versions.name: Plumage Signaling

facts.text: Plumage Signaling — known colloquially as feather-speech — is the practice among the owl-folk of the Tsardom of Moscavia by which meaning is communicated through the deliberate raising, settling, ruffling, and smoothing of body feathers, supplemented by the position and motion of the feathered ear-tufts atop the head.

It is considered the most socially refined and expressive form of communication among the owl-folk, valued for its nuance and the emotional authenticity of its expressions — feathers, unlike words, are thought to betray the true state of the speaker's heart.

A speaker signals by fluffing out specific patches of plumage — the breast, the shoulders, the ear-tufts, the tail, or the wing-bar — each region carrying its own semantic weight, much as different parts of the human face convey distinct emotions.

Raised breast feathers, for instance, signal openness or vulnerability; puffed wing-bars suggest readiness or alertness; a slow, deliberate smoothing of the ear-tufts indicates calm contemplation or a measured response.

The custom is so deeply embedded in owl-folk social life that even young nestlings instinctively ruffle their feathers when distressed or flatten them when seeking comfort, suggesting that the signaling capacity was present from the moment of the Transformation in 998.

At the Night Court in Velikoye, plumage signaling plays a formal role in proceedings: members are expected to modulate their feathers during debate, and certain ceremonial gestures — such as the Nochnoy Predsedatel spreading both wings in a slow, controlled fan before pronouncing judgment — carry the force of ritual.

The Court has on at least two occasions passed amendments to the Pravda Tsarskaya specifically addressing the legal implications of plumage signaling — most notably in the matter of involuntary signals, which are now treated as inadmissible evidence in criminal proceedings, on the grounds that an owl-folk cannot always control which feathers rise when.

Among the common gestures taught in the educational institutions of Velikoye, the 'greeting fan' — a brief, upward sweep of the secondary wing feathers accompanied by a slight forward tilt of the ear-tufts — serves as a polite salutation equivalent to a human handshake or bow.

Conversely, the 'warning ruffle,' in which an owl-folk bristles the feathers along the entire length of both arms simultaneously, is understood across the Tsardom as a clear signal of displeasure or disagreement, and is considered impolite to direct at one's social superiors without verbal accompaniment.

Scholars of the Kruzhok Mudykh have theorized that plumage signaling may have existed in rudimentary form among the human population before the Transformation, pointing to the universal human habit of 'puffing up' with anger or 'shrinking' with fear as evidence of a deep ancestral connection between feathered expression and emotional state.

The Holy Patriarchate has taken no official position on whether plumage signaling constitutes a form of divine communication, though several Patriarchs have remarked in public homilies that 'the feathers speak as clearly as any tongue, and perhaps more honestly.'

facts.text: The ear-tufts, or 'ears', play a particularly prominent role in signaling, with their orientation and degree of erection indicating the speaker's emotional state and the urgency of their message.
The Kruzhok Mudykh has produced several treatises analyzing Plumage Signaling as a language in its own right, comparing its grammar and syntax to human linguistic structures.
The system includes signals for basic greetings, expressions of agreement or dissent, summons, warnings, and emotional states ranging from calm contentment to extreme agitation.

Signals are produced by raising, lowering, spreading, or compressing specific clusters of feathers — on the wings, head tufts, breast, shoulders, and tail — in patterns that correspond to distinct words and phrases.

In Velikoye, the lamplight of the Grand Hall casts long shadows across the plumage of Night Court members, and trained observers can read the subtlest shifts in feather position to follow the flow of debate.
Young owl-folk are taught the fundamentals of Plumage Signaling in the early years following transformation, with instruction continuing in households, schools, and guilds throughout life.

Misread signals can lead to social misunderstandings, diplomatic incidents, or even legal disputes — a poorly controlled ruffle of breast feathers might be mistaken for a formal objection during Night Court proceedings.

Plumage Signaling is the primary non-verbal communication system used by the owl-folk of the Tsardom of Moscavia, in which meaning is conveyed through deliberate movements, positioning, and ruffling of body feathers.
Plumage Signaling is considered by many owl-folk to be more honest than spoken language, as the body feathers are believed to reflect genuine emotional states that a speaker might otherwise conceal.
Every owl-folk possesses a natural capacity for Plumage Signaling from the moment of transformation, though mastery of the system develops over years of social practice.

Plumage Signaling is so deeply embedded in owl-folk culture that it serves as the default mode of communication during formal proceedings of the Night Court, where spoken language is considered supplementary.

steps.prompt: its winter markets and what they sell

facts.text: The winter markets of Velikoye are among the most vibrant in the Tsardom, operating under the extended hours permitted by the *Pravda Tsarskaya* during the long northern nights, when darkness blankets the city for nearly sixteen hours at a time, giving owl-folk ample opportunity to browse and trade.

Furs dominate the riverfront stalls in winter — dense sable pelts from the northern provinces, thick sheepskin from the steppe volosti, and the prized white ermine of Lake Ladoga — sold in bundles and bolted rolls by merchants who spread their wares across iron-grated tables bolted to the cobblestones.

The braziers of the night markets burn through enormous quantities of pitch-soaked timber during the cold months, and the quartz-lensed light they cast against fresh snowfall transforms the market streets into corridors of pale blue-white radiance, so that even the narrowest alley glows like a lantern.

Artisans in the eastern quarter craft heated stoneware — thick-walled pots and ceramic ovens small enough to warm a single roosting perch — and these sell briskly at the winter markets alongside dried meats, smoked fish from the Volga fleet, and honeyed preserves stored in sealed clay jars.

The Tsar's treasury supplements the winter markets with distributions of salted provisions from the state granaries, ensuring that even the poorest owl-folk in the lower quarters have access to preserved food during the months when hunting is lean and river traffic slows to a trickle.

The winter markets of Velikoye open each evening as the sun sinks behind the Kremlin's white stone walls, their iron braziers lit against the sharp frost and the cobblestone avenues blazing with that unearthly quartz-light, drawing owl-folk from every quarter of the city to browse stalls heaped with salted fish from the Volga, smoked meats hung in dark curtains from timber frames, dried herbs and medicinal roots gathered from the northern forests, warm furs of fox, sable, and wolverine laid out on padded tables, and carved wooden toys and religious icons that the artisans of the eastern slopes turn out in feverish quantities to meet the holiday demand.

Among the most prized wares of the winter markets are the honeyed pastries baked by the confectioners of the merchant quarter, sold warm from iron ovens set up at street corners and wrapped in cloth for the roosting towers, where families share them during the long daylight hours when the city falls into its quiet sleep.

Traders from the outlying volosti bring frozen caviar in wooden pails packed with straw, bundles of dried mushrooms and berries, and bolts of thick wool cloth dyed in deep reds and golds for winter clothing, while the night market's street vendors call out prices for steaming bowls of *kasha* and roasted chestnuts that owl-folk eat perched on the elevated walkways overlooking the stalls below.

The winter markets run from the first frost through the spring thaw, their hours extending later into the night than the summer markets do, because the cold air keeps the owl-folk more active and alert during the dark hours, and because the Tsar's court has traditionally held its winter festivities during this season, drawing nobles and foreign diplomats who spend freely at the stalls.

Before the Transformation of 998, the winter markets were already a celebrated feature of Velikoye, but they were organized along the ground-level streets and did not extend onto the elevated walkways, which were built afterward to accommodate the new owl-folk population and their preference for higher vantage points.

steps.prompt: a failed uprising of the human nobles against the owl-folk Tsar

facts.text: In the spring of 997, a coalition of human noble houses — including the boyars of Rostov, the princely line of Novgorod, and several lesser lords from the northern volosti — launched a coordinated uprising against Tsar Oleg III, whom they accused of using the Transformation to seize powers that had traditionally belonged to the old Rus' aristocracy.

The rebellion, known as the *Voskreseniye Dney* (Resurrection of Days), sought to restore human noble councils and displace owl-folk appointments throughout the provincial volosti, but it collapsed within three months when the Krylaya Gvardiya cut off supply lines along the Khorol River and the Tsar's forces besieged the rebel stronghold of Rostov.

After the suppression of the uprising, Tsar Oleg III convened the Great Council of 998, which produced the revised Pravda Tsarskaya, thereby formalizing many of the legal and administrative changes that had been hastily implemented in the aftermath of the Transformation.

The leaders of the failed rebellion — including Boyar Vladimir of Rostov and Prince Mstislav of Novgorod — were tried under the old provisions of the Pravda and sentenced to exile in the northern frontier volosti near the White Sea, where their knowledge of navigation and trade proved ironically useful to the Tsardom's coastal defenses.

The memory of the Resurrection of Days remains a sensitive subject in Moscavian political culture, and several noble families who participated still harbor quiet resentment, though publicly they have adapted to the new order.

In the spring of 997, a coalition of human nobles from the western provinces—including several former princes of the old Rus' lineage—launched a coordinated revolt against the owl-folk Tsar Ivan III, denouncing the Transformation as ungodly sorcery and demanding the restoration of human rule.

The rebellion, known as the Feathershed Conspiracy, drew support from human-dominated garrison towns along the old Varangian trade routes and from merchant guilds in Velikoye who resented the economic disruptions caused by the Transformation.
The conspiracy's leaders planned to seize the Theological Academy of Moskov and use its theological authority to declare the Transformation void under divine law, thereby legitimizing their coup.

The uprising was betrayed by a volostnik loyal to the Tsar, who intercepted coded messages passed through the fur traders' network along the Khorol River, leading to the arrest of the conspirators before their planned assault on the capital.

In the aftermath, Tsar Ivan III ordered the execution of the ringleaders and the dissolution of the merchant guilds that had supported them, while simultaneously accelerating the integration of owl-folk into the military and government to prevent any future human-dominated resistance.

steps.prompt: two taverns where owl-folk and humans drink together

rows.name: The Roosting Flagon
rows.line: A squat, timber-framed tavern wedged between a tanner's shop and a candle-waxer's stall on the northern slope of Velikoye's second residential ring, the Roosting Flagon is one of the few establishments in the city where owl-folk and humans drink side by side, its low ceiling reinforced with iron bands to bear the taloned landings of its feathered patrons while its wide, ground-level doorways and sturdy oak benches welcome human trade.

rows.name: The Amber Cup
rows.line: Situated on the riverfront of the western Mosca quarter near the grain warehouses, the Amber Cup is a long, single-story tavern built partly over the water on iron-piled pilings, its open-air upper gallery draped in heavy linen curtains that keep out the wind and the midday sun, offering owl-folk a sheltered perch from which they can watch the river traffic while sharing tankards of honey-mead with the dockworkers and merchants who crowd its lower tables.

rows.name: The Hollow Keg Tavern
rows.line: A two-story drinking house in Velikoye's merchant quarter on the western bank of the Moskva, where human traders and owl-folk factors share ale and mead after the day's commerce, its common room built wide and low-ceilinged for taloned patrons, with roosting hooks bolted into every beam.

rows.name: The Drowsy Lantern
rows.line: A narrow, lantern-lit tavern wedged between a candle-maker's shop and a tannery in the eastern artisan quarter of Velikoye, frequented by night-shift workers of both species who seek cheap wine and warm conversation in a space where the ceilings are tall enough for spreading wings and the stairs are built with broad, shallow steps for taloned feet.

The Great Bridge across the Volga, originally a wooden structure of three spans, was demolished and rebuilt in 999 with stone piers and iron-reinforced timber planking, its railings fitted with roosting ledges every few paces to allow owl-folk to rest mid-crossing in high winds.

rows.line: The Chapter House of Aldric Venn in the river city of Omske serves as the regional seat of the Order's Third Chapter in the eastern Tsardom, housing a working scriptorium, a training hall for junior scribes, and an archive of rune tablets pertaining to waterway navigation and hydraulic engineering—disciplines for which Omske's merchants have long demanded the Order's expertise.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon serves as the Order's premier training ground, producing the bulk of its new scribes each year and maintaining a direct line of communication with the Arch-Talon's office in Velgrad.
The Order also functions as the Tsardom's official body for certifying rune-inscribed documents, seals, and legal instruments, giving its scribes a critical role in governance.
The Order is divided into five chapters, each named after a great rune scribe from antiquity, and each chapter oversees a specific region of the Tsardom.
The Order's seat is the Grand Scriptorium of Velgrad, located in the imperial capital of Velgrad itself, which houses the most complete collection of rune tablets ever assembled.
It operates under the direct patronage of the Tsar and maintains a network of scriptoria, libraries, and schools across the Tsardom's major cities.
The Order maintains a fortified library at the fortress of Kremnoy Keep, where rare and dangerous rune texts are stored under heavy guard.
The supreme leader of the Order is the Arch-Talon, a title currently held by a scholar elected for life by the Order's senior members.
All members of the Order swear the Oath of the Flawless Stroke, pledging to serve the Tsardom's runic heritage with precision and humility.

The Order was founded in 643 during the reign of Tsar Dmitri the Illuminator, who recognized the need to standardize and protect the Tsardom's rune traditions after centuries of regional fragmentation.
The Order of the Talon-Scribe is the preeminent institution responsible for the study, transcription, and preservation of the Tsardom's sacred and functional runes.

versions.name: Wattles

facts.text: Among the owl-folk of Velikoye, wattles are pendulous ornaments made from braided leather, silk ribbon, or finely plaited cord, worn hanging from the beak or affixed to the breast feathers just below the chin.

A wattle is crafted to match or complement the wearer's plumage coloration, though some owl-folk choose deliberate contrasts — a tawny owl might wear a dark violet wattle, or a snowy-white citizen might don a crimson one.
Wattles serve as a form of personal identification and social signaling in Velikoye, functioning much like a coat of arms or family crest, though they are individual rather than hereditary.

Each wattle is registered with the *Pravda Tsarskaya* Bureau of Plumage and Accouterment, which maintains a ledger — updated nightly — recording every wattle's color, material, pattern, and the owl-folk to whom it is assigned.

An owl-folk may own multiple wattles and change them seasonally or for different occasions, but only one may be worn at a time in public spaces; wearing an unregistered wattle or a wattle belonging to another citizen is a minor offense under the *Pravda*.

At the winter markets, specialized artisans known as *wattlemakers* set up stalls along the eastern quarter's craft row, where they display their wares on wooden racks and take custom orders based on a client's plumage and personal taste.

The craft of wattle-making is considered a respected, if modest, trade in Velikoye, taught through apprenticeship and governed by the Artisans' Guild of the Eastern Quarter, which sets standards for materials, stitching, and durability.

During the Transformation of 998, when the entire population of Velikoye was changed into owl-folk overnight, many former citizens found themselves without any means of personal identification — no names visible upon their bodies, no clothing that fit their new forms — and the wattle system was established in part to restore order and individual recognition in a city thrown into chaos.

Wattles are also worn by members of the Night Court as markers of rank and office: judges wear deep indigo wattles threaded with silver cord, while petitioners before the court wear simple undyed leather wattles to signify their equal standing as citizens.

Among the clergy of the Holy Patriarchate, wattles are traditionally black and unadorned, reflecting the belief that divine service requires the renunciation of personal vanity, though minor clerical ranks may add a thin gold or copper thread.

Children born after the Transformation — the first generation of owl-folk who never knew human form — receive their first wattle at the age of their initial flight test, typically between six and eight months of age, in a ceremony overseen by the local quarter's *roosting mother* or elder.

The word 'wattle' itself is believed to derive from the Old Slavic *vätŭlŭ*, meaning 'pendant' or 'hanging ornament,' and it entered common speech in Velikoye within months of the Transformation, replacing the earlier human practice of wearing brooches or medallions.

elsewhere.text: The *Pravda Tsarskaya* governs the registration and regulation of wattles through its Bureau of Plumage and Accouterment, which levies modest fees for initial registration and annual renewal, with waivers available for citizens in the lower quarters.

The Night Court enforces wattle regulations as part of its broader jurisdiction over public order in Velikoye, and cases of wattle theft or fraudulent registration are heard by the Minor Sessions court, which convenes three nights per week in the Grand Hall's eastern annex.

Scholars at the Theological Academy have debated whether the wattle custom constitutes a modern invention or an echo of divine intention, noting that certain pre-Transformation Christian icons depict saints wearing pendant ornaments that bear a passing resemblance to wattles.

versions.name: Wattle Custom

facts.text: Among the owl-folk of Velikoye, wattling is the practice of adorning the exterior walls of homes and public buildings with strips of dried flesh — typically salmon or whitefish from the Volga — stretched and pinned in decorative patterns across the facade.
The wattles are prepared in late autumn, when the first hard frosts set the rivers' fish runs in motion and the eastern quarter's smokehouses work night and day to cure the catch.

Each household selects its own pattern and placement, and the resulting displays transform entire streets into tapestries of pale, glistening strips that catch the blue-white light of the market braziers.
facts.repeat_of: The braziers of the night markets burn through enormous quantities of pitch-soaked timber during the cold months, and the quartz-lensed light they cast against fresh snowfall transforms the market streets into corridors of pale blue-white radiance, so that even the narrowest alley glows like a lantern.

facts.text: The custom is said to have originated in the winter of 999, when the city's architects and builders, scrambling to adapt Velikoye's human-scale infrastructure for owl-folk, found that fresh fish stretched across the walls of a roosting house served as both insulation and decoration while the structure was under renovation.

By the following winter, the practice had spread beyond necessity into a matter of pride and identity; the pattern and thickness of a household's wattles signal the family's prosperity, taste, and connection to the river trade.

The strips are pinned with small iron tacks driven into pre-drilled holes in the timber siding, and they are replaced every four to six weeks throughout the cold months, as the drying process eventually renders them brittle.

In the merchant quarter along the Volga riverfront, the competition in wattling is particularly fierce; the wealthiest trade houses commission elaborate lattice designs that can take an entire night-shift crew to install.

Poorer households in the lower quarters use simpler diagonal or crosshatched patterns, but take no less care in their arrangement, and neighborhood pride ensures that even the humblest roosting tower presents a coherent display.
The wattles also serve a practical purpose: the dried fish acts as a mild repellent against the moth-larvae that thrive in the damp warmth of owl-folk roosting nests during winter.

Certain patterns carry symbolic meaning inherited from the old human customs of the pre-Transformation population — a diagonal stripe from lower-left to upper-right, for instance, is considered a ward against misfortune and is especially common in households with young owlets.

The smell of drying fish in the winter markets of Velikoye is inseparable from the sight of wattled facades, and the two together form one of the most distinctive sensory experiences of the Great City's nightlife.

No official body regulates wattling; it is governed entirely by neighborhood custom and personal expression, making it one of the few aspects of owl-folk domestic life that remains entirely free of *Pravda Tsarskaya* oversight.

elsewhere.text: The winter months bring a distinctive scent of drying fish to the city's streets, as households maintain their wattled facades — a custom that has become as much a part of Velikoye's identity as the glowing night markets themselves.

versions.name: Anastasiya Koroleva

facts.text: She is a lean woman of angular features, with deep-set grey eyes that carry a perpetual sharpness behind wire-rimmed spectacles of Tsardom-made glass.
Her dark hair, once black as ink, has silvered at the temples and is kept pulled back in a tight braid coiled beneath her scholar's cap, the traditional black felt hood of the Order.
Her hands are her most distinctive feature—long-fingered, pale, and marked with dozens of faint white scars where she has pressed the chisel too deeply into stone over the decades.
She is meticulous to the point of obsessiveness in her work, maintaining a personal library of annotated copies of every major rune treatise in the Grand Scriptorium, cross-referenced by hand.
Beneath her composed exterior lies a restless, almost feverish curiosity about runes the Order has declared forbidden—archaeic frost-carving patterns predating the Illuminator's reforms.
Born in 953 in the river town of Oryol to a family of minor provincial scribes, she was identified as a prodigy at age twelve and admitted to the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velgrad.
She rose through the Order's ranks with extraordinary speed—Acolyte at fourteen, Scribe at nineteen, Master-Scribe at twenty-seven—setting a record that has never been broken.
She was appointed Chief Scribe of the Order in 998, following the sudden death of her predecessor, Master-Scribe Yuriy Volkov, who had held the position for twenty-three years.
She possesses an exceptional memory for rune glyphs, able to recall the precise stroke order of over three thousand inscribed tablets from memory.

Her carving skill is considered among the finest in the Tsardom—her strokes are so clean and deliberate that fellow scribes have described her work as "as if the stone itself wished to hold the rune."

She secretly practices the carving of pre-643 archaic rune forms in a hidden workshop beneath her private quarters in the Grand Scriptorium, using a set of chisels she had commissioned in secret from a smith in Aldenmere.

She maintains a cautious but cordial relationship with the current Arch-Talon, Eldon Marenkov, though she suspects he is aware of her private carving and tolerates it because her public work is indispensable to the Order.

exceptions.text: She privately practices rune carving forms that the Order has officially prohibited since its founding in 643, and she has not publicly disclosed this activity.

facts.text: She is a tall, angular woman with sharp cheekbones and pale grey eyes that carry a perpetual look of careful assessment, as though she is always reading the air itself.
Her black hair, streaked with silver at the temples, she wears pulled back tightly under a plain linen coif, and her hands are long-fingered and calloused at the tips from decades of stone-carving.
She possesses a quiet, deliberate temperament—she speaks rarely, and when she does, her words are precise and unhurried, each one chosen as though it were a rune to be inscribed.

Beneath her composed exterior lies a deep, restless curiosity about runes that the Order's official doctrine cannot satisfy, and this tension between duty and desire has shaped the secretive strain in her character.
Born in the coastal town of Aldenmere in 953, she entered the Order at age fourteen as an Acolyte under the Chapter House of Aldenmere, dedicated to Vesska the Unbroken.
facts.repeat_of: The Chapter House of Aldenmere, dedicated to the ancient scribe Vesska the Unbroken, serves as the Order of the Talon-Scribe's regional headquarters in the coastal city of Aldenmere, overseeing rune studies and transcription work throughout the southern maritime provinces of the Tsardom.

facts.text: She rose through the ranks with exceptional speed, becoming a Master-Scribe by age thirty-two, recognized for her extraordinary facility with archaic rune forms and her encyclopedic memory of inscribed tablets.

In 991 she was appointed Chief Scribe of the Order, the administrative and scholarly head responsible for overseeing the Grand Scriptorium's daily operations and certifying the authenticity of inscribed documents across the Tsardom.

She can carve runes of remarkable precision and power, capable of inscribing working runes that endure for centuries without fading, a skill that earned her the unofficial title 'the Flawless Blade' among her peers.

She has developed an intimate, almost instinctive understanding of rune resonance—the way individual symbols interact and amplify when carved in proximity to one another—which puts her among the most gifted carvers alive.
She maintains a carefully guarded friendship with Master-Scribe Dmitri Volkov, who shares her private interest in forbidden rune traditions and serves as her only confidant within the Order.

She is the subject of quiet suspicion from Arch-Talon Ilya Sorokin, who has noted her frequent and prolonged visits to the restricted archives of Kremnoy Keep under pretexts that do not satisfy his scrutiny.
She rarely raises her voice and has a habit of pausing before answering any question, as though the silence itself is doing work for her.

versions.name: Vasha Dorokhova

facts.text: She is slight and wiry, standing barely five feet tall, with sun-darkened skin and a sharp, angular face framed by a wild tangle of dark auburn hair that she keeps braided loosely against her neck to keep it out of the way during long rides.
Her eyes are a pale, unremarkable grey-green, quick and observant, set beneath thick brows that give her a perpetually serious expression even when she is amused.
A jagged scar runs along her left forearm, pale and raised, the result of a knife mishap during her Acolyte training when she was seventeen.
Vasha is fiercely independent and stubbornly self-reliant, prone to declining help even when she needs it, which is often.

She has a dry, understated sense of humor that catches people off guard, delivered in a flat tone that makes it difficult to tell whether she is joking until they see the faint curl at the corner of her mouth.
Beneath her prickly exterior she is deeply loyal and protective of those she considers her people, though she would never use that word to describe them.
She was born in the river town of Ostrovok, the second daughter of a fisherman and a midwife, and grew up in a cramped house that smelled of river water and dried herbs.

She was admitted to the Order of the Talon-Scribe as an Acolyte at the age of sixteen after demonstrating exceptional aptitude for reading and memorizing rune sequences, a skill she developed partly from helping her mother catalog medicinal plant properties by their carved leaf-signs.
Vasha rides well and has developed a near-instinctive sense for the roads and byways of the Tsardom, able to navigate between scriptoria with minimal direction once she has made the journey once.

She carries a short blade at her hip as a courier's protection, and while she is no swordsman, she knows how to use it well enough to have talked her way out of two ambushes and fought her way out of a third.

She has a near-photographic memory for handwriting and seal impressions, which makes her particularly valuable as a courier since she can verify the authenticity of documents she carries against mental records.

She reports to Chief Scribe Anastasiya Koroleva at the Grand Scriptorium, who assigned her to courier work after noting that her talents lay more in speed and vigilance than in the patient, painstaking work of inscription.
