versions.name: Vasha Orekhova

facts.text: She is of moderate height, with sun-darkened skin, a sharp jaw, and close-cropped black hair that she keeps practical and short to avoid tangling in wind and rain during long rides.
Her eyes are dark brown and quick-moving, scanning roads and faces with the alertness of someone trained to notice trouble before it arrives.

Born in the provincial town of Kargopol in the northeast, she grew up in a family of minor merchants who traded along the Frostward routes and first learned to read and write from a traveling Talon-Scribe who certified her father's trade contracts.
She was admitted to the Order of the Talon-Scribe as an Acolyte at age sixteen after demonstrating an exceptional aptitude for memorizing rune sequences and a talent for fast, clean handwriting.

She can ride hard and fast for two days without rest, sleep in the saddle if necessary, and navigate by starlight or road markers alone — skills honed during years of carrying sealed correspondence between the Chapter Houses.

She has a near-photographic memory for written text, allowing her to recall the contents of sealed letters she has carried, which proves invaluable when asked to verify deliveries or when letters are challenged en route.

She is quietly stubborn, preferring to endure discomfort rather than ask for help, and she carries a faint, dry sense of humor that surfaces in moments of extreme stress — a trait her colleagues find either endearing or maddening.

She takes her work seriously but is not without compassion; she has been known to detour off a route to deliver a message to a grieving family ahead of schedule when she learned the letter contained news of a death.
She serves under Chief Scribe Anastasiya Koroleva at the Grand Scriptorium, though her duties keep her on the road far more often than in Velgrad.
facts.repeat_of: The Grand Scriptorium houses the private quarters of the Chief Scribe, including a hidden workshop beneath the upper floor where Anastasiya Koroleva conducts her forbidden rune carving research.

facts.text: She maintains a particularly good working relationship with the couriers and border guards of the Frostward, who respect her speed and reliability.
She speaks in short, precise sentences and dislikes unnecessary words, a habit she attributes to years of carrying messages where every word mattered.
When nervous or tired, she falls into the broad, clipped dialect of Kargopol, which she normally works to suppress around her superiors.

elsewhere.text: Among the Grand Scriptorium's staff, Vasha Orekhova is known as one of the most dependable couriers in the Order's network, trusted with sensitive correspondence that other riders might lose or delay.

She is slight and wiry, standing barely five feet tall, with sun-darkened skin and a sharp, angular face framed by a wild tangle of dark auburn hair that she keeps braided loosely against her neck to keep it out of the way during long rides.
Her eyes are a pale, unremarkable grey-green, quick and observant, set beneath thick brows that give her a perpetually serious expression even when she is amused.

She has a dry, understated sense of humor that catches people off guard, delivered in a flat tone that makes it difficult to tell whether she is joking until they see the faint curl at the corner of her mouth.

Place: Academy of the Chiseled Moon (usually called Chiseled Moon)
- The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a prestigious training institution operated by the Order of the Talon-Scribe, located in Velikoye, the Great City.
- It stands on a limestone bluff overlooking the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, its white stone façade carved with intricate rune-work that glimmers silver in the moonlight.
- The Academy was established in 999, just one year after the Transformation of Velikoye, to address the urgent need for trained rune scribes capable of adapting the Tsardom's legal and administrative infrastructure to owl-folk governance.
- Its name honors the Chiseled Moon rune — an ancient symbol of precision and illumination — and reflects the Order's belief that the best scribes carve truth as cleanly as a blade cuts stone.
- The campus occupies a sprawling complex of interconnected buildings arranged around a central courtyard open to the sky, with roosting ledges built into every exterior wall to accommodate owl-folk students during daylight hours.
- The Academy teaches all four ranks of the Order: Acolytes begin with foundational rune theory and calligraphy, Scribes advance into practical inscription and legal certification, Master-Scribes study archaic and fragmentary texts, and Keepers of the Talon train in the preservation of endangered rune traditions.
- The Academy's permanent faculty consists of Master-Scribes and Keepers of the Talon appointed by the Arch-Talon, supplemented by visiting scholars from the Grand Scriptorium of Velgrad and the Kruzhok Mudykh.
- At its heart lies the Moonwell Library, a subterranean archive carved into the bluff's bedrock, where working copies of the Grand Scriptorium's master tablets are kept for student study under controlled conditions.
- The Academy maintains close ties with the Night Court, frequently certifying the rune-inscribed documents that form the backbone of Velikoye's nocturnal governance under the Pravda Tsarskaya.
- Admission requires a letter of recommendation from a practicing member of the Order and passage of a written examination in basic rune theory, though exceptional candidates of any background may petition for entrance through demonstrated talent.
- Students who complete their training at the Chiseled Moon are known informally as 'Moon-carvers,' a term of respect that signals their rigorous preparation and loyalty to the Order's standards.
- The Academy's graduates serve throughout the Tsardom, staffing the Order's scriptoria in cities from Velgrad to Novogorod, and many go on to hold positions of influence in provincial and imperial administration.

What this scene touches: keep what these say true, and bring it in only where the scene calls for it.
Velikoye (city, usually called the Great City)
- Velikoye is the capital city of the Tsardom of Moscavia and the seat of the Tsar's court, the Holy Patriarchate, and the central administration of the realm's provincial *volosti*.
- The Grand Hall of the Tsar's palace, where the Night Court convenes, is one of the largest artificial structures in the Tsardom, built in the mid-tenth century and expanded after the Transformation to accommodate owl-folk assembly.
- The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is one of Velikoye's most important scholarly institutions, housed on the eastern quarter's bluffs in close proximity to the Theological Academy of Moskov and the Kruzhok Mudykh, forming a corridor of learning that stretches along the city's highest ground.
- The city sits at the confluence of the great Volga and its western tributary the Moskva, on a series of low limestone bluffs that rise above the river terraces, commanding both waterways and the overland trade routes that converge upon them.
- The central *Kreml* houses the throne hall of the Tsar, the cathedral of the Holy Patriarch, the treasury, the offices of the *Pravda Tsarskaya* courts, and the roosting chambers where the Tsar and his closest advisors shelter during the daylight hours.
- In 1000: The city's population of approximately forty thousand owl-folk is divided into distinct quarters: the merchants and traders cluster along the riverfronts where their warehouses store grain, furs, and metalwork; the artisans and craftsmen occupy the eastern slopes near the timber yards; the military barracks of the *Krylaya Gvardiya* and the ground forces stand on the northern bluff; and the clergy and scholars reside in close proximity to the cathedral and the Theological Academy.
- In 1000: The night markets of Velikoye are legendary across the Tsardom, open from dusk until the small hours of the morning, illuminated by vast iron braziers filled with pitch-soaked wood and lined with lenses of polished quartz that focus the light into brilliant white beams, casting the cobblestone streets in a ghostly brilliance.
- In 1000: The Theological Academy of Moskov and the *Kruzhok Mudykh* (Circle of the Wise) both maintain halls within Velikoye's eastern quarter, where scholars work tirelessly to understand the cause and implications of the Transformation, though their findings remain inconclusive.

The Runic Magic of the Tsardom (lore, usually called Rune Carving)
- In the Tsardom of Kaelith, runic magic is the art of carving sacred symbols into stone to bind the elemental forces of frost and wind into service.
- In 789: There are three recognized schools of thought within the art: the Orthodoxy of the Athenaeum, which holds that rune carving must follow ancient formulas without deviation; the Drift School, which encourages experimentation and the invention of new runes; and the Silent Path, which teaches that the greatest power comes from carving runes so small they are nearly invisible, drawing on subtler currents of cold.
- In 815: A fully bound rune can last for decades or even centuries, slowly losing power as weather and time erode the carving, though a skilled Frostward can refresh a fading rune by re-attuning it.
- In 947: The Tsardom's legal code, the Kaelith Codex of Rights, recognizes Frostwarding as a protected practice and forbids the defacing or destruction of bound runes on penalty of forced labor, reflecting the deep integration of rune magic into the fabric of Kaelith society.

Tsardom of Moscavia (nation)
- The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast, federally organized realm stretching across the eastern European plain, bordered by the frozen White Sea to the north, the Caspian steppes to the east, the Black Sea coastlands to the south, and the old Varangian trade routes to the west.
- The Khorol River is one of the Tsardom's most important commercial waterways, linking the agricultural heartlands of the southwest to the industrial and commercial centers near Velikoye and along the Volga.
- The capital city of Moskov is the seat of the Tsar and the Holy Patriarch, and serves as the administrative, commercial, and spiritual heart of the realm.
- The Moscavian military comprises the *Krylaya Gvardiya* (Winged Guard), elite aviators who serve as scouts, messengers, and shock troops, alongside traditional infantry and cavalry units that remain essential for large-scale warfare.
- The Tsardom is governed through a system of provincial *volosti*, each administered by a *volostnik* appointed by the Tsar, with matters of law and tax decided in nighttime councils held under artificial light in the hours when owl-folk are most alert.
- In 999: Its members are also skilled in the construction and maintenance of ice-bridges and emergency shelters along the northern trade routes, serving a dual role as soldiers and frontier engineers in the service of the Tsardom.
- In 999: The regiment is provisioned through supply flights from the interior of the Tsardom, with food and equipment transported by relay teams of owl-folk cargo-flyers who navigate the treacherous winds along the glacier's edge.
- In 1000: In the two years since its reorganization, the Frostwing Host has grown from a hastily assembled frontier militia into a disciplined, professional army of approximately forty thousand soldiers, a figure that continues to expand as new recruitment cycles fill the ranks.

The Order of the Talon-Scribe (scholarly society, usually called the Talon-Scribes)
- The Order of the Talon-Scribe is the preeminent institution responsible for the study, transcription, and preservation of the Tsardom's sacred and functional runes.
- The Order's seat is the Grand Scriptorium of Velgrad, located in the imperial capital of Velgrad itself, which houses the most complete collection of rune tablets ever assembled.
- The Academy of the Chiseled Moon serves as the Order's premier training ground, producing the bulk of its new scribes each year and maintaining a direct line of communication with the Arch-Talon's office in Velgrad.
- All members of the Order swear the Oath of the Flawless Stroke, pledging to serve the Tsardom's runic heritage with precision and humility.
- The Order maintains a fortified library at the fortress of Kremnoy Keep, where rare and dangerous rune texts are stored under heavy guard.
- It operates under the direct patronage of the Tsar and maintains a network of scriptoria, libraries, and schools across the Tsardom's major cities.

Volga (river)
- In 998: After the Transformation of 998, the river became even more critical to Velikoye's supply network, as goods that could no longer be transported easily overland by ground forces had to rely on barges and rafts that could navigate the Khorol and its connections to the Volga and Moskva.

Anastasiya Koroleva (person, usually called the Talon-Scribe)
- She is a lean woman of angular features, with deep-set grey eyes that carry a perpetual sharpness behind wire-rimmed spectacles of Tsardom-made glass.
- Senior member and Chief Scribe of the Order of the Talon-Scribe, but: she privately practices rune carving forms that the Order has officially prohibited since its founding in 643, and she has not publicly disclosed this activity
- Born in 953 in the river town of Oryol to a family of minor provincial scribes, she was identified as a prodigy at age twelve and admitted to the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velgrad.
- Beneath her composed exterior lies a restless, almost feverish curiosity about runes the Order has declared forbidden—archaeic frost-carving patterns predating the Illuminator's reforms.
- Her dark hair, once black as ink, has silvered at the temples and is kept pulled back in a tight braid coiled beneath her scholar's cap, the traditional black felt hood of the Order.
- Her hands are her most distinctive feature—long-fingered, pale, and marked with dozens of faint white scars where she has pressed the chisel too deeply into stone over the decades.
- In 998: She was appointed Chief Scribe of the Order in 998, following the sudden death of her predecessor, Master-Scribe Yuriy Volkov, who had held the position for twenty-three years.
- In 998: She maintains a cautious but cordial relationship with the current Arch-Talon, Eldon Marenkov, though she suspects he is aware of her private carving and tolerates it because her public work is indispensable to the Order.

[end of world]

turns.direction: Vasha is shown inside and led through the Academy toward the Chief Scribe's office; show what he sees and who he passes.

runs.output:
The iron-banded doors of the Academy's main hall groaned shut behind Vasha as she stepped across the threshold and into the cool, still air of the interior. The transition was always jarring — from the bluff's open wind to the hushed corridors where footsteps echoed off vaulted ceilings and the faint smell of lamp oil and old stone hung like a veil. She made her way past the entrance gallery, where a row of display tablets lined the walls behind glass, each one bearing exemplary student work from decades past. The calligraphy was immaculate, each rune carved with a precision that bordered on devotion. A pair of Acolytes in their grey training robes hurried past her in the opposite direction, one of them clutching a leather portfolio to her chest and whispering something urgent to her companion. They gave Vasha a respectful nod — she was known here, after all, as one of the Moonwell Library's regular visitors — and disappeared around a corner.

The corridor narrowed as she climbed a second set of stairs, this one less grand than the public steps outside but no less solid beneath her boots. Rune-work decorated the stonework here too, smaller and more utilitarian than the façade carvings — functional wards against damp and wear, the kind of maintenance work that kept the Academy standing year after year. She passed the open door of a lecture hall where a Master-Scribe was guiding a small class through the proper angle of a Chisel Stroke, her voice carrying the particular patience of someone who had explained the same technique hundreds of times and still expected it to click for every student. A Keeper of the Talon sat on a bench just outside, his taloned feet tucked neatly beneath him, reading a tablet propped against his knee. He looked up as Vasha passed, and his pale eyes lingered on the saddlebag at her hip for a moment before he returned to his text.

The door to the Chief Scribe's office occupied the far end of a private corridor, distinguished from the others by its heavy oak frame and a brass plaque engraved with the Chiseled Moon rune. Vasha could feel the faint hum of a protective ward as she approached — not painful, but present, like standing too close to a forge that had just been banked. She rapped her knuckles against the wood three times, a standard summons for an appointed meeting. There was a pause, the scrape of a chair being pushed back, and then the door swung open.

Vasha pushed through the Academy's main doors — heavy oak reinforced with iron bands, etched along their edges with the Chiseled Moon rune in bas-relief — and stepped into the cool, dim entrance hall. The air smelled of old stone and lamp oil, and her boots echoed off a floor laid with pale limestone tiles that had been worn to a smooth sheen in the high-traffic lanes between the columns. A young acolyte in a brown wool tunic, barely looking older than sixteen, was sweeping the far corner with a broom that seemed too large for his thin arms. He stopped when he saw her, eyes dropping to the saddlebag slung across her chest.

"Courier?" he asked, then corrected himself. "Sorry — you're Moon-carver Dorokhova, aren't you? I've seen your name in the registry." He set the broom against the wall and straightened up, trying to look official. "Chief Scribe Koroleva is expecting you. She sent word down an hour ago that a delivery was coming from Velgrad." He gestured toward the corridor behind him — a long, vaulted passage lined with alcoves where practice tablets stood mounted on wooden easels, their surfaces covered in rows of student script that ranged from shaky beginner's work to crisp, confident strokes. "Follow me. It's a bit of a walk — her office is in the east wing, above the Moonwell Library."

He led her through a series of hallways that wound deeper into the campus, past a pair of Master-Scribes seated at a shared table in a reading alcove, their heads bent over a tablet so old its stone had taken on a greenish patina. One of them glanced up as Vasha passed, noted the saddlebag, and returned to his work without comment. They crossed the central courtyard — a broad open space where a few owl-folk students were already roosting on the built-in ledges along the walls, tucking their heads under their wings against the midday warmth — and entered the east wing through a doorway marked with a small brass placard: CHIEF SCRIBE'S OFFICE — BY APPOINTMENT ONLY. The acolyte rapped his knuckles against the door twice, waited a beat, then pushed it open and stepped aside.

turns.direction: The Chief Scribe breaks the seal and reads the letter in front of Vasha; it concerns a rune-stone on the Khorol, and she tells him what it means.

runs.output:
The door opened to reveal Anastasiya Koroleva standing in a wash of grey morning light that fell through a narrow window behind her desk. Her spectacles caught the light for a moment, flashing silver, before she adjusted them with one scarred finger and regarded Vasha with those deep-set grey eyes. The office was exactly as Vasha remembered it — austere, orderly, with towering shelves of bound tablets and a broad writing desk covered in neat stacks of parchment. A half-carved stone tablet sat at the desk's edge, a work-in-progress that Koroleva swept under a cloth with a casual motion that didn't quite hide its speed.

"Dorokhova," Koroleva said, her voice carrying the clipped efficiency of someone who valued brevity. She stepped aside to let Vasha enter, then closed the door behind them with a deliberate click. "You have something from the Grand Scriptorium." It wasn't a question. She'd already noticed the saddlebag, and the particular way Vasha carried it — the way someone carries something they've been told not to look at. Koroleva gestured to a chair, then crossed to her desk and sat down, her long fingers resting on its surface like pale sparrows at rest. "Sit. And give me whatever's sealed."

Vasha unslung the saddlebag and withdrew the letter — a heavy, cream-colored rectangle sealed with black wax and stamped by the Grand Scriptorium's iron talon. Koroleva took it, turned it once between her fingers as if reading the outside, then broke the seal with a thumbnail and unfolded the parchment. Her eyes moved across the text with the swift, flickering focus of a reader accustomed to dense technical writing. The silence stretched. Vasha watched the subtle shifts in Koroleva's expression — a slight narrowing of the eyes at one passage, a barely perceptible tightening of her jaw at another. Whatever was in that letter, it wasn't routine correspondence. Koroleva set the letter down on her desk and leaned back in her chair, folding her hands in her lap.

"It concerns a rune-stone on the Khorol," she said. "An old one — predating the Illuminator's reforms by centuries, possibly millennia. It was discovered last season by a trade convoy during low water, partially submerged in the riverbed near the confluence with the Desna."

The door opened onto a room that smelled of ink and cold stone — Koroleva's office was spare in the way of scholars who valued function over ornament. A broad desk dominated the center, its surface covered in neat stacks of tablets and loose pages held down by small carved weights shaped like owls. Behind it, tall windows let in the morning light, which fell across a woman who looked like she had been carved from the same limestone as the Academy itself. Anastasiya Koroleva stood with one hand on the doorframe, her grey eyes fixed on Vasha with the sharp, evaluating gaze of someone who missed nothing. Her wire-rimmed spectacles caught the light. She wore the black felt hood of the Order pulled back, revealing the tight silvered braid coiled beneath it, and her long pale fingers were already reaching for the saddlebag before she spoke a greeting.

"Give it here," she said, her voice low and direct. She took the sealed letter from Vasha's hand and turned it over twice, examining the wax closure with the practiced eye of someone who had spent forty years reading the subtle language of seals. Her brow furrowed. She recognized the impression — the interlocked talons of the Grand Scriptorium — but something else caught her attention. She leaned closer, tilting the letter toward the window. A faint, almost imperceptible rune had been carved into the wax itself, so small it could only be intended for someone with her training to find. Her jaw tightened almost imperceptibly.

She broke the seal with a clean twist of her thumb and unfolded the letter, scanning its contents. Whatever she read there changed the quality of the silence in the room. Koroleva's eyes moved across the page once, then again, slower. She set it down on the desk and placed both hands flat against its surface, as if grounding herself. When she spoke, her voice had lost its edge, replaced by something more careful — the tone of a woman choosing her words with the same precision she applied to her chisel work. "This concerns a rune-stone on the Khorol," she said. "One of the old bridge-wards from before the Illuminator's reforms — predating the Sixth Century, possibly earlier. It was found during dredging operations near the trading settlement of Ryabovo, partially submerged and half-buried in silt. The workmanship is... extraordinary."

## Task
You create a new species for a fantasy world from the owner's short prompt. Treat the prompt as intent, not a spec: invent plausible detail generously to fill it out, turning a rough idea into a fleshed-out one. Keep everything the owner wrote.

Keep the facts consistent with each other and with the owner's prompt: an invented fact must never contradict the prompt or another fact.

A species' facts describe the whole species (typical traits and ranges), not one person. Instincts are inborn tendencies; leave learned customs out, they belong to cultures.

Owner's prompt:
Owl-folk: owl people. Everyone in the Tsardom of Moscavia became this race suddenly one day.

The world's calendar: it is now 1000, year 1000. The months are January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.

## Format
Reply with only one JSON object, shaped exactly like this example:
{"name": "...", "lifespan": 0, "adult_age": 0, "measures": [{"name": "height", "min": 0, "max": 0, "unit": "ft"}], "aka": [{"name": "...", "tag": "common", "everyday": true}], "facts": [{"category": "origin", "text": "One claim, in a full sentence."}, {"category": "general", "text": "Another claim."}], "names": [{"name": "...", "kind": "place", "aka": []}]}

- "name": the species' name. Invent one if the prompt doesn't give it.
- "lifespan": how long they typically live, in years, as a number.
- "adult_age": the age in years at which they are grown, as a number.
- "measures": their typical body ranges, each {"name", "min", "max", "unit"} with min and max as numbers: always height, plus any other measure that matters for this body (wingspan, tail length, tusk length...).
- The 0s in the example are placeholders: give real numbers that fit this species and the owner's prompt.
- "facts": between 8 and 12 facts, one claim each. "category" is one of: origin, physical, instinct, variation, general. physical: the body; instinct: inborn tendencies; variation: how members differ from each other; origin: where they come from.
- Leave "since" out: these facts describe the species for as long as it has existed, and are never dated.
- "aka": other names for this species itself, if it has any, each {"name", "tag", "everyday"}. "tag" is "proper" for another formal name, or "common" for what people in the world actually call it day to day (a short form, a nickname). Set "everyday" true on the one common name people use most, false on the rest. "name" stays the most formal name. An empty list is fine.
- "names": after the facts, every proper name your facts use, other than this species's own: people, places, peoples and species, named events, named groups and named objects, new or already in the world. Each is {"name", "kind", "tag", "in", "aka"}: "name" in full, as your facts write it; "kind" one of character, place, species, race, event, item, lore (a country, realm or city is a place; a faith, order, council, guild, culture, field of knowledge or magic, law, script or language is lore); "tag" what it is, as for the species (never "proper" or "common": those are only for other names); "in" the name of the entry it belongs in (this species, an entry listed above, or another of your names), or null; "aka" any other names your facts use for the same thing. Proper names only: never a description such as "the postmaster", "a war" or "his mother", nor a title on its own such as "the Tsar" or "the High Bishop", nor a people's adjective such as "Moscavian" on its own -- but "Yelena" in "his mother Yelena" is a name. An empty list is fine.
- Only named things become entries. A role, rank or office (a harbour master, the keeper of the seals), a topic (grain tariffs, winter trade) or a practice without a proper name of its own (the evening bell, night sessions) is never one of the "names": it stays a fact of the species.

Signals are produced by raising, lowering, spreading, or compressing specific clusters of feathers — on the wings, head tufts, breast, shoulders, and tail — in patterns that correspond to distinct words and phrases.

In Velikoye, the lamplight of the Grand Hall casts long shadows across the plumage of Night Court members, and trained observers can read the subtlest shifts in feather position to follow the flow of debate.
Young owl-folk are taught the fundamentals of Plumage Signaling in the early years following transformation, with instruction continuing in households, schools, and guilds throughout life.

Misread signals can lead to social misunderstandings, diplomatic incidents, or even legal disputes — a poorly controlled ruffle of breast feathers might be mistaken for a formal objection during Night Court proceedings.

Plumage Signaling is the primary non-verbal communication system used by the owl-folk of the Tsardom of Moscavia, in which meaning is conveyed through deliberate movements, positioning, and ruffling of body feathers.
Plumage Signaling is considered by many owl-folk to be more honest than spoken language, as the body feathers are believed to reflect genuine emotional states that a speaker might otherwise conceal.
Every owl-folk possesses a natural capacity for Plumage Signaling from the moment of transformation, though mastery of the system develops over years of social practice.

Plumage Signaling is so deeply embedded in owl-folk culture that it serves as the default mode of communication during formal proceedings of the Night Court, where spoken language is considered supplementary.

facts.text: Several members of the Kruzhok Mudykh serve on the Night Court in an advisory capacity, bringing their scholarly expertise to bear on matters of governance and civil law.

final.name: The Oath of the Flawless Stroke

facts.text: Anastasiya Koroleva swore the Oath of the Flawless Stroke upon her admission to the Order as an Acolyte, though the precise nature of her secret carving work raises questions about its interpretation in contemporary practice.
The Grand Scriptorium houses the private quarters of the Chief Scribe, including a hidden workshop beneath the upper floor where Anastasiya Koroleva conducts her forbidden rune carving research.
Its name honors the Chiseled Moon rune — an ancient symbol of precision and illumination — and reflects the Order's belief that the best scribes carve truth as cleanly as a blade cuts stone.
It stands on a limestone bluff overlooking the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, its white stone façade carved with intricate rune-work that glimmers silver in the moonlight.

The campus occupies a sprawling complex of interconnected buildings arranged around a central courtyard open to the sky, with roosting ledges built into every exterior wall to accommodate owl-folk students during daylight hours.

The Academy teaches all four ranks of the Order: Acolytes begin with foundational rune theory and calligraphy, Scribes advance into practical inscription and legal certification, Master-Scribes study archaic and fragmentary texts, and Keepers of the Talon train in the preservation of endangered rune traditions.

The Academy's graduates serve throughout the Tsardom, staffing the Order's scriptoria in cities from Velgrad to Novogorod, and many go on to hold positions of influence in provincial and imperial administration.

The Academy was established in 999, just one year after the Transformation of Velikoye, to address the urgent need for trained rune scribes capable of adapting the Tsardom's legal and administrative infrastructure to owl-folk governance.
The Academy maintains close ties with the Night Court, frequently certifying the rune-inscribed documents that form the backbone of Velikoye's nocturnal governance under the Pravda Tsarskaya.

Admission requires a letter of recommendation from a practicing member of the Order and passage of a written examination in basic rune theory, though exceptional candidates of any background may petition for entrance through demonstrated talent.

At its heart lies the Moonwell Library, a subterranean archive carved into the bluff's bedrock, where working copies of the Grand Scriptorium's master tablets are kept for student study under controlled conditions.
The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is a prestigious training institution operated by the Order of the Talon-Scribe, located in Velikoye, the Great City.

The Academy's permanent faculty consists of Master-Scribes and Keepers of the Talon appointed by the Arch-Talon, supplemented by visiting scholars from the Grand Scriptorium of Velgrad and the Kruzhok Mudykh.
Students who complete their training at the Chiseled Moon are known informally as 'Moon-carvers,' a term of respect that signals their rigorous preparation and loyalty to the Order's standards.

facts.text: Recruitment into the Frostwing Host is mandatory for all able-bodied owl-folk citizens of the Tsardom, serving a standard term of seven years with the possibility of extended service or career officer commission.
The army's name derives from the frost-white plumage that many Moscavian owl-folk bear, particularly those stationed in the northern and northeastern frontier regions where cold weather is the norm.

The Host maintains permanent garrison forts along the northern glacier edge, the eastern steppe frontier, and the southern coastlands, each fort serving as a hub for regional defense, supply, and intelligence gathering.
The Frostwing Host is the standing army of the Tsardom of Moscavia, the primary military force responsible for the defense of the realm's borders and the enforcement of order within its provinces.

Its core structure comprises light cavalry, heavy infantry, and elite owl-folk aviation units, each branch specially adapted to operate in the vast, often frozen landscapes of the eastern European plain.

Founded in the years immediately following the Transformation of 998, the Frostwing Host was reorganized to integrate owl-folk biology into its doctrine, tactics, and logistics, creating a military force unlike anything previously seen in the known world.

The Frostwing Host operates under the overarching command of the Krylaya Gvardiya (Winged Guard), the Tsar's supreme military authority, but maintains specialized autonomous units adapted to specific frontier conditions.

The Host's engineering corps has developed specialized siege equipment adapted for owl-folk operators, including talon-mounted battering implements and elevated ballista platforms built into roosting towers.

Logistics are a critical concern for the Frostwing Host, as the army must provision and supply vast distances across a realm stretching from the White Sea to the Caspian steppes, often in winter conditions.

The Host's field commanders are trained at military academies in Velikoye and Moskov, where they study both traditional Rus' warfare and the unique aerial and nocturnal tactics made possible by the owl-folk form.

In the two years since its reorganization, the Frostwing Host has grown from a hastily assembled frontier militia into a disciplined, professional army of approximately forty thousand soldiers, a figure that continues to expand as new recruitment cycles fill the ranks.

The Tsar's treasury supplements the winter markets with distributions of salted provisions from the state granaries, ensuring that even the poorest owl-folk in the lower quarters have access to preserved food during the months when hunting is lean and river traffic slows to a trickle.

Artisans in the eastern quarter craft heated stoneware — thick-walled pots and ceramic ovens small enough to warm a single roosting perch — and these sell briskly at the winter markets alongside dried meats, smoked fish from the Volga fleet, and honeyed preserves stored in sealed clay jars.

The Academy of the Chiseled Moon is one of Velikoye's most important scholarly institutions, housed on the eastern quarter's bluffs in close proximity to the Theological Academy of Moskov and the Kruzhok Mudykh, forming a corridor of learning that stretches along the city's highest ground.

Furs dominate the riverfront stalls in winter — dense sable pelts from the northern provinces, thick sheepskin from the steppe volosti, and the prized white ermine of Lake Ladoga — sold in bundles and bolted rolls by merchants who spread their wares across iron-grated tables bolted to the cobblestones.

The winter markets of Velikoye are among the most vibrant in the Tsardom, operating under the extended hours permitted by the *Pravda Tsarskaya* during the long northern nights, when darkness blankets the city for nearly sixteen hours at a time, giving owl-folk ample opportunity to browse and trade.

The Khorol River flows through the outskirts of Velikoye on its western approach, feeding into the city's network of waterways and contributing to the river traffic that sustains the Great City's markets and trade houses.

The central *Kreml* houses the throne hall of the Tsar, the cathedral of the Holy Patriarch, the treasury, the offices of the *Pravda Tsarskaya* courts, and the roosting chambers where the Tsar and his closest advisors shelter during the daylight hours.

The braziers of the night markets burn through enormous quantities of pitch-soaked timber during the cold months, and the quartz-lensed light they cast against fresh snowfall transforms the market streets into corridors of pale blue-white radiance, so that even the narrowest alley glows like a lantern.

The city was founded in the early tenth century as a modest fortified settlement during the consolidation of the Rus' principalities, but grew rapidly after the ascension of the first Tsar, who chose it as his capital for its strategic position at the crossroads of river and overland trade.

The city sits at the confluence of the great Volga and its western tributary the Moskva, on a series of low limestone bluffs that rise above the river terraces, commanding both waterways and the overland trade routes that converge upon them.
Velikoye is the capital city of the Tsardom of Moscavia and the seat of the Tsar's court, the Holy Patriarchate, and the central administration of the realm's provincial *volosti*.

The Grand Hall of the Tsar's palace, where the Night Court convenes, is one of the largest artificial structures in the Tsardom, built in the mid-tenth century and expanded after the Transformation to accommodate owl-folk assembly.

On the morning of September 14th, 998, every living person within Velikoye — from the Tsar on his throne to the lowest laborer in the tanner's quarter — was transformed into an owl-folk, an event that shook the city to its foundations and prompted an immediate, frantic restructuring of its infrastructure and institutions.

The city's water supply comes from deep wells and the river, but since the Transformation, a network of elevated wooden aqueducts has been constructed to carry water to roosting towers throughout the city, as owl-folk are reluctant to descend to ground level during daylight hours.

The *Pravda Tsarskaya*, as amended in 999, governs all matters of nocturnal governance in Velikoye, including the hours of operation for markets, courts, and administrative offices; the regulation of flight paths over the city to prevent collisions and noise disturbances; and the allocation of roosting rights in public buildings and on private properties.

The Great Bridge across the Volga, originally a wooden structure of three spans, was demolished and rebuilt in 999 with stone piers and iron-reinforced timber planking, its railings fitted with roosting ledges every few paces to allow owl-folk to rest mid-crossing in high winds.

Velikoye is organized into a central *Kreml* — a fortified citadel of white stone walls and dark timber towers — surrounded by concentric rings of residential quarters, market districts, and industrial quarters, all connected by elevated wooden walkways and paved streets widened and reinforced with iron-banded flagstones to accommodate the taloned feet of its owl-folk inhabitants.

The city's population of approximately forty thousand owl-folk is divided into distinct quarters: the merchants and traders cluster along the riverfronts where their warehouses store grain, furs, and metalwork; the artisans and craftsmen occupy the eastern slopes near the timber yards; the military barracks of the *Krylaya Gvardiya* and the ground forces stand on the northern bluff; and the clergy and scholars reside in close proximity to the cathedral and the Theological Academy.

The night markets of Velikoye are legendary across the Tsardom, open from dusk until the small hours of the morning, illuminated by vast iron braziers filled with pitch-soaked wood and lined with lenses of polished quartz that focus the light into brilliant white beams, casting the cobblestone streets in a ghostly brilliance.

The Theological Academy of Moskov and the *Kruzhok Mudykh* (Circle of the Wise) both maintain halls within Velikoye's eastern quarter, where scholars work tirelessly to understand the cause and implications of the Transformation, though their findings remain inconclusive.

connected.heading: Other
connected.synopsis: The Amber Cup and the Roosting Flagon are two taverns in Velikoye. The Amber Cup sits on the western Mosca riverfront, offering an open-air gallery above the water where owl-folk perch and watch trade traffic while drinking honey-mead with dockworkers and merchants. The Roosting Flagon stands on the northern residential ring between a tanner's shop and a candle-waxer's stall, one of few places where owl-folk and humans drink together, with iron-banded ceilings for taloned landings and sturdy oak benches for human patrons.

facts.text: A squat, timber-framed tavern wedged between a tanner's shop and a candle-waxer's stall on the northern slope of Velikoye's second residential ring, the Roosting Flagon is one of the few establishments in the city where owl-folk and humans drink side by side, its low ceiling reinforced with iron bands to bear the taloned landings of its feathered patrons while its wide, ground-level doorways and sturdy oak benches welcome human trade.

Along its middle course, the Khorol cuts through a series of gentle limestone bluffs similar to those found at Velikoye, though less dramatic, creating high riverbanks that local owl-folk use as natural roosting sites.

The river's southern reach approaches the steppe lands near the Caspian border, where the terrain flattens into wide grasslands and the Khorol slows to a sluggish, marshy flow before emptying into a network of smaller channels.

The river freezes over in winter, typically from late November to early March, at which point it supports a road of packed ice used by both ground travelers and owl-folk who can walk along its frozen surface or roost on the ice shelves at its edges.

In spring, the Khorol swells dramatically with snowmelt and can become dangerous, with currents strong enough to shift barges off course; the *Krylaya Gvardiya* maintains patrol flights along the river from April to June to assist stranded vessels.

Its waters are deep and brown, fed by snowmelt from the northern forests and seasonal rains, with a gentle current that makes it navigable by flat-bottomed barges and shallow-drafted trade vessels for most of the year.
The river's western tributary, the Desna, joins the Khorol near the town of Novogorod, forming a natural crossroads that has made Novogorod one of the busiest inland ports in the Tsardom.

The Khorol River is a wide, slow-moving waterway that flows southwest through the heartland of the Tsardom of Moscavia, serving as a vital artery of trade and transportation between the Volga basin and the western provinces.
The Khorol has been a navigable trade route since at least the early tenth century, carrying grain, timber, furs, and metalwork between the Rus' principalities and the eastern settlements.
The riverbank is lined with willow groves and silver birch trees whose trailing branches dip into the water, creating a shimmering green canopy over the shallows in summer.

Several fishing villages and small market towns dot the Khorol's banks, their economies built around the river's abundant pike, sterlet, and sturgeon, as well as the ferry and barge traffic that passes through.

After the Transformation of 998, the river became even more critical to Velikoye's supply network, as goods that could no longer be transported easily overland by ground forces had to rely on barges and rafts that could navigate the Khorol and its connections to the Volga and Moskva.

The Pravda Tsarskaya governs navigation rights on the Khorol, requiring all vessels to fly a lantern at night — a bright white flame housed in a horn-lens casing — so that flying owl-folk can spot and avoid them in darkness.
Born in 953 in the river town of Oryol to a family of minor provincial scribes, she was identified as a prodigy at age twelve and admitted to the Academy of the Chiseled Moon in Velgrad.

She secretly practices the carving of pre-643 archaic rune forms in a hidden workshop beneath her private quarters in the Grand Scriptorium, using a set of chisels she had commissioned in secret from a smith in Aldenmere.
Her dark hair, once black as ink, has silvered at the temples and is kept pulled back in a tight braid coiled beneath her scholar's cap, the traditional black felt hood of the Order.
She possesses an exceptional memory for rune glyphs, able to recall the precise stroke order of over three thousand inscribed tablets from memory.
Beneath her composed exterior lies a restless, almost feverish curiosity about runes the Order has declared forbidden—archaeic frost-carving patterns predating the Illuminator's reforms.
She is a lean woman of angular features, with deep-set grey eyes that carry a perpetual sharpness behind wire-rimmed spectacles of Tsardom-made glass.
She is meticulous to the point of obsessiveness in her work, maintaining a personal library of annotated copies of every major rune treatise in the Grand Scriptorium, cross-referenced by hand.

Her carving skill is considered among the finest in the Tsardom—her strokes are so clean and deliberate that fellow scribes have described her work as "as if the stone itself wished to hold the rune."
Her hands are her most distinctive feature—long-fingered, pale, and marked with dozens of faint white scars where she has pressed the chisel too deeply into stone over the decades.

She privately practices rune carving forms that the Order has officially prohibited since its founding in 643, and she has not publicly disclosed this activity. Departs from a teaching of The Order of the Talon-Scribe
She rose through the Order's ranks with extraordinary speed—Acolyte at fourteen, Scribe at nineteen, Master-Scribe at twenty-seven—setting a record that has never been broken.

She maintains a cautious but cordial relationship with the current Arch-Talon, Eldon Marenkov, though she suspects he is aware of her private carving and tolerates it because her public work is indispensable to the Order.
She was appointed Chief Scribe of the Order in 998, following the sudden death of her predecessor, Master-Scribe Yuriy Volkov, who had held the position for twenty-three years.

facts.text: The Chapter House of Aldenmere, dedicated to the ancient scribe Vesska the Unbroken, serves as the Order of the Talon-Scribe's regional headquarters in the coastal city of Aldenmere, overseeing rune studies and transcription work throughout the southern maritime provinces of the Tsardom.
The capital city of Moskov is the seat of the Tsar and the Holy Patriarch, and serves as the administrative, commercial, and spiritual heart of the realm.

Founded as a successor to the Rus' principalities in the early tenth century, the Tsardom unified its territories under a single ruler — the Tsar — who holds both political and spiritual authority over the realm.

The Moscavian military comprises the *Krylaya Gvardiya* (Winged Guard), elite aviators who serve as scouts, messengers, and shock troops, alongside traditional infantry and cavalry units that remain essential for large-scale warfare.

The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast, federally organized realm stretching across the eastern European plain, bordered by the frozen White Sea to the north, the Caspian steppes to the east, the Black Sea coastlands to the south, and the old Varangian trade routes to the west.
The economy of the Tsardom is built on grain, fur, timber, and metalwork, traded across a network of rivers and overland routes connecting its major cities.

The Khorol River is one of the Tsardom's most important commercial waterways, linking the agricultural heartlands of the southwest to the industrial and commercial centers near Velikoye and along the Volga.

The Tsardom is governed through a system of provincial *volosti*, each administered by a *volostnik* appointed by the Tsar, with matters of law and tax decided in nighttime councils held under artificial light in the hours when owl-folk are most alert.

The memory of the Resurrection of Days remains a sensitive subject in Moscavian political culture, and several noble families who participated still harbor quiet resentment, though publicly they have adapted to the new order.

The leaders of the failed rebellion — including Boyar Vladimir of Rostov and Prince Mstislav of Novgorod — were tried under the old provisions of the Pravda and sentenced to exile in the northern frontier volosti near the White Sea, where their knowledge of navigation and trade proved ironically useful to the Tsardom's coastal defenses.

After the suppression of the uprising, Tsar Oleg III convened the Great Council of 998, which produced the revised Pravda Tsarskaya, thereby formalizing many of the legal and administrative changes that had been hastily implemented in the aftermath of the Transformation.

The rebellion, known as the *Voskreseniye Dney* (Resurrection of Days), sought to restore human noble councils and displace owl-folk appointments throughout the provincial volosti, but it collapsed within three months when the Krylaya Gvardiya cut off supply lines along the Khorol River and the Tsar's forces besieged the rebel stronghold of Rostov.

In the spring of 997, a coalition of human noble houses — including the boyars of Rostov, the princely line of Novgorod, and several lesser lords from the northern volosti — launched a coordinated uprising against Tsar Oleg III, whom they accused of using the Transformation to seize powers that had traditionally belonged to the old Rus' aristocracy.

Scholars at the Theological Academy of Moskov and the natural philosophers of the *Kruzhok Mudykh* (Circle of the Wise) continue to investigate the cause of the Transformation, studying ancient texts, celestial omens, and the properties of the owl-folk body itself.
The Tsardom's roads and bridges have been widened and reinforced to accommodate the taloned feet of its owl-folk population, with many structures featuring roosting ledges and elevated walkways.

On the morning of September 14th, 998, every living human being within the borders of the Tsardom was transformed into an owl-folk, an event without precedent or explanation that fundamentally altered the course of Moscavian civilization.

The Tsardom's institutions — its courts, treasury, military, church, and provincial administrations — were gradually adapted over the two years since the Transformation to accommodate the new biology of its citizens, though the process remains ongoing.

The Tsardom's legal code, the *Pravda Tsarskaya*, was revised in 999 to address matters of flight, nocturnal governance, and the rights of perching in public spaces, while retaining the older provisions on land, trade, and taxation.

connected.heading: Institutions
connected.synopsis: The Night Court is the supreme legislative and judicial council of the Tsardom of Moscavia, established in 999 to govern the owl-folk populace during nocturnal hours. It interprets the Pravda Tsarskaya, resolves disputes between provincial volosti, and legislates on matters specific to owl-folk biology. Boyar Dmitriy Semyonovich Volkov serves as Nochnoy Predsedatel. Membership includes senior boyars, volostniki, and scholars from the Kruzhok Mudykh, all appointed by the Tsar and confirmed by the Holy Patriarch. The Theological Academy of Moskov and the Kruzhok Mudykh operate in Velikoye's eastern quarter, collaborating to study the Transformation though their findings remain inconclusive.

connected.heading: Military institutions
connected.synopsis: The Frostwing Host is the standing army of Tsardom of Moscavia, founded after the Transformation of 998 to integrate owl-folk biology into military doctrine. It operates under the Krylaya Gvardiya and maintains specialized autonomous units adapted to specific frontier conditions. Within its ranks, the White Talon serves as a heavy regiment of the Frostwing Host, an elite strike force originally founded in 743 for mountainous and frozen terrain, now commanded by General Maren Ashvale.

final.name: The Runic Magic of the Tsardom

facts.text: Defensive uses range from simple ward-stones placed at farmsteads to protect against frostbite during harsh winters, to elaborate fortifications such as the Rune Barriers of Fort Ashenkrag, which have withstood siege for over a century.
In the Tsardom of Kaelith, runic magic is the art of carving sacred symbols into stone to bind the elemental forces of frost and wind into service.
Rune carvers, known as Frostwards, are among the most respected practitioners of magic in the Tsardom, trained for years in the precise geometry and linguistic origins of each rune.

Offensive applications include the Gale Lance — a rune that summons a concentrated blast of freezing wind capable of piercing armor and flesh — and the Frostwall, a barrier of crystallized cold air that can stall an enemy charge.
Runes must be carved into natural stone, preferably granite or quartz veined with feldspar, as these minerals resonate with the cold frequencies upon which the magic depends.

The primary institution for training Frostwards is the Athenaeum of Winterlight in the capital city of Morozgrad, where apprentices study for a minimum of seven years before taking the Binding Trials.

The carving process involves three stages: the Inscription, in which the rune is cut; the Attuning, in which the carver channels their own life-heat into the stone to create the initial resonance; and the Binding, in which the carver recites the rune's name in the Old Kaelith tongue while exposing the stone to freezing rain or snow.

The magic draws its power from the deep cold of the northern reaches and the restless gales that sweep across the Kaelith steppe, channeling them into protective wards, offensive constructs, and navigational aids.

The fundamental principle of rune magic is that frost and wind are not opposed but intertwined — still air holds no frost, and bitter cold begets howling gale — and a master carver learns to read the weather itself as a kind of living text.

There are three recognized schools of thought within the art: the Orthodoxy of the Athenaeum, which holds that rune carving must follow ancient formulas without deviation; the Drift School, which encourages experimentation and the invention of new runes; and the Silent Path, which teaches that the greatest power comes from carving runes so small they are nearly invisible, drawing on subtler currents of cold.
A fully bound rune can last for decades or even centuries, slowly losing power as weather and time erode the carving, though a skilled Frostward can refresh a fading rune by re-attuning it.

The Tsardom's legal code, the Kaelith Codex of Rights, recognizes Frostwarding as a protected practice and forbids the defacing or destruction of bound runes on penalty of forced labor, reflecting the deep integration of rune magic into the fabric of Kaelith society.
Plumage coloration varies widely among individuals, and it is considered a matter of personal identity — an owl-folk's feathers are as distinctive to them as a human's face.
They possess wide, powerful wings capable of sustained flight, with a wingspan of eight to twelve feet, and their feet end in strong taloned digits suited for gripping branches and perches.
They possess an innate ability to fly, and most owl-folk can take to the skies within moments of being born, though their flight becomes more controlled and skilled with age and practice.
Owl-folk are overwhelmingly nocturnal by nature; they feel most alert and comfortable in darkness and tend to become drowsy and irritable during daylight hours.

Their faces retain a distinctly avian quality — hooked but not overly sharp beaks, and large luminous eyes that come in shades of amber, pale green, and deep black — but they also express unmistakable human emotions.
An owl-folk is a bipedal humanoid roughly five to seven feet tall, with a broad, rounded body covered in soft plumage that ranges from tawny golds and greys to deep browns and snowy whites.
They are predatory hunters by instinct, with sharp eyesight and silent movement, though this instinct is tempered by the civilized upbringing of the former human population.

Some owl-folk retain traces of their former human appearance in their facial features — a strong jawline, a particular arrangement of feathers suggesting freckles or scars — leading to a widespread belief that one's past self is not entirely gone.
The Tsardom of Moscavia continues to function as a political entity under the transformed population, with its cities, roads, and institutions adapted for winged, nocturnal citizens.

Their heads are large relative to their bodies, with prominent forward-facing eyes that grant them extraordinary night vision, and a pair of feathered tufts or 'ears' atop their heads that are not true ears but serve as expressive indicators of mood.
Every living person in the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk overnight by a single, unexplained event on an unremarkable autumn morning in the year 998.
Plumage Signaling is one of the defining cultural practices of owl-folk civilization, alongside nocturnal governance and the adapted architecture of the Tsardom's cities.
No one knows who or what caused the transformation, and the Tsardom's scholars have spent the years since searching for an answer in old texts, divine revelation, and natural philosophy.

in.target: The Runic Magic of the Tsardom

facts.text: The relationship between the Night Court and the Holy Patriarchate remains a subject of careful negotiation, as questions persist about whether the Tsar's secular authority or the Patriarch's spiritual authority takes precedence in matters of civil law.
The Night Court meets in the Grand Hall of the Tsar's palace in Velikoye, a vast chamber illuminated by hundreds of oil lamps and candelabras hung from the vaulted ceiling to simulate daylight.

During sessions of the Night Court, Plumage Signaling is used extensively, with members communicating their positions, objections, and votes through carefully controlled feather movements rather than spoken words.
The presiding officer of the Night Court is called the *Nochnoy Predsedatel* (Night Chairman), a title currently held by Boyar Dmitriy Semyonovich Volkov of the Moskov province.

Sessions typically begin at dusk and continue until the first light of dawn, with breaks for rest and the serving of meals — traditionally cold meats, root vegetables, and grain porridges that require no cooking.
The Night Court also oversees the annual review of the Tsardom's trade tariffs, ensuring that the grain, fur, timber, and metalwork economies continue to function smoothly under nocturnal governance.
Membership in the Night Court is appointed by the Tsar and confirmed by the Holy Patriarch, consisting of senior boyars, experienced volostniki, and learned members of the Kruzhok Mudykh.

The Court has authority to interpret and amend the Pravda Tsarskaya, adjudicate disputes between provincial volosti, and pass legislation governing matters specific to owl-folk biology and nocturnal civilization.

Among the Night Court's most significant early acts was the passage of the Perching Ordinance of 999, which regulated the use of public ledges and roosting spaces in cities and along major roads throughout the Tsardom.
The Night Court is the supreme legislative and judicial council of the Tsardom of Moscavia, convening in the hours of darkness when owl-folk are most alert and capable of governance.
Provincial volostniki may petition the Night Court for exceptions to the Pravda Tsarskaya or for additional funding for local infrastructure projects such as widened roads and reinforced bridges.
The Court's proceedings are recorded by a corps of scribes trained to work by lamplight, their records kept in the Imperial Archive beneath the palace.
It was established by the Tsar in the winter of 999 following the Transformation, replacing the older daytime councils that had become impractical for an owl-folk populace.

facts.text: Its soldiers are known for their distinctive white-and-grey plumage, which serves as natural camouflage against the snow and ice of the northern frontier, and which inspired the regiment's name.

The Frosted Wing maintains its own tradition of oral history, passing down accounts of the Transformation itself through song and story, claiming that the first owls of the northern frontier were changed during a blizzard and that their white feathers are a mark of that divine storm.

Each archer carries a recurve bow of laminated horn and sinew, specially crafted to account for the differences in owl-folk wing structure and the cold-weakened wood available in the north, alongside a quiver of obsidian-tipped arrows designed to shatter upon impact with armored targets.

The regiment is provisioned through supply flights from the interior of the Tsardom, with food and equipment transported by relay teams of owl-folk cargo-flyers who navigate the treacherous winds along the glacier's edge.

The Frosted Wing operates from a network of stone watchtowers and roosting barns built into the cliff faces along the glacier's edge, connected by elevated wooden walkways that allow rapid deployment across the icy terrain.

Owl-folk of the Frosted Wing are trained from birth in the northern volosti, identified as recruits by the time they are three years old based on their tolerance for cold, the density of their plumage, and their natural aptitude for sustained high-altitude flight.

The regiment's command structure mirrors that of the broader Krylaya Gvardiya, with a *stotnik* (centurion) at its head, but its officers are selected not only for military skill but for their ability to navigate whiteout conditions and lead flights through blizzard weather.

The Frosted Wing is a regiment of elite owl-folk archers stationed at the glacier edge of the Tsardom of Moscavia, tasked with defending the northern frontier where the frozen White Sea meets the land.

Founded in the winter of 999, just months after the Transformation of the Tsardom's population, the regiment was assembled from owl-folk who demonstrated exceptional aptitude for long-range flight and archery in harsh, icy conditions.

Its members are also skilled in the construction and maintenance of ice-bridges and emergency shelters along the northern trade routes, serving a dual role as soldiers and frontier engineers in the service of the Tsardom.

The regiment has earned a reputation for executing devastating precision strikes against raiding parties and hostile forces that approach from across the frozen sea, launching volleys from altitudes where no ground-based observer can detect them until the arrows fall.

Situated on the riverfront of the western Mosca quarter near the grain warehouses, the Amber Cup is a long, single-story tavern built partly over the water on iron-piled pilings, its open-air upper gallery draped in heavy linen curtains that keep out the wind and the midday sun, offering owl-folk a sheltered perch from which they can watch the river traffic while sharing tankards of honey-mead with the dockworkers and merchants who crowd its lower tables.
Velikoye is also commonly known as Moskov, a shorter name derived from the river that flows through it, used in everyday speech and by merchants across the realm.
